blocks.h: 1. What the Sustainable Development Goals are

blocks.p: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are the core of "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development", adopted by the United Nations General Assembly by resolution A/RES/70/1 on 25 September 2015 and in effect from 1 January 2016. They succeeded the Millennium Development Goals, which ran to 2015.
The structure is worth stating precisely, because the numbers are marks:

ul: 17 Goals and 169 targets, measured against a global indicator framework;
organised around five areas - People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership;
carrying the central pledge to leave no one behind;
balancing the three dimensions of sustainable development - economic, social and environmental;

declared to be integrated and indivisible, and global in nature and universally applicable - they apply to developed and developing States alike, which is the principal break from the Millennium Development Goals.

blocks.h: 2. The role of the SDGs in promoting global sustainability

blocks.p: The SDGs are not a treaty. They impose no legal obligation on any State and create no enforcement mechanism. The interesting question - and the one this limb is really asking - is therefore how a non-binding instrument achieves anything at all. It does so through six mechanisms:

ol: A common language and a common framework. Governments, financiers, corporations, classification societies and NGOs all now describe their environmental and social objectives against the same seventeen headings. That comparability is itself the achievement - it allows performance to be compared across sectors and borders in a way that was impossible before.
Universality. Because the Goals apply to every State rather than only to developing ones, they reframe sustainability as a shared project instead of an aid programme.

Integration. The Goals are expressly indivisible, which forces the recognition of trade-offs and co-benefits - decarbonising shipping (13) affects air quality and health (3), energy systems (7), industry and infrastructure (9) and ocean health (14) simultaneously.
Measurement. 169 targets and a formal indicator framework turn aspiration into something that can be reported and audited. What is measured gets managed.

Accountability by transparency rather than sanction. Review runs through the High-Level Political Forum and voluntary national reviews. There is no penalty - the pressure is reputational and peer-driven.

Mobilisation of finance and of the private sector. This is the mechanism with the most practical bite for shipping. The SDGs have become the reference framework for ESG reporting, sustainable finance, green loans and charterers' requirements, so alignment has become a condition of access to capital and to cargo rather than a matter of goodwill.

blocks.p: The honest qualification, which a management-level answer should make: the same non-binding character is the SDGs' principal weakness. Progress depends on national will and on finance, delivery is uneven, and the framework is vulnerable to "SDG-washing" - the badging of existing activity against a convenient Goal. It is a framework for direction and comparison, not a regulatory instrument. In the maritime sector the actual obligations come from IMO conventions; the SDGs supply the direction those conventions are steered by.

blocks.h: 3. Why the maritime sector matters, and how IMO aligns

blocks.p: Shipping is the dominant carrier of world trade by volume, and is simultaneously a material source of greenhouse gas and air emissions, a vector for invasive species, a source of operational and accidental marine pollution, and a global employer of seafarers. It therefore touches a large number of the Goals directly and is one of the few sectors regulated by a dedicated United Nations specialised agency.

The IMO has mapped its own work to the Goals and identifies SDG 14 as the Goal most directly relevant to its mandate, while its technical cooperation and capacity-building work is directed at a wider set. The two Goals chosen below are those where the maritime connection is strongest and the industry's actions are most concrete.

blocks.h: 4. SDG 13 Climate Action - relevance to shipping

blocks.p: SDG 13 is "take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts".
Its relevance to shipping is twofold, and both halves should be stated:

ul: shipping is a source. It is the most carbon-efficient mode of freight transport per tonne-kilometre, but the absolute volume of trade makes it a material emitter, and unlike shore industry it is a transboundary sector which no single State can regulate - which is precisely why it was left to IMO rather than being counted in national inventories under the Paris Agreement;

shipping is also exposed. Sea level rise, increased storm severity and changing ice conditions affect ports, coastal infrastructure and routeing - so the industry has an operational as well as a moral interest in the outcome.

blocks.p: The regulatory expression of SDG 13 in this sector is the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023, which superseded the 2018 Initial Strategy. Its levels of ambition are:

ul: net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around, i.e. close to, 2050;

indicative checkpoints for 2030 and 2040, expressed as percentage reductions in total annual GHG emissions from international shipping against a 2008 baseline, each stated as a minimum with a higher "striving for" level;
uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and energy sources to represent a share of the energy used by international shipping by 2030;
and a move from carbon intensity to well-to-wake, full lifecycle accounting of emissions.

blocks.p: The position at this sitting must be stated carefully. The short-term measures - the EEXI, the operational CII and the enhanced SEEMP - entered into force on 1 January 2023, so 2023 is the first full CII data year and the first ratings were issued during 2024. The mid-term measures - a technical measure such as a GHG fuel standard, and an economic measure such as a pricing mechanism - were still under development. MEPC 82, held from 30 September to 4 October 2024, carried that work forward and also opened a review of the short-term measures, referring it to a correspondence group and an intersessional working group reporting to MEPC 83 in 2025. No mid-term measure had been adopted.
The actions divide usefully into four groups, and giving them in this order shows engineering judgement rather than a list of green words:

rows: Operational - available now, at low capital cost

Speed optimisation and slow steaming; weather routeing; just-in-time arrival negotiated with terminals; trim optimisation; hull and propeller condition management - coating selection, in-water inspection and polishing; voyage and cargo planning to reduce ballast legs
The SEEMP's four-step cycle is the management instrument through which these are planned, implemented, monitored and evaluated

Waste heat recovery; shaft generators; propeller and rudder energy-saving devices, ducts and fins; air lubrication; wind assistance - rotor sails, suction wings, kites; engine derating and turbocharger cut-out; variable-frequency drives on pumps and fans; LED lighting and improved HVAC control
Each must be justified against the ship's actual trade - the SEEMP Guidelines warn that some measures are mutually exclusive

LNG as a transitional fuel, with methane slip managed; methanol, ammonia and hydrogen; biofuels and drop-in blends; batteries and hybrid propulsion for suitable trades; onshore power supply (cold ironing) in port; dual-fuel and fuel-ready designs so a ship built now is not stranded
The Strategy's move to well-to-wake accounting is what makes the choice of fuel PRODUCTION pathway, not just the fuel, the decisive question

Fleet renewal with more efficient tonnage; charter party clauses allocating efficiency responsibility and permitting speed optimisation; digital performance monitoring and transparent emissions reporting; crew and shore-staff training in energy-efficient operation; participation in R&D funding and first-mover fuel initiatives
The split incentive between owner and charterer is the single largest non-technical obstacle, and is solved contractually

blocks.h: 6. SDG 14 Life Below Water - relevance to shipping

blocks.p: SDG 14 is "conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development", and it is the Goal most directly connected to IMO's mandate. Target 14.1 - to prevent and significantly reduce marine pollution of all kinds - is the one shipping bears on most directly, and targets on marine ecosystems and on ocean acidification follow closely behind.
Shipping's impacts on the marine environment are:

ul: operational and accidental pollution - oil, noxious liquid substances, sewage, garbage and plastics;
invasive aquatic species transferred in ballast water and as biofouling on hulls - one of the most serious and least reversible impacts, because a translocated species cannot be recovered;
toxic anti-fouling systems;
air emissions that acidify and enrich the sea - SOx and NOx deposition, and CO2 driving ocean acidification, which is where SDG 13 and SDG 14 meet;
underwater radiated noise, affecting marine mammals;
ship strikes on cetaceans;
end-of-life ship recycling, where poor practice contaminates the coastal environment.

blocks.p: The IMO instruments that implement this are MARPOL Annexes I to VI; the Ballast Water Management Convention 2004, in force 8 September 2017, with its D-1 exchange and D-2 performance standards; the AFS Convention 2001; the London Convention and Protocol on dumping; and the IMO Action Plan on marine plastic litter from ships.

One instrument requires care at this sitting. The Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009 had its entry-into-force criteria met in June 2023, when Bangladesh and Liberia became Contracting States, and enters into force twenty-four months later on 26 June 2025. At the date of this examination it is therefore adopted and ratified but NOT YET IN FORCE - it comes into force six months after this paper was sat. That distinction between ratified and in force is exactly the kind of point a Class I examiner rewards, and getting it wrong in either direction is a visible error.

ol: Ballast water and biofouling. Operate and maintain the ballast water management system to the D-2 standard properly rather than nominally - crew training, sampling, and honest recording in the Ballast Water Record Book; and manage biofouling through a biofouling management plan, hull coating selection, in-water inspection and cleaning with capture. Biofouling management is a double win: it is also one of the largest available fuel-efficiency measures, so it serves SDG 13 at the same time.

Zero-discharge discipline for garbage and plastics. Full segregation and Garbage Record Book accuracy under MARPOL Annex V, an absolute prohibition on plastics overboard, retention on board where reception facilities are inadequate, and elimination of single-use plastics in ship's stores - the industry's direct contribution to target 14.1.

Oil and chemical pollution prevention. Rigorous Oil Record Book discipline and functioning oily-water separators with no bypass; bunkering procedures, checklists and scuppers plugged; the SOPEP or SMPEP exercised rather than filed; tank cleaning and slops managed properly.
Sewage and grey water - treatment plants maintained and operated, and discharge only in accordance with Annex IV; voluntary grey water retention in sensitive areas.

Air emissions that reach the sea - compliance with the sulphur limit and with ECA requirements, correct scrubber washwater management, and NOx-compliant operation, all of which reduce acidifying and eutrophying deposition.
Anti-fouling systems compliant with the AFS Convention, with a valid International Anti-fouling System Certificate.

Underwater radiated noise and ship strikes - design and operational measures to reduce radiated noise, particularly propeller cavitation, and compliance with routeing measures, areas to be avoided and speed restrictions in whale habitats.

Responsible ship recycling - maintaining an accurate and updated Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and selecting recycling facilities operating to the Hong Kong Convention standard in advance of its entry into force, rather than waiting to be compelled.
Protection of special areas and PSSAs - observing the stricter discharge and routeing requirements in Special Areas, Emission Control Areas and Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas.
Beyond compliance - participation in ocean data collection, industry initiatives on plastics and biofouling, and transparent environmental reporting.

blocks.p: The point on which to end - and the one that distinguishes a management-level answer from a general essay - is that for a shipowner in December 2024 the SDGs are no longer only an ethical framework; they have become a commercial and financing one.

ul: Access to capital. Banks lending under sustainable-finance frameworks require alignment and portfolio emissions disclosure, so a fleet's carbon intensity affects its cost of borrowing.
Access to cargo. Major charterers set emissions and environmental criteria in their vetting and chartering decisions, so CII rating affects employability.
Asset value. A ship that cannot meet tightening carbon intensity requirements through its economic life faces early obsolescence, which makes newbuilding fuel choice a balance-sheet decision.
Regulatory direction. The SDGs are not enforceable, but they signal reliably where binding IMO regulation is heading - so alignment is also the cheapest available form of regulatory risk management.
Licence to operate - crew recruitment and retention, port and coastal State relations, and public reputation.

blocks.p: In short: the SDGs set the direction, IMO conventions turn that direction into obligation, and the SEEMP and the ship's management system turn obligation into daily practice. A management-level officer's role sits at the last of those three, and the value of understanding the first is knowing why the third keeps changing.

Sixteen marks in one limb, and the stem prints three distinct tasks: explain the role of the SDGs in promoting global sustainability; choose any two and discuss their relevance to the maritime sector; and highlight specific actions the shipping industry can take. The third task carries the most marks and is where most answers thin out into generalities.

The word that governs the whole answer is "specific". "Reduce emissions" and "protect the marine environment" score nothing. Weather routeing, hull and propeller condition management, onshore power supply, D-2 ballast water compliance, an accurate Inventory of Hazardous Materials - these score, because they are things an engineer actually does. The route therefore devotes a full step to actions under each chosen Goal.

Note also that the stem says "choose any two". That is a genuine choice, and choosing well is part of the answer. SDG 13 and SDG 14 are the strongest pair because they are the two with dedicated IMO instruments behind them, which lets you cite regulation rather than sentiment. SDG 8 (decent work, via the MLC), SDG 7 (clean energy), SDG 9 (industry and infrastructure) and SDG 3 (health and wellbeing) are all defensible alternatives - but say which two you have chosen and why, in one line, before you start.

Most candidates answer this limb by describing what the SDGs are. The question asks about their role in promoting sustainability, which is a different and more interesting question, because the SDGs are not a treaty and bind nobody.

So the marks are in explaining how a non-binding instrument works at all: a common language and comparability; universality applying to every State; integration forcing recognition of trade-offs; measurement through 169 targets and an indicator framework; accountability by transparency through the High-Level Political Forum and voluntary national reviews rather than by sanction; and - the one with the most practical bite for shipping - mobilisation of finance and the private sector through ESG reporting, sustainable finance and charterers' requirements.

Adding the honest weakness - that non-binding status means uneven delivery and exposure to "SDG-washing", and that in this sector the actual obligations come from IMO conventions while the SDGs supply direction - turns a descriptive answer into an evaluative one, which is what management level means.

ul: A/RES/70/1, adopted 25 September 2015, in effect 1 January 2016.
17 Goals, 169 targets, with a global indicator framework.
Five Ps - People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership.
Leave no one behind - the central pledge.
Integrated and indivisible; global in nature and universally applicable - the break from the Millennium Development Goals.
Review through the High-Level Political Forum and voluntary national reviews.

blocks.p: Naming the resolution and the two dates is cheap and immediately marks the answer out. So does saying 17 and 169 rather than "a number of goals and targets".

blocks.h: The three things that must be right for December 2024

blocks.p: This question has no single hard date in it, which makes it more dangerous rather than less - the temptation is to write about decarbonisation as it stands whenever you are revising. Three positions must be fixed at the sitting:

ol: The operative IMO climate instrument is the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023, with its net-zero-by-or-around-2050 ambition. It superseded the 2018 Initial Strategy and its far weaker 50%-by-2050 target. Citing the 2018 Strategy as current is a straightforward error at this sitting.

The mid-term measures were NOT adopted. A technical measure such as a GHG fuel standard and an economic measure such as a pricing mechanism were under development. MEPC 82 (30 September to 4 October 2024) carried the work forward and referred the review of the short-term measures onward to MEPC 83 in 2025. Describing any mid-term measure as adopted is future contamination.
The Hong Kong Convention was ratified but NOT YET IN FORCE. Its criteria were met in June 2023 and it enters into force on 26 June 2025 - six months after this examination.

blocks.p: That third point is the best single opportunity on this question. A sitting that falls six months before a convention's entry into force lets you demonstrate the adopted / ratified / in force distinction with a concrete, current example - and it is precisely what a candidate revising from later material would get wrong, because by then the Convention is simply in force.

blocks.h: The stage of the decarbonisation regime at this sitting

blocks.p: Worth holding, because it lets you write about the CII with confidence rather than vaguely: EEXI, the operational CII and the enhanced SEEMP entered into force on 1 January 2023. So at December 2024, 2023 is the first full CII data year and the first ratings have been issued during 2024 on that data. The regime is live and biting, not prospective - which is the correct tense for this sitting and is different from how a January 2024 answer would have read.

A point worth one sentence and worth a mark, because it demonstrates the Goals' claimed indivisibility rather than merely asserting it: CO2 absorbed by the ocean drives acidification, so reducing shipping's greenhouse gas emissions serves SDG 14 as well as SDG 13. The same is true in the other direction - biofouling management prevents invasive species transfer under SDG 14 and is one of the largest available fuel-efficiency measures under SDG 13.
If you can give one example of a single action serving both chosen Goals, you have shown you understand what "integrated and indivisible" means in practice.

ul: Describing what the SDGs are and never addressing their role - how a non-binding framework achieves anything.
Giving generic actions. The stem says "specific actions". Name the measure an engineer would actually implement.
Not stating which two Goals have been chosen, or choosing two with weak maritime connections.
Citing the 2018 Initial Strategy as the current IMO GHG strategy. It was superseded by MEPC.377(80) on 7 July 2023.
Describing an IMO mid-term measure as adopted. None was, at this sitting.
Describing the Hong Kong Convention as in force. It enters into force 26 June 2025, six months after this sitting.
Treating the SDGs as legally binding. They are not - the binding obligations are in the IMO conventions.
Confusing the SDGs with the Paris Agreement, which is a separate treaty and does not cover international shipping in national inventories.
Asserting a percentage for shipping's share of global emissions or of world trade. The figures vary widely by source; make the argument without them.
Writing only about the environment. SDG 8 decent work, delivered through the MLC, and SDG 5 gender equality are also live maritime connections.

"Are the SDGs binding on India?" No - they are a General Assembly resolution, not a treaty. The binding maritime obligations come from IMO conventions, which India implements through the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and subordinate rules.
"Which SDG is closest to IMO's mandate?" SDG 14, life below water - though IMO maps its work across many.

"What is the current IMO GHG strategy and what does it aim at?" The 2023 Strategy, MEPC.377(80) of 7 July 2023 - net-zero by or around 2050, with indicative checkpoints for 2030 and 2040 and a 2030 ambition for zero or near-zero fuels.
"Is the Hong Kong Convention in force?" Not at this sitting - criteria met June 2023, entry into force 26 June 2025.
"Give one action that serves two Goals at once." Biofouling management - it prevents invasive species transfer (14) and reduces fuel consumption (13).

"Why does well-to-wake accounting matter?" Because it counts emissions from fuel production as well as combustion, so the production pathway - not just the fuel - determines whether a fuel is genuinely low-carbon.
When were the SDGs adopted and by what instrument? UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/70/1, 25 September 2015, effective 1 January 2016.
How many Goals and targets? 17 Goals and 169 targets.
What are the five Ps? People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership.
What is SDG 13 and SDG 14? Climate action; and conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources.
Which IMO convention addresses invasive species? The Ballast Water Management Convention 2004, in force 8 September 2017, with the D-1 and D-2 standards.
Name three operational measures to reduce fuel consumption. Speed optimisation, weather routeing, hull and propeller condition management.
Name three alternative fuels and one problem with each. LNG - methane slip; methanol - lower energy density; ammonia - toxicity and NOx.
What is cold ironing? Onshore power supply, allowing a ship in port to shut down auxiliary engines.
What document must be maintained for ship recycling? The Inventory of Hazardous Materials.
How do the SDGs affect a shipowner commercially? Through access to capital, access to cargo, asset value and regulatory direction.

blocks.p: For the instrument: 70/1, 2015, 17 and 169, five Ps, leave no one behind.
For the role limb, six mechanisms: LANGUAGE, UNIVERSALITY, INTEGRATION, MEASUREMENT, TRANSPARENCY, FINANCE - then the honest weakness.

For SDG 13 actions, four groups in ascending capital cost: OPERATE better - RETROFIT - REFUEL - RENEW. For SDG 14 actions, work outward from the ship: what leaves the hull (garbage, oil, sewage, ballast), what is on the hull (anti-fouling, biofouling), what the hull does (noise, ship strikes), and what happens at the end (recycling).

SDG 13 - urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts
SDG 14 - conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources; target 14.1 on marine pollution

MEPC.377(80), 7 July 2023 - the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy; net-zero by or around 2050; 2030 and 2040 indicative checkpoints; 2030 zero or near-zero fuel uptake; well-to-wake accounting. Superseded the 2018 Initial Strategy

blocks.p: Four limitations are recorded, and three of them are deliberate refusals to assert a number. No figure is given for shipping's share of global greenhouse gas emissions or of world trade - both circulate very widely, are quoted at materially different values by different sources and study years, and none was verified for this sitting; the argument is made qualitatively instead, which costs nothing because the examiner is not testing the statistic. No SDG progress figure is asserted for the same reason. And the numerical values of the 2030 and 2040 indicative checkpoints are described in structure - a percentage reduction against a 2008 baseline, stated as a minimum with a higher striving-for level - rather than quoted, because those values were not re-read from the resolution in this session. The net-zero-by-or-around-2050 ambition and the 2030 zero or near-zero fuel ambition are asserted, both having been established directly.

Two currency instructions for any later editor. The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy is the operative strategy here and no mid-term measure may be described as adopted - the work was referred onward to MEPC 83 in 2025, after this examination. And the Hong Kong Convention must remain "not yet in force" in this object: it entered into force on 26 June 2025, six months after this paper was sat, and an editor working from current material would find it described as in force and would introduce a state of affairs that did not exist at the sitting.

notes: The intake recorded STABLE / LOW with no classes. Checked rather than trusted. The SDG instrument itself is entirely stable, but the MARITIME limb of the answer is built on instruments that were moving fast in 2024, so the risk is raised to MEDIUM.

THE DANGER ON THIS QUESTION IS DIFFUSE RATHER THAN POINTED. There is no single hard date in the stem, which makes it MORE dangerous rather than less: the natural failure mode is to describe maritime decarbonisation as it stands whenever the answer is written. Three positions were fixed at the sitting date rather than inherited.

FINDING 1 - THE OPERATIVE STRATEGY. The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80), was adopted 7 JULY 2023 and SUPERSEDED the 2018 Initial Strategy. It is the operative strategy at this sitting: net-zero by or around 2050, indicative checkpoints for 2030 and 2040 against a 2008 baseline, and a 2030 ambition for zero or near-zero technologies, fuels and energy sources, with a move to well-to-wake accounting. Citing the 2018 Initial Strategy and its 50%-by-2050 target would be stale by eighteen months at this sitting.

FINDING 2 - MID-TERM MEASURES NOT ADOPTED. At this sitting the mid-term measures - a technical measure such as a GHG fuel standard and an economic measure such as a pricing mechanism - were UNDER DEVELOPMENT. MEPC 82, held 30 September to 4 October 2024, carried that work forward and separately opened the review of the short-term measures, referring it to a correspondence group and an intersessional working group reporting to MEPC 83 in 2025. NO mid-term measure is described as adopted anywhere in this object. A donor or a reviser working from 2025 or 2026 material would carry that outcome and it must not be back-read.

FINDING 3 - CONVENTION NOT YET IN FORCE, AND THE SITTING FALLS SIX MONTHS BEFORE IT. The Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009 had its entry-into-force criteria met in JUNE 2023, when Bangladesh and Liberia became Contracting States, and enters into force twenty-four months later on 26 JUNE 2025. At this December 2024 sitting it is ADOPTED AND RATIFIED BUT NOT YET IN FORCE. The answer states this expressly and uses it as the question's clearest adopted-versus-ratified-versus-in-force illustration. An editor updating from current material would find it simply 'in force' and would destroy the point.

DECARBONISATION STAGE AT THIS SITTING, stated in the correct tense: EEXI, the operational CII and the enhanced SEEMP entered into force 1 January 2023, so 2023 is the FIRST full CII data year and the first ratings were issued DURING 2024. The regime is live and biting at this sitting, not prospective - which is materially different from how a January 2024 answer would read.

STABLE AT THIS SITTING, checked not assumed: A/RES/70/1 of 25 September 2015 and the 17 Goals and 169 targets; the Ballast Water Management Convention 2004, in force 8 September 2017, and its D-1 and D-2 standards; the AFS Convention 2001; the London Convention and Protocol; and MARPOL Annexes I to VI. The SEEMP guidance operative at this sitting is MEPC.395(82) of 4 October 2024, consistent with Q8 on this paper.
NO CLAIM IN THIS ANSWER DEPENDS ON THE EXAMINATION DAY within December 2024. The nearest boundary, the Hong Kong Convention, is six months after the latest possible sitting day.

steps.title: What the Sustainable Development Goals are
points: the core of the 2030 Agenda, UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/70/1
adopted 25 September 2015, in effect 1 January 2016; successor to the Millennium Development Goals
17 Goals and 169 targets, with a global indicator framework
five areas - People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership
the central pledge to LEAVE NO ONE BEHIND
balancing the economic, social and environmental dimensions
integrated and indivisible; global in nature and UNIVERSALLY applicable - the break from the MDGs

steps.title: The role of the SDGs in promoting global sustainability
points: THEY ARE NOT A TREATY - no legal obligation and no enforcement; so the question is how they work at all
a common language and framework, giving comparability across sectors and borders
universality - every State, not only developing States
integration - forcing recognition of trade-offs and co-benefits
measurement - 169 targets and an indicator framework turn aspiration into something auditable
accountability by TRANSPARENCY - High-Level Political Forum and voluntary national reviews, not sanction
mobilisation of finance and the private sector - ESG, sustainable finance, charterers' requirements: the mechanism with real bite for shipping
HONEST WEAKNESS - non-binding means uneven delivery and SDG-washing; in this sector the OBLIGATIONS come from IMO conventions

steps.title: Why the maritime sector matters, and how IMO aligns
points: shipping is the dominant carrier of world trade by volume
a material source of GHG and air emissions, a vector for invasive species, a source of marine pollution, and a global employer
a transboundary sector no single State can regulate - which is why it sits with IMO
IMO has mapped its work to the Goals and identifies SDG 14 as closest to its mandate
STATE WHICH TWO GOALS YOU HAVE CHOSEN AND WHY - SDG 13 and 14 have dedicated IMO instruments behind them

steps.title: SDG 13 Climate Action - relevance to shipping
points: SDG 13 - take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts
shipping as a SOURCE - most carbon-efficient per tonne-km, but material in absolute terms
transboundary, so left to IMO rather than national inventories under the Paris Agreement
shipping as EXPOSED - sea level rise, storm severity, changing ice conditions affect ports and routeing
the regulatory expression: 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, MEPC.377(80), 7 July 2023, SUPERSEDING the 2018 Initial Strategy
net-zero by or around, i.e. close to, 2050
indicative checkpoints for 2030 and 2040 against a 2008 baseline, each a minimum with a striving-for level
2030 ambition for zero or near-zero technologies, fuels and energy sources; move to WELL-TO-WAKE accounting
AT THIS SITTING - EEXI, CII and enhanced SEEMP in force since 1 January 2023; 2023 the first full data year; first ratings issued during 2024
AT THIS SITTING - mid-term measures UNDER DEVELOPMENT, not adopted; MEPC 82 referred work to MEPC 83 in 2025

steps.title: SDG 13 - specific actions
points: OPERATIONAL - speed optimisation, weather routeing, just-in-time arrival, trim optimisation, hull and propeller condition management, voyage planning to cut ballast legs
the SEEMP four-step cycle is the management instrument for all of these
RETROFIT - waste heat recovery, shaft generators, energy-saving devices, air lubrication, wind assistance, derating, VFDs, LED and HVAC control
FUELS - LNG with methane slip managed, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, biofuels, batteries and hybrids, onshore power supply, dual-fuel and fuel-ready designs
well-to-wake accounting makes the fuel PRODUCTION PATHWAY the decisive question
FLEET AND COMMERCIAL - fleet renewal, charter party clauses allocating efficiency responsibility, digital performance monitoring, training, R&D participation
the split incentive between owner and charterer is the largest non-technical obstacle, and is solved contractually

steps.title: SDG 14 Life Below Water - relevance to shipping
points: SDG 14 - conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources; the Goal closest to IMO's mandate
target 14.1 - prevent and significantly reduce marine pollution of all kinds
operational and accidental pollution - oil, NLS, sewage, garbage, plastics
invasive species via ballast water and biofouling - among the least reversible impacts
toxic anti-fouling systems
SOx and NOx deposition, and CO2 driving ocean ACIDIFICATION - where SDG 13 and 14 meet
underwater radiated noise; ship strikes on cetaceans
end-of-life recycling contaminating the coastal environment
instruments - MARPOL Annexes I to VI; BWM Convention 2004 in force 8 September 2017 with D-1 and D-2; AFS 2001; London Convention and Protocol; IMO marine plastic litter action plan
HONG KONG CONVENTION - criteria met June 2023, ENTERS INTO FORCE 26 JUNE 2025, so NOT YET IN FORCE at this sitting

steps.title: SDG 14 - specific actions
points: ballast water - operate and maintain the BWMS to D-2 properly, crew training, sampling, honest Ballast Water Record Book
biofouling - management plan, coating selection, in-water inspection and cleaning with capture; ALSO a major fuel-efficiency measure
garbage and plastics - segregation, Garbage Record Book accuracy, absolute prohibition on plastics overboard, retention where reception facilities are inadequate, eliminate single-use plastics
oil and chemicals - Oil Record Book discipline, functioning OWS with no bypass, bunkering procedures and checklists, SOPEP/SMPEP exercised
sewage and grey water - treatment plants maintained; Annex IV discharge only; voluntary grey water retention in sensitive areas
air emissions reaching the sea - sulphur limit and ECA compliance, scrubber washwater management, NOx-compliant operation
anti-fouling systems compliant with AFS, with a valid IAFS Certificate
underwater radiated noise and ship strikes - reduce propeller cavitation; observe routeing measures, ATBAs and speed restrictions in whale habitats
responsible recycling - accurate and updated Inventory of Hazardous Materials; select facilities to the Hong Kong Convention standard AHEAD of its entry into force
observe Special Areas, ECAs and Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas; beyond-compliance participation and transparent reporting

steps.title: The management-level conclusion
points: for a shipowner the SDGs are now a COMMERCIAL and FINANCING framework, not only an ethical one
access to capital - sustainable finance frameworks and portfolio emissions disclosure affect the cost of borrowing
access to cargo - charterers set environmental criteria, so CII rating affects employability
asset value - a ship that cannot meet tightening carbon intensity faces early obsolescence, making newbuilding fuel choice a balance-sheet decision
regulatory direction - the SDGs signal where binding IMO regulation is heading, so alignment is cheap regulatory risk management
licence to operate - crew recruitment and retention, port and coastal State relations, reputation
CLOSING LINE - the SDGs set the direction, IMO conventions turn direction into obligation, and the SEEMP turns obligation into daily practice

questions.understand_first: The stem prints three tasks and they are worth very different amounts. Explaining what the SDGs ARE is quick. Explaining their ROLE is the interesting part, because the SDGs are a General Assembly resolution that binds nobody - so the real question is how a non-binding framework changes behaviour at all, and the answer is comparability, universality, measurement, transparency and above all the mobilisation of finance and charterers. The third task, SPECIFIC ACTIONS, carries the most marks and is where answers usually collapse into generalities: 'reduce emissions' scores nothing, 'weather routeing, hull and propeller condition management, onshore power supply' scores. Choose SDG 13 and SDG 14 because each has dedicated IMO instruments behind it, which lets you cite regulation instead of sentiment - and remember the maritime instruments were moving fast in 2024, so the strategy, the mid-term measures and the Hong Kong Convention must each be stated at their December 2024 status.
questions.memory_cue: Instrument: 70/1, 2015, 17 and 169, five Ps, leave no one behind (1). Role, six mechanisms: LANGUAGE, UNIVERSALITY, INTEGRATION, MEASUREMENT, TRANSPARENCY, FINANCE (2) - then the honest weakness. SDG 13 actions in ascending cost: OPERATE - RETROFIT - REFUEL - RENEW (5). SDG 14 actions outward from the ship: what LEAVES the hull, what is ON the hull, what the hull DOES, what happens at the END (7). Close on capital, cargo, asset value, direction (8).

quick_revision.critical_regulation: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/70/1 of 25 September 2015, sets 17 Goals and 169 targets which are integrated and indivisible, global in nature and universally applicable; in the maritime sector the binding expression of SDG 13 is the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80) of 7 July 2023, which superseded the 2018 Initial Strategy and sets net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around 2050 with indicative checkpoints for 2030 and 2040.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering with generic aspirations when the stem asks for specific actions the shipping industry can take - 'reduce emissions' scores nothing where 'weather routeing, hull and propeller condition management, onshore power supply, D-2 ballast water compliance' scores. Three currency traps sit alongside it, and all three are things a candidate revising from later material would get wrong: the operative IMO climate instrument is the 2023 Strategy MEPC.377(80), not the superseded 2018 Initial Strategy; no mid-term measure had been adopted at this sitting, the work having been referred onward to MEPC 83 in 2025; and the Hong Kong Convention was NOT YET IN FORCE - its criteria were met in June 2023 but it enters into force on 26 June 2025, six months after this examination.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the SDGs and maritime sector question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the SDGs are. 2 Their role in promoting sustainability. 3 Why the maritime sector matters and which two Goals you choose. 4 SDG 13 relevance. 5 SDG 13 specific actions. 6 SDG 14 relevance. 7 SDG 14 specific actions. 8 The management-level conclusion.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem prints three tasks and the third - specific actions - carries the most marks, so it gets a full step under each chosen Goal.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What instrument established the SDGs, when, and what does it contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/70/1, 'Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development', adopted 25 September 2015 and in effect from 1 January 2016. It contains 17 Goals and 169 targets, organised around five areas - People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership - with the pledge to leave no one behind, and declares the Goals integrated and indivisible, global in nature and universally applicable.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the resolution and the two dates, and giving 17 and 169, immediately marks the answer out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The SDGs bind nobody. How do they promote sustainability at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Through six mechanisms: a common language giving comparability across sectors and borders; universality, applying to every State rather than only developing ones; integration, forcing recognition of trade-offs and co-benefits; measurement, through 169 targets and an indicator framework; accountability by transparency, through the High-Level Political Forum and voluntary national reviews rather than sanction; and mobilisation of finance and the private sector through ESG reporting, sustainable finance and charterers' requirements - the mechanism with the most practical bite for shipping.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks about their ROLE, not what they ARE, and this is the distinction most answers miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the operative IMO climate instrument at this sitting, and what does it set?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023, which superseded the 2018 Initial Strategy. It sets net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around, i.e. close to, 2050; indicative checkpoints for 2030 and 2040 against a 2008 baseline; an ambition for uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and energy sources by 2030; and a move to well-to-wake lifecycle accounting.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the 2018 Initial Strategy and its weaker 50%-by-2050 target is stale by eighteen months at this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What was the status of the IMO mid-term GHG measures at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under development, and NOT adopted. A technical measure such as a GHG fuel standard and an economic measure such as a pricing mechanism were being developed; MEPC 82, held 30 September to 4 October 2024, carried the work forward and referred the review of the short-term measures to a correspondence group and an intersessional working group reporting to MEPC 83 in 2025.
retrieval_cards.why: Material written for any later sitting carries the outcome of that work, and back-reading it is future contamination.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Was the Hong Kong Convention in force at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Its entry-into-force criteria were met in June 2023, when Bangladesh and Liberia became Contracting States, and it enters into force twenty-four months later on 26 June 2025 - six months AFTER this examination. At this sitting it is adopted and ratified but not yet in force.
retrieval_cards.why: The clearest adopted-versus-ratified-versus-in-force illustration available on this question, and it inverts for any later sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give specific SDG 13 actions in four groups by ascending capital cost.
retrieval_cards.answer: OPERATE - speed optimisation, weather routeing, just-in-time arrival, trim optimisation, hull and propeller condition management. RETROFIT - waste heat recovery, shaft generators, energy-saving devices, air lubrication, wind assistance, variable-frequency drives. REFUEL - LNG with methane slip managed, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, biofuels, batteries, onshore power supply, dual-fuel and fuel-ready designs. RENEW - fleet renewal, charter party clauses addressing the split incentive, digital performance monitoring, training.
retrieval_cards.why: Ordering by capital cost shows engineering judgement rather than a list of green words.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which IMO instruments implement SDG 14, and what are the ballast water standards?
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Annexes I to VI; the Ballast Water Management Convention 2004, in force 8 September 2017, with the D-1 ballast water exchange standard and the D-2 ballast water performance standard; the AFS Convention 2001; the London Convention and Protocol; and the IMO Action Plan on marine plastic litter from ships. The Hong Kong Convention 2009 was not yet in force at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: SDG 14 is the Goal closest to IMO's mandate, so this is where regulation can be cited rather than sentiment.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give specific SDG 14 actions, working outward from the ship.
retrieval_cards.answer: What leaves the hull - D-2 ballast water compliance with honest record keeping, zero plastics overboard and Garbage Record Book discipline, oily-water separator with no bypass, Annex IV sewage treatment, sulphur and ECA compliance with scrubber washwater management. What is on the hull - AFS-compliant anti-fouling with a valid IAFS Certificate, and a biofouling management plan with in-water cleaning and capture. What the hull does - reduce underwater radiated noise from propeller cavitation, and observe routeing measures and speed restrictions in whale habitats. What happens at the end - an accurate Inventory of Hazardous Materials and recycling at Hong Kong Convention standard yards.
retrieval_cards.why: The outward-from-the-hull structure is what makes the list specific rather than generic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give one action that serves both chosen Goals, and explain the link.
retrieval_cards.answer: Biofouling management. It prevents the transfer of invasive aquatic species, serving SDG 14, and simultaneously reduces hull resistance and therefore fuel consumption and emissions, serving SDG 13. The link runs the other way too: CO2 absorbed by the ocean drives acidification, so reducing greenhouse gas emissions under SDG 13 protects marine ecosystems under SDG 14.
retrieval_cards.why: It demonstrates the Goals' claimed indivisibility in practice instead of merely asserting it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are the SDGs legally binding, and where do the maritime obligations actually come from?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are not binding - they are a UN General Assembly resolution, not a treaty, with no enforcement mechanism. The binding maritime obligations come from IMO conventions, principally MARPOL, the BWM Convention and the AFS Convention, which States implement domestically - in India through the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and subordinate rules. The SDGs set direction; the conventions create obligation.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the distinction that makes the 'role' limb answerable, and it prevents the answer overclaiming.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why do the SDGs matter commercially to a shipowner?
retrieval_cards.answer: Access to capital - sustainable finance frameworks and portfolio emissions disclosure affect the cost of borrowing. Access to cargo - charterers apply environmental criteria, so CII rating affects employability. Asset value - a ship unable to meet tightening carbon intensity requirements faces early obsolescence, making newbuilding fuel choice a balance-sheet decision. Regulatory direction - the SDGs signal where binding IMO regulation is heading. And licence to operate - crew recruitment, port State relations and reputation.
retrieval_cards.why: This is what turns a general essay into a management-level answer.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: One limb, sixteen marks, three printed tasks: explain the role of the SDGs in promoting global sustainability; choose ANY TWO SDGs and discuss their relevance to the maritime sector; and highlight SPECIFIC actions the shipping industry can take to support their achievement. The choice of Goals is genuine and should be stated and justified in one line.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks, undivided. Roughly three for what the SDGs are, three for the role limb - which is the analytically hardest part because the instrument is non-binding - two for framing the maritime connection and choosing the Goals, and eight across the two chosen Goals split between relevance and actions, with the actions carrying the larger share.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can explain how a non-binding framework changes behaviour, and can then name concrete engineering and management actions rather than aspirations. The currency test is whether the maritime instruments are stated at their December 2024 status - the 2023 Strategy rather than the 2018 one, no mid-term measure adopted, and the Hong Kong Convention not yet in force.
primary_source_plan: Take the instrument, date, Goal and target counts, the five areas and the pledge from A/RES/70/1 itself
Establish the mechanisms of the review architecture - HLPF, voluntary national reviews, indicator framework
ESTABLISH THE OPERATIVE IMO CLIMATE INSTRUMENT AT DECEMBER 2024 BEFORE WRITING ANY DECARBONISATION CONTENT - the strategy was replaced in 2023 and the measures were moving through 2024
Fix the status of the mid-term measures at the sitting, from the MEPC 82 outcome
Fix the decarbonisation stage - EEXI, CII and enhanced SEEMP in force since 1 January 2023, first ratings during 2024
For SDG 14, take the instrument list and the BWM standards, and SEPARATELY verify the Hong Kong Convention's entry-into-force date against the sitting month
Assert no emissions-share or trade-share percentage that cannot be sourced and dated
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The SDG instrument itself is entirely stable, but the maritime limb rests on instruments that moved during 2023 and 2024 - the GHG Strategy was replaced in July 2023, the short-term measures came into force in January 2023 with first ratings during 2024, the mid-term measures were still in development, and the Hong Kong Convention was six months from entry into force. The danger is diffuse rather than pointed, which makes it easier to get wrong.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The SDGs are universal and the IMO instruments apply internationally. Where national implementation is mentioned it must be the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and subordinate rules, not the MS Act 2025.
technical_ambiguities: Whether the SDGs are legally binding - they are not
Whether the 2018 or the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy is operative - the 2023 Strategy, MEPC.377(80)
Whether any mid-term measure had been adopted - none had
Whether the Hong Kong Convention was in force - it was not, entering into force 26 June 2025
Whether shipping is counted in national inventories under the Paris Agreement - international shipping is not, which is why IMO regulates it
Whether a percentage can be given for shipping's emissions share - not without a verified source
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: What the SDGs are, briefly and numerically; then the role limb answered as the mechanisms by which a non-binding framework works, with the honest weakness stated; then the maritime framing and an explicit choice of SDG 13 and SDG 14; then for each Goal, relevance followed by a substantial block of specific actions, tabulated for SDG 13 by ascending capital cost and listed for SDG 14 working outward from the hull; closing on the commercial and financing consequences for a shipowner.

questions.short_title: IMO Code on Noise Levels On Board Ships
questions.text_verbatim: Explain the purpose and significance of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Code on Noise Levels Onboard Ships (Noise Code). Discuss the key provisions of the Noise Code, including the maximum allowable noise limits, areas of application, and measures to reduce noise levels onboard. Highlight the impact of noise on crew health and performance, and describe the compliance requirements for ship design, equipment, and operational practices under this Code. (16)

The purpose of the Code, in its own words, and its three-part rationale

Noise exposure limits - the Lex(24) criterion, the 85 dB(A) threshold and the peak limit

blocks.h: 1. What the Noise Code is, and what made it mandatory

blocks.p: The Code on noise levels on board ships is the annex to resolution MSC.337(91), adopted by the Maritime Safety Committee on 30 November 2012. It replaced in practice the earlier recommendatory Code of resolution A.468(XII) of 1981.

It was made mandatory by resolution MSC.338(91), adopted on the same day, which inserted a new SOLAS regulation II-1/3-12, "Protection against noise", in force 1 July 2014. Regulation II-1/3-12.3 provides that ships shall be constructed to reduce onboard noise and to protect personnel from noise in accordance with the Code. The same amendment deleted the former SOLAS regulation II-1/36, which had been the Convention's only previous mention of noise protection - so the new regulation did not merely add a requirement, it replaced a general exhortation with a measurable standard.

One nuance is worth stating early because it recurs throughout: although the Code is legally treated as a mandatory instrument under SOLAS, certain provisions remain recommendatory. Paragraph 1.1.3 lists them - paragraphs 1.3.2 and 1.3.3, 3.4.2 and 3.4.3, the whole of chapter 5, section 6.3, section 7.3 and appendices 2, 3 and 4. So the maximum limits in chapter 4 are mandatory, while the exposure limits in chapter 5 are recommendatory. Candidates who say the whole Code is mandatory, or that none of it is, both lose the point.
Paragraph 1.2 states the purpose: to limit noise levels and reduce seafarers' exposure to noise, in order to -

ol: provide for safe working conditions, having regard to the need for speech communication and for hearing audible alarms, and to an environment in which clear-headed decisions can be made in control stations, navigation and radio spaces and manned machinery spaces;
protect the seafarer from excessive noise levels which may give rise to noise-induced hearing loss; and
provide an acceptable degree of comfort in rest, recreation and other spaces, and conditions for recuperation from the effects of exposure to high noise levels.

blocks.p: The significance is in the ordering. Limb 1 is a safety objective, not a health one - noise that masks an alarm or degrades a decision is a navigational and operational hazard. Limb 2 is occupational health. Limb 3 is habitability, and it introduces the idea of recuperation: the Code does not only cap the working environment, it requires a quiet place to recover in, which is why cabin limits are the tightest in the table.

Paragraph 1.1.1 adds the design philosophy: the Code is intended to provide the basis for a design standard, with compliance based on the satisfactory conclusion of sea trials resulting in the issue of a Noise Survey Report; ongoing operational compliance is predicated on the crew being trained in personal protection and the maintenance of mitigation measures, enforced through the processes put in place under SOLAS chapter IX - the ISM Code.

Ships. Paragraph 1.3.1: the Code applies to new ships of 1,600 gross tonnage and above. "New ship" is defined at 1.4.22 by reference to SOLAS regulation II-1/3-12.1, which applies the regulation to ships of 1,600 GT and above:

ul: for which the building contract is placed on or after 1 July 2014; or
in the absence of a building contract, the keels of which are laid or which are at a similar stage of construction on or after 1 January 2015; or
the delivery of which is on or after 1 July 2018.

blocks.p: Older ships are not simply exempt. Regulation II-1/3-12.2 catches ships delivered before 1 July 2018 whose keels were laid on or after 1 January 2009 but before 1 January 2015: for those, measures shall be taken to reduce machinery noise in machinery spaces to levels acceptable to the Administration, and if it cannot be sufficiently reduced the source shall be insulated or isolated, or a refuge from noise provided if the space must be manned, with ear protectors provided as necessary.

The Code itself is permissive in two further directions, and both are among the recommendatory provisions: paragraph 1.3.2 - the provisions on hazardous noise levels, mitigation and personal protective gear may be applied to existing ships of 1,600 GT and above so far as reasonable and practical; and paragraph 1.3.3 - the Code may be applied to new ships of less than 1,600 GT.

Excluded ship types - paragraph 1.3.4, eleven of them: dynamically supported craft; high-speed craft; fishing vessels; pipe-laying barges; crane barges; mobile offshore drilling units; pleasure yachts not engaged in trade; ships of war and troopships; ships not propelled by mechanical means; pile driving vessels; and dredgers. SOLAS II-1/3-12.4 cross-refers to this same list.

Spaces and conditions. The Code applies to ships in port or at sea with seafarers on board (1.3.5). It is not intended to apply to passenger cabins and other passenger spaces except so far as they are work spaces (1.3.8). It covers only ship-related noise sources such as machinery and propulsion, and not wind, wave or ice noise, alarms or public address systems (1.3.10). Where major repairs, alterations and modifications are made to an existing ship, the areas changed shall meet the new-ship requirements so far as the Administration deems reasonable and practicable (1.3.9). And the Administration may grant a dispensation in special circumstances where compliance is documented to be impossible despite reasonable technical noise reduction - but not for cabins, unless exceptional circumstances prevail (1.3.6).

Paragraph 4.1.1: these are maximum levels, not desirable levels, and where reasonably practicable it is desirable to be lower. Paragraph 4.1.2: they are assessed before the ship is put in service, by equivalent continuous sound level measurement. The limits are in dB(A):

rows: Workshops other than those forming part of machinery spaces
Look-out posts, including navigating bridge wings and windows
Radio rooms (equipment operating but not producing audio signals)
Galleys, without food processing equipment operating

blocks.p: Three points earn marks beyond the numbers. First, only the accommodation spaces differ by ship size - cabins, messrooms, recreation rooms and offices are 5 dB(A) tighter on ships of 10,000 GT and above; every work, navigation and service space limit is the same for both sizes. Second, the machinery space limit of 110 dB(A) is not a level anyone may be exposed to unprotected: paragraph 4.1.3 states that it assumes hearing protectors meeting chapter 7 are worn, and that personnel entering spaces above 85 dB(A) should be required to wear them. Third, the machinery control room at 75 dB(A) against a machinery space at 110 is the Code's clearest single design statement: a 35 dB(A) step, bought by the control room enclosure, so that speech and alarms work where the decisions are made.

Chapter 4 caps the space; chapter 5 caps the person. Paragraph 5.1.1 ties them together: the chapter 4 limits are designed so that, if complied with, seafarers will not be exposed to an Lex(24) exceeding 80 dB(A) - the equivalent continuous noise exposure over each 24-hour period. For a new ship this is verified from sea trial measurements by calculating the expected exposure of each category of crew member.

ul: 5.1.2 - in spaces above 85 dB(A), suitable hearing protection should be used, or time limits applied, to maintain an equivalent level of protection.
5.1.4 - no crew member should be exposed unprotected to peak values exceeding 135 dB(C).
5.3.1 - even wearing hearing protectors, no seafarer should be exposed above 120 dB(A) or to an Leq(24) above 105 dB(A).

5.3.5 - for exposures of less than eight hours, seafarers without protection should not be exposed above 85 dB(A); where they remain more than eight hours, an Leq(24) of 80 dB(A) should not be exceeded - so for at least a third of each 24 hours each seafarer should be in an environment below 75 dB(A).

5.4 - as an alternative to the zone method, no unprotected seafarer above an Leq(24) of 80 dB(A), and daily exposure in spaces requiring protectors not to exceed four hours continuously or eight hours in total.

5.5 - a hearing conservation programme for those working where LAeq exceeds 85 dB(A): initial and periodic audiometric tests by a trained and qualified person, instruction on the hazards and on proper use of protectors, maintenance of audiometric records, and periodic analysis of those records.

blocks.p: Section 5.3 expresses all this as five zones, A to E, on a plot of level against duration: zone A no exposure at all; zones B and C occasional exposure only, with protectors attenuating 25 to 35 dB(A) and at least 25 dB(A) respectively; zone D daily exposure with protectors of at least 25 dB(A) and a hearing conservation programme to be considered; zone E no protection required. Remember the note under the figure: to work in zones A to D, protectors bringing the level at the ear below 85 dB(A) are required; in zone E they are not required but should be accessible if the level is over 80 dB(A) for more than eight hours.

blocks.h: 6. Measures to reduce noise on board

blocks.p: The Code's own hierarchy is unambiguous, at section 7.1: hearing protection is supplied only when the application of means for controlling sound at source does not reduce the level, and the provision of hearing protectors shall not be considered a substitute for effective noise control. Measures therefore run source - path - receiver:

ul: At source - selection of quieter machinery and low-noise fans and compressors; resilient mounting of engines, gensets, pumps and gearboxes; balancing and alignment; flexible couplings in piping and exhaust systems; attention to propeller design and hull clearance to limit propeller-excited hull noise; silencers on engine intakes, exhausts and ventilation.

On the path - acoustic enclosure of dominant sources; insulation and damping treatments on bulkheads, decks and casings; floating floors and resilient deck coverings; avoiding structure-borne short circuits between machinery seatings and accommodation; arrangement and layout - siting cabins and hospitals away from casings, machinery, funnel uptakes and mooring machinery, which is the cheapest measure of all because it costs nothing at the design stage and is unaffordable later.

At the receiver - the machinery control room as an acoustic refuge; the refuge from noise required for older ships under SOLAS II-1/3-12.2; hearing protectors under chapter 7; and administrative controls - job rotation, limiting continuous exposure to four hours and eight hours in total, and scheduling noisy work.

blocks.p: Appendix 3 of the Code, Suggested methods of attenuating noise, collects these; it is one of the recommendatory appendices.

blocks.h: 7. Impact on crew health and on performance

blocks.p: The Code separates these, and so should the answer.

Health. The primary effect is noise-induced hearing loss, defined at 1.4.24 as a hearing loss originating in the nerve cells within the cochlea attributable to the effects of sound. It is cumulative, painless and irreversible - which is precisely why it is regulated by exposure dose over 24 hours rather than by momentary discomfort, and why audiometric testing under 5.5 is the only way it is detected before it is disabling. Very high peaks - above the 135 dB(C) limit at 5.1.4 - risk acoustic trauma, immediate mechanical damage rather than gradual loss. Beyond hearing, sustained noise contributes to disturbed sleep and impaired recuperation, fatigue, elevated stress response and cardiovascular strain - which is why paragraph 1.2.3 speaks of comfort in rest and recreation spaces and of conditions for recuperation, and why cabin limits are the tightest in the Code.
Performance. Paragraph 1.2.1 identifies the operational consequences directly:

ul: masking of speech communication - orders and reports misheard, on the bridge, in the engine room and during mooring and emergency operations;
masking of audible alarms - the safety case for the 60 dB(A) radio room and 65 dB(A) bridge limits;
degradation of clear-headed decision-making in control stations, navigation and radio spaces and manned machinery spaces - the Code's own phrase;
fatigue and reduced alertness carried into the next watch through disturbed rest, which links this Code directly to the fatigue regime and to MLC Regulation 4.3 on health and safety protection;
reduced situational awareness, including the loss of the diagnostic information an engineer takes from the sound of running machinery when protectors are worn.

blocks.p: The two are connected. A noisy ship is not only a ship whose crew lose hearing over a career; it is a ship on which an alarm is missed tonight. That is why noise sits in SOLAS chapter II-1 as a construction requirement and not merely in occupational health guidance.

blocks.h: 8. Compliance requirements - design, equipment and operation

rows: The Code is a design standard. Predict levels, arrange spaces, specify machinery and treatments to meet the chapter 4 limits; provide acoustic insulation between accommodation spaces to the chapter 6 indices
Verify by measurement under chapter 3 conditions; sea trials; produce the Noise Survey Report in the appendix 1 format before the ship is put in service

Hearing protectors able to reduce levels to 85 dB(A) or less, selected by the HML method of ISO 4869-2:1994; noise-cancelling headsets permitted if equivalent in the unpowered condition; warning notices at entrances

Exposure control and time limits; a section in the Safety Management System on the company's hearing protection policy, exposure limits and training, logged in training records; a hearing conservation programme with audiometric testing; the Noise Survey Report carried on board and accessible for the crew

blocks.p: The Noise Survey Report (section 4.3) is the certificate-equivalent of this Code, and its detail is examinable: one report per ship, comprising information on the noise levels in the various spaces, showing the reading at each specified measuring point, with the points marked on a general arrangement plan or accommodation drawings attached to the report or otherwise identified; in the appendix 1 format; and it shall always be carried on board and be accessible for the crew.

Acoustic insulation between accommodation spaces (chapter 6) is the requirement most often forgotten. The airborne sound insulation of bulkheads and decks within the accommodation must meet, as a minimum, the weighted sound reduction index Rw of ISO 717-1:

ul: cabin to cabin - Rw 35;
messrooms, recreation rooms, public spaces and entertainment areas to cabins and hospitals - Rw 45;
corridor to cabin - Rw 30;
cabin to cabin with a communicating door - Rw 30.

blocks.p: These are determined by laboratory test to ISO 10140-2 (6.2.2); where erection of materials is in doubt, field measurements may be taken and the apparent index R'w should comply with a tolerance of up to 3 dB (6.3.2).

Warning notices (section 7.4). Where the noise level in machinery spaces or other spaces exceeds 85 dB(A), entrances shall carry a warning notice comprising symbol and supplementary sign in the working language of the ship; if only a minor portion of the space is affected, the particular location or equipment shall be identified at eye level, visible from each direction of access. The Code prints four bands:

rows: DANGEROUS NOISE - USE OF HEARING PROTECTORS MANDATORY
CAUTION: DANGEROUS NOISE - USE OF HEARING PROTECTORS MANDATORY - SHORT STAY ONLY
CAUTION: EXCESSIVELY HIGH-NOISE LEVEL - USE OF HEARING PROTECTORS MANDATORY - NO STAY LONGER THAN 10 MINUTES

blocks.p: Sixteen marks in one limb, but the stem is really a five-part checklist and the examiner will mark against it: purpose and significance; key provisions including maximum allowable noise limits, areas of application and measures to reduce noise; the impact on crew health and performance; and the compliance requirements for ship design, equipment and operational practices. Miss one and you lose that block of marks however good the rest is. The route follows the printed order deliberately, so the answer can be marked straight down the page.

The discriminator on this question is numbers. Almost every candidate can write that noise is bad for hearing and that ear defenders should be worn. Very few can give the machinery space limit, the cabin limits and the fact that they differ by ship size, the 85 dB(A) threshold, the Lex(24) 80 dB(A) criterion and the four Rw values. Those are where the marks are, and they exist only in the Code.

blocks.h: The one distinction that separates a good answer from a correct one

blocks.p: Chapter 4 is mandatory; chapter 5 is not. Paragraph 1.1.3 lists the provisions that remain recommendatory, and the whole of chapter 5 - the exposure limits - is on that list, along with 1.3.2 and 1.3.3, 3.4.2 and 3.4.3, section 6.3, section 7.3 and appendices 2, 3 and 4.

So the space limits in the table are a hard SOLAS requirement; the personal exposure limits, the zones and the hearing conservation programme are recommendatory even though the Code is a mandatory instrument. This is genuinely counter-intuitive, it is stated expressly in the Code, and saying it correctly demonstrates the Code has been opened rather than summarised.

blocks.h: Application dates: the part most answers get wrong

blocks.p: "Applies to new ships of 1,600 GT and above" is only the first half. The three date criteria come from SOLAS II-1/3-12.1, not from the Code: contract on or after 1 July 2014; absent a contract, keel laid on or after 1 January 2015; or delivery on or after 1 July 2018. Any one of the three brings the ship in.

And older ships are not simply outside. Regulation II-1/3-12.2 imposes a real duty on ships delivered before 1 July 2018 whose keels were laid on or after 1 January 2009 but before 1 January 2015: reduce machinery space noise to levels acceptable to the Administration, and failing that insulate or isolate the source or provide a refuge from noise if the space must be manned. An answer that mentions this second tier is describing the regulation; one that stops at the first is describing half of it.

ul: 110 machinery spaces - and it assumes protectors are worn (4.1.3).
75 machinery control rooms - the 35 dB(A) step that makes the control room work.
85 workshops and non-specified work spaces - and also the threshold for warning notices and for requiring protectors.
65 navigating bridge and chartrooms; 60 radio rooms; 70 look-out posts and bridge wings.
60 / 55 cabins and hospitals - the only figures where ship size matters, tighter on 10,000 GT and above.
90 normally unoccupied spaces; 75 galleys, serveries and pantries, and open recreation areas.
Lex(24) 80 dB(A) - the exposure criterion the whole table is designed to deliver.
135 dB(C) unprotected peak; 120 dB(A) and Leq(24) 105 dB(A) even with protectors.
Rw 35 / 45 / 30 / 30 - cabin-cabin, public spaces to cabins, corridor-cabin, cabin-cabin with communicating door; 3 dB field tolerance.

blocks.p: If time is short, the four that carry most credit are 110, 75, 85 and 60/55, because they let you describe the whole design logic - protect the ear in the machinery space, protect speech in the control room, mark the hazard threshold, and protect sleep in the cabin.

blocks.h: Health versus performance - answer both, separately

blocks.p: The stem says "the impact of noise on crew health and performance", which is two things. Health is the cochlear, cumulative, irreversible hearing loss, plus acoustic trauma from peaks, plus disturbed sleep, fatigue and stress. Performance is masking of speech and alarms, degraded decision-making in control stations, reduced alertness on the following watch, and loss of the diagnostic sound cues an engineer relies on when protectors are worn.

The sentence that ties them together, and is worth stating explicitly: a noisy ship is not only one whose crew lose hearing over a career, it is one on which an alarm is missed tonight - which is why the requirement sits in SOLAS chapter II-1 as a construction standard rather than in health guidance alone.

ul: Saying the whole Code is mandatory. Chapter 5, sections 6.3 and 7.3, paragraphs 1.3.2, 1.3.3, 3.4.2, 3.4.3 and appendices 2 to 4 are recommendatory - paragraph 1.1.3.
Giving 1,600 GT without the three date criteria from SOLAS II-1/3-12.1.
Saying existing ships are exempt. The 2009-2015 build window carries a real machinery-noise duty under II-1/3-12.2.
Quoting one set of limits and not noticing that accommodation limits are 5 dB(A) tighter at 10,000 GT and above.
Presenting 110 dB(A) as an acceptable unprotected exposure. It assumes hearing protectors are worn.
Treating hearing protectors as the primary control. Section 7.1 says they are not a substitute for effective noise control.
Omitting chapter 6 acoustic insulation entirely - the four Rw values are quick marks.
Omitting the Noise Survey Report, which is the compliance document and must be carried on board and be accessible to the crew.
Forgetting that the Code covers only ship-related sources - not wind, wave, ice, alarms or public address (1.3.10).
Answering only on health when the stem also asks about performance.
"Is the Noise Code mandatory?" Its application is mandatory under SOLAS II-1/3-12, but specified parts of it remain recommendatory - and chapter 5 is one of them.

"Your machinery space measures 108 dB(A). Compliant?" Against the chapter 4 limit of 110, yes - but personnel entering must wear protectors, the entrance must carry the 85-110 band notice, and the individual's Lex(24) still has to be controlled.
"Can the Administration dispense with a cabin limit?" Only in exceptional circumstances - dispensations under 1.3.6 shall not include cabins unless exceptional circumstances prevail.
"Which SOLAS regulation did this replace?" MSC.338(91) deleted the former regulation II-1/36 when it inserted II-1/3-12.
"What must the noise survey report show?" The reading at each specified measuring point, with the points marked on a general arrangement plan or accommodation drawings.
"How long may a seafarer work in a space requiring protectors?" Section 5.4 - not more than four hours continuously or eight hours in total in a day.
Which resolution is the Noise Code, and which made it mandatory? MSC.337(91); MSC.338(91) inserting SOLAS II-1/3-12, in force 1 July 2014.
What is the limit in a machinery space and in a machinery control room? 110 and 75 dB(A).
What is the cabin limit? 60 dB(A), or 55 on ships of 10,000 GT and above.
At what level must a warning notice be posted? Above 85 dB(A).
What is the daily exposure criterion? Lex(24) not exceeding 80 dB(A).
What peak may an unprotected seafarer not exceed? 135 dB(C).
What sound reduction index is required cabin to cabin? Rw 35; and Rw 45 from public spaces to cabins and hospitals.

Which ships are excluded? The eleven types at Code paragraph 1.3.4 - dynamically supported craft, high-speed craft, fishing vessels, pipe-laying barges, crane barges, MODUs, pleasure yachts not in trade, warships and troopships, ships not mechanically propelled, pile driving vessels and dredgers.
What document evidences compliance? The Noise Survey Report, in the appendix 1 format, carried on board and accessible to the crew.

blocks.p: Walk the ship from the noisiest space inward and the whole table falls out: machinery space 110 -> control room 75 -> workshop 85 -> bridge 65 -> radio 60 -> cabin 60 (55 big ship). The single number that ties the Code together is 85 - it is the workshop limit, the warning-notice threshold, the level above which protectors are required, and the level protectors must bring the ear below.

For the structure of the Code: 1 general, 2 equipment, 3 measurement, 4 LIMITS, 5 EXPOSURE, 6 INSULATION, 7 PROTECTION - and the answer's five demands map onto chapters 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7. For measures: SOURCE - PATH - RECEIVER, in that order, because the Code insists protectors are last.

blocks.p: Every dB figure, date and paragraph number in this answer comes from MSC.337(91) and MSC.338(91) read in full. Three limitations are recorded. MIW holds no licensed IMO consolidated SOLAS edition, so regulation II-1/3-12 is taken from its adopting resolution rather than from a consolidated text - sound for the regulation as adopted, and no later amendment to it was identified as at this sitting. Figure 1 of the Code is a graph and is described by its numerical anchors rather than redrawn. And no epidemiological statistic on hearing loss prevalence among seafarers is asserted; the health effects given are those the Code itself identifies.

On currency, this question is unusually quiet: the Code is unamended at this sitting and nothing in 2024 touched it. That is worth knowing precisely because the rest of this paper is not quiet - Q6 and Q8 both turn on instruments that moved during 2024. Here the risk is not staleness but imprecision.

notes: The intake recorded STABLE / LOW. Checked rather than trusted, per the standing rule, and CONFIRMED - this is one of the genuinely quiet questions on the paper.

MSC.337(91) was adopted 30 November 2012 and is UNAMENDED at this sitting. SOLAS regulation II-1/3-12, inserted by MSC.338(91), entered into force 1 July 2014 and no amendment to it was identified as at December 2024.

ALL THREE APPLICATION DATES ARE HISTORIC AT THIS SITTING. Contract on or after 1 July 2014, keel on or after 1 January 2015, delivery on or after 1 July 2018 - the latest of them is more than six years before this examination, so no forward-looking phasing statement is appropriate. An answer written for an earlier sitting might have described the 1 July 2018 delivery criterion as still to come; at December 2024 it is long past.
THE 2009-2015 BUILD WINDOW at II-1/3-12.2 is likewise entirely historic and is stated as a settled duty on that cohort, not as a transitional measure.

NO 2024 MOVEMENT. Nothing adopted or entering into force during 2024 touches the Noise Code, SOLAS II-1/3-12 or the underlying measurement standards relied on. Verified rather than assumed, because the paper anchor establishes that three other questions on this paper DID move during 2024.

PREDECESSOR INSTRUMENTS ARE HISTORIC, NOT CURRENT. A.468(XII) of 1981 is the recommendatory predecessor and survives only as the footnote reference in II-1/3-12.2; A.343(IX) on listening posts is expressly NOT superseded by the Code and remains alongside it. Neither is presented as the operative standard.

questions.understand_first: This looks like a general essay on noise and it is not. Every one of the five things the stem asks for - purpose, maximum allowable limits, areas of application, measures to reduce noise, and compliance requirements for design, equipment and operation - has an exact answer inside one short instrument, and the marks are in the exactness. The Code's own logic is worth grasping before the numbers: it is a DESIGN standard, proved on sea trials and recorded in a Noise Survey Report, and it caps two different things in two different chapters - chapter 4 caps the SPACE, chapter 5 caps the PERSON. The single most surprising fact, stated expressly at paragraph 1.1.3, is that although the Code is mandatory under SOLAS, the whole of chapter 5 remains recommendatory. And the number that ties the Code together is 85 dB(A): the workshop limit, the warning-notice threshold, the level above which protectors are required, and the level protectors must bring the ear below.
