quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS regulation II-1/3-12, inserted by resolution MSC.338(91) and in force 1 July 2014, requires ships to be constructed to reduce onboard noise and to protect personnel from noise in accordance with the Code on noise levels on board ships adopted by resolution MSC.337(91); it applies to ships of 1,600 gross tonnage and above contracted on or after 1 July 2014, or keel-laid on or after 1 January 2015, or delivered on or after 1 July 2018.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing a general essay on noise and hearing protection instead of producing the Code's actual numbers. The stem asks for FIVE things - purpose and significance, maximum allowable limits, areas of application, measures to reduce noise, impact on health AND performance, and compliance requirements for design, equipment and operation - and each is a separate block of marks. Three specific traps: the whole Code is NOT mandatory (paragraph 1.1.3 keeps all of chapter 5 recommendatory); the 110 dB(A) machinery space limit ASSUMES hearing protectors are worn and is not a permissible unprotected exposure; and only the ACCOMMODATION limits change with ship size, being 5 dB(A) tighter at 10,000 GT and above.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Noise Code question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the Code is and what made it mandatory. 2 Purpose and significance. 3 Areas of application. 4 Maximum allowable limits. 5 Noise exposure limits. 6 Measures to reduce noise. 7 Impact on health and on performance. 8 Compliance in design, equipment and operation.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem is a five-part checklist and the route follows its printed order so the answer can be marked straight down the page.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which resolution is the Noise Code, and what made it mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Code is the annex to resolution MSC.337(91), adopted 30 November 2012. Resolution MSC.338(91) inserted SOLAS regulation II-1/3-12, Protection against noise, in force 1 July 2014, which requires ships to be constructed in accordance with the Code. The same amendment deleted the former SOLAS regulation II-1/36.
retrieval_cards.why: The deletion of II-1/36 shows the regulation replaced a general exhortation with a measurable standard.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the whole of the Noise Code mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Paragraph 1.1.3 lists provisions that remain recommendatory, options for compliance or informative: paragraphs 1.3.2 and 1.3.3, 3.4.2 and 3.4.3, THE WHOLE OF CHAPTER 5, section 6.3, section 7.3 and appendices 2, 3 and 4. So the chapter 4 space limits are mandatory while the chapter 5 exposure limits are not.
retrieval_cards.why: Counter-intuitive, stated expressly, and the clearest sign the Code has been opened rather than summarised.

retrieval_cards.prompt: To which ships does the Code apply, and from what dates?
retrieval_cards.answer: New ships of 1,600 GT and above. Under SOLAS II-1/3-12.1: building contract placed on or after 1 July 2014; or, absent a contract, keel laid or at a similar stage on or after 1 January 2015; or delivery on or after 1 July 2018. Any one criterion brings the ship in.
retrieval_cards.why: The three dates come from the SOLAS regulation, not from the Code, and most answers give only the tonnage.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are older ships simply exempt from noise requirements?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. SOLAS II-1/3-12.2 catches ships delivered before 1 July 2018 whose keels were laid on or after 1 January 2009 but before 1 January 2015: measures shall be taken to reduce machinery space noise to levels acceptable to the Administration; if it cannot be sufficiently reduced the source shall be insulated or isolated, or a refuge from noise provided if the space must be manned, with ear protectors provided as necessary.
retrieval_cards.why: The second tier of the regulation, and the part most answers omit entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the maximum noise levels for machinery spaces, machinery control rooms, the navigating bridge, radio rooms and cabins.
retrieval_cards.answer: Machinery spaces 110 dB(A); machinery control rooms 75 dB(A); navigating bridge and chartrooms 65 dB(A); radio rooms 60 dB(A); cabins and hospitals 60 dB(A), or 55 dB(A) on ships of 10,000 GT and above.
retrieval_cards.why: The 110-to-75 step across the control room bulkhead is the Code's clearest design statement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which limits change with ship size, and what does the 110 dB(A) figure assume?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only the accommodation spaces - cabins and hospitals, messrooms, recreation rooms and offices - are 5 dB(A) tighter on ships of 10,000 GT and above. Work, navigation and service space limits are identical for both sizes. Paragraph 4.1.3 states that the 110 dB(A) limit assumes hearing protectors meeting chapter 7 are worn, and that personnel entering spaces above 85 dB(A) should be required to wear them.
retrieval_cards.why: Two traps in one: quoting a single column, and presenting 110 dB(A) as a permissible unprotected exposure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the principal noise exposure limits in chapter 5.
retrieval_cards.answer: The chapter 4 limits are designed so that Lex(24) does not exceed 80 dB(A). Above 85 dB(A) protection or time limits apply. No unprotected exposure to peaks above 135 dB(C). Even wearing protectors, not above 120 dB(A) or Leq(24) 105 dB(A). Daily exposure in spaces requiring protectors not to exceed four hours continuously or eight hours in total. Where a seafarer is over eight hours in a high-noise space, Leq(24) 80 dB(A) should not be exceeded, so at least a third of each 24 hours should be below 75 dB(A).
retrieval_cards.why: Chapter 4 caps the space; chapter 5 caps the person. Both are needed for a complete answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the acoustic insulation requirements of chapter 6.
retrieval_cards.answer: Weighted sound reduction index Rw to ISO 717-1: cabin to cabin 35; messrooms, recreation rooms, public spaces and entertainment areas to cabins and hospitals 45; corridor to cabin 30; cabin to cabin with a communicating door 30. Determined by laboratory test to ISO 10140-2; in the field the apparent index R'w should comply with a tolerance of up to 3 dB.
retrieval_cards.why: Four quick numbers that most answers omit entirely because they forget chapter 6 exists.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Noise Survey Report and what must it contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: A report made for each ship, comprising information on the noise levels in the various spaces on board and showing the reading at each specified measuring point, with the points marked on a general arrangement plan or accommodation drawings attached to the report or otherwise identified. It is in the format of appendix 1 and shall always be carried on board and be accessible for the crew.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the compliance document for this Code - the equivalent of a certificate - and 'accessible for the crew' is the part that is forgotten.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does section 7.1 say about the place of hearing protectors?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are supplied when the application of means for controlling sound at source does not reduce the noise level to that specified, and their provision shall NOT be considered to be a substitute for effective noise control.
retrieval_cards.why: It fixes the source-path-receiver hierarchy and stops the answer becoming a paragraph about ear defenders.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What warning notices does the Code require, and at what levels?
retrieval_cards.answer: Where noise in machinery or other spaces exceeds 85 dB(A), entrances shall carry a warning notice with symbol and supplementary sign in the ship's working language. The four bands are 80-85 dB(A) high noise, use hearing protectors; 85-110 dangerous noise, use mandatory; 110-115 mandatory and short stay only; above 115 mandatory and no stay longer than ten minutes.
retrieval_cards.why: The ten-minute limit above 115 dB(A) is exact, memorable and rarely quoted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Separate the health effects of noise from the performance effects.
retrieval_cards.answer: Health: noise-induced hearing loss originating in the cochlea - cumulative, painless and irreversible; acoustic trauma from peaks; disturbed sleep, impaired recuperation, fatigue, stress and cardiovascular strain. Performance: masking of speech communication and of audible alarms; degraded clear-headed decision-making in control stations, navigation and radio spaces; reduced alertness on the following watch; loss of diagnostic machinery sound cues when protectors are worn.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for both, and they are different arguments - one is a career, the other is tonight's watch.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: One limb, sixteen marks, but the stem prints a five-part checklist: the purpose and significance of the Code; its key provisions including maximum allowable noise limits, areas of application and measures to reduce noise; the impact of noise on crew health AND performance; and the compliance requirements for ship design, equipment and operational practices. Each is a separate block of marks.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks, undivided. Roughly: two for what the Code is and what made it mandatory, two for purpose and significance, three for application including the date criteria and exclusions, three for the limits table, two for exposure limits, two for reduction measures, one for health and performance, and three for compliance including the survey report, insulation indices and warning notices. Numbers are the discriminator throughout.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate has opened MSC.337(91) and the SOLAS regulation rather than writing generally about noise. The tell-tales are: the three application date criteria; the distinction between the mandatory chapter 4 limits and the recommendatory chapter 5 exposure limits; the fact that only accommodation limits vary with ship size; the 110 dB(A) figure being conditional on protectors being worn; the four Rw values; and the Noise Survey Report being carried on board and accessible to the crew.

Obtain MSC.338(91) separately for SOLAS regulation II-1/3-12, because the application DATES are in the regulation and not in the Code

Read chapter 7 for the protector performance requirement and the four warning-notice bands
Check for any amendment to the Code or to II-1/3-12 taking effect before December 2024

decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. SOLAS applies internationally and India is a Party. No Indian statute is load-bearing and the Merchant Shipping Act is not engaged.

Whether the 110 dB(A) machinery space limit permits unprotected exposure - it does not; it assumes protectors
Whether the limits vary with ship size - only the accommodation limits do
Whether existing ships are exempt - the 2009 to 2015 build window carries a real duty
Whether the application dates are in the Code or the SOLAS regulation - they are in the regulation

blocks.h: 1. What the NIR is, and what it replaced

blocks.p: The New Inspection Regime (NIR) of the Paris Memorandum of Understanding on Port State Control entered into force on 1 January 2011. It was implemented in parallel with the European Union's port State control Directive, so within the EU and EFTA member States it is law as well as an administrative arrangement.
It changed the regime in three fundamental ways:

ol: the Target Factor was replaced by the Ship Risk Profile. Under the old system a ship accumulated points and was targeted when it crossed a threshold. Under the NIR every ship carries a continuously recalculated risk profile placing it in one of three categories, and that profile determines how often it is inspected and what kind of inspection it gets;

the commitment changed from each member State inspecting 25% of individual ships calling at its ports to a shared commitment of the region as a whole to inspect ALL ships visiting its ports and anchorages. Coverage became collective rather than proportional, so a ship can no longer evade inspection by routing to a State that has met its quota;
the company responsible for ISM management is ranked by performance for the first time, and that ranking feeds the profile of every ship in its fleet.

blocks.p: The regional scope covers the European coastal States and the coastal States of the North Atlantic basin from North America to Europe. At this sitting the Memorandum records 27 maritime authorities as members, with the Russian Federation suspended until further notice.

The Ship Risk Profile classifies every ship as a High Risk Ship (HRS), a Standard Risk Ship (SRS) or a Low Risk Ship (LRS). A ship that is neither high nor low risk is a standard risk ship - so SRS is the residual category, not a middle band anyone qualifies for.
It is calculated from generic and historic parameters, using the record of inspections in the Paris MoU area over the last 36 months:

rows: Chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker, bulk carrier and passenger ship are the higher-risk types
Ships over 12 years old attract higher risk
Position on the White, Grey or Black List; and whether the flag has completed the IMO audit
The performance of the RO(s) that issued the ship's statutory certificates, itself listed as high, medium, low or very low
The ISM company's performance ranking - see below
Deficiencies recorded at inspections in the region over 36 months
Detentions in the region over 36 months

blocks.p: Two features of the calculation matter practically. It is recalculated daily, so a profile is never static. And because company performance is one of the inputs, the inspection result of one ship can immediately affect the profile of every other ship in the same ISM company - a genuinely new form of collective consequence.

In broad terms a Low Risk Ship is a newer ship of a non-high-risk type, on a White List flag whose administration has completed the IMO audit, classed and certified by a high-performing recognized organization, operated by a high-performing company, with few deficiencies and no detentions over the period. A High Risk Ship is at the opposite end - a higher-risk type, older, on a Black or Grey List flag, with a poorly performing RO or company and a record of deficiencies and detentions. The precise weightings are set out in Table 1 of Annex 7 of the Memorandum and a candidate is not expected to reproduce them.

This was the genuinely novel element of the NIR. The Paris MoU applies a formula taking into account the deficiencies and detentions of the whole of a company's fleet over the last 36 months, identified through the IMO company number, and compares it against the average of all vessels inspected in the Paris MoU region. The company is then ranked very low, low, medium or high. Any refusal of access imposed on one of its ships has a negative impact on the ranking.

The policy intent is to reach past the individual ship to the quality of management, and to remove the advantage previously enjoyed by an operator who kept one showpiece vessel in good order while running the rest of the fleet down.

blocks.h: 4. The selection scheme - windows and priorities

blocks.p: The profile determines the periodic inspection window measured from the last inspection in the Paris MoU region:

rows: May be inspected from month 5; must be inspected after month 6
May be inspected from month 10; must be inspected after month 12
May be inspected from month 24; must be inspected after month 36

blocks.p: The window restarts after any inspection. Priorities follow directly from it:

ul: Priority II - the window has opened. The ship may be selected for a periodic inspection.
Priority I - the window has passed. The ship will be selected and must be inspected.
before the window opens, and absent any factor below, the ship has no priority status and member States are not obliged to inspect it - though they may.

blocks.p: Two categories of event override the timetable entirely:

ul: an overriding factor makes the ship Priority I irrespective of the window - for example a collision, grounding or stranding, or a discharge of harmful substances, a suspension or withdrawal of class for safety reasons, or a report that the ship is operating dangerously;

an unexpected factor makes the ship Priority II irrespective of the window - for example failure to comply with the ETA reporting obligations, outstanding deficiencies, or reported cargo problems, particularly with noxious or dangerous cargo.

blocks.p: The NIR retained the three inspection types but changed who receives which:

ul: Initial inspection - verification of certificates and documents, the overall condition of the ship, and compliance with on-board conditions;
More detailed inspection - conducted where clear grounds are established that the condition of the ship, equipment or crew does not substantially meet the requirements;
Expanded inspection - a defined-scope examination of risk areas.

blocks.p: On a periodic inspection, an expanded inspection is mandatory for every High Risk Ship, and for every bulk carrier, chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker or passenger ship older than 12 years, whatever its profile. A Standard or Low Risk Ship that is not one of those types receives an initial inspection, escalating to a more detailed inspection if clear grounds appear. Any additional inspection - one triggered by an overriding or unexpected factor - is at least a more detailed inspection, and may be an expanded inspection at the PSCO's professional judgement where the ship is high risk or one of the listed types.
The NIR could not work without knowing where ships are, so it introduced a reporting chain:

ul: ETA72 - 72 hours before arrival, from ships eligible for an expanded inspection: all High Risk Ships and all bulk carriers, chemical tankers, gas carriers, oil tankers and passenger ships over 12 years old. The notification must include ship identification, planned duration of call, planned operations, planned surveys and substantial repair work, the date of the last expanded inspection in the region, and for tankers the hull configuration (single hull, single hull with segregated ballast tanks, or double hull), the condition of cargo and ballast tanks (full, empty or inerted) and the volume and type of cargo;
ETA24 - 24 hours before arrival, from all ships, at any time and regardless of the inspection window, or on leaving the previous port if the voyage is shorter than 24 hours;
ATA and ATD - the actual times of arrival and departure, a new obligation covering all ships calling at all ports and anchorages in the region.

blocks.p: The information is transferred by the relevant authority into THETIS, the NIR information database, fed through SafeSeaNet. THETIS is what makes a shared regional commitment possible: it calculates the profile, holds the inspection history and tells any member State which ships in its ports are due. Failure to report is itself an unexpected factor, and so exposes the ship to inspection regardless of its window - which is the enforcement mechanism for the reporting duty.
The NIR extended banning from certain ship types to all ship types and from Black List flags to Grey List flags as well:

ul: a ship flying a Black-listed flag is banned after the third detention in the last 36 months;
a ship flying a Grey-listed flag is banned after the third detention in the last 24 months;
after a second banning, any subsequent detention leads to a ban regardless of the flag's listing;
a ship that jumps detention or fails to sail to an agreed repair yard is banned.

blocks.p: The bans escalate and cannot be lifted before: 3 months after the first; 12 months after the second; 24 months after the third, with more stringent conditions to be met before the 24 months elapse; and the fourth is a permanent ban.

The flag lists themselves are published annually from a three-year rolling period of inspections and detentions, for flags with at least 30 inspections in the period. The lists operative at this examination are the 2023 performance lists, applied from 1 July 2024.

ol: Risk-proportionate effort. Inspection resource is directed at the ships most likely to be substandard instead of being spread evenly, which is a better use of a finite number of PSCOs.

A real reward for quality. A Low Risk Ship faces inspection every 24 to 36 months rather than annually - fewer interruptions, less off-hire risk, lower cost, and a commercial and chartering advantage.
No escape by routing. The shared regional commitment to inspect all ships removes the old possibility of avoiding attention by calling at States that had met their 25% quota.
It reaches the company, not just the ship. Company performance makes fleet-wide management quality consequential, which is where substandard operation actually originates.

Transparency and predictability. The profile can be calculated by the operator in advance through the Paris MoU ship risk calculator, so a company can see the effect of a deficiency before the next port.
Escalating, published banning. Persistent offenders are progressively excluded from the region entirely, and the reputational effect on flags and ROs drives improvement upstream.
Harmonisation. A common database, common criteria and common procedures across the member States reduce inconsistency between ports.

Collective punishment through company performance. A well-run ship's profile can deteriorate because of detentions on sister vessels it has no connection with, and a newly acquired ship inherits the company's record.

Parameters largely outside the operator's control. Flag and RO performance are set by the conduct of other owners entirely; a diligent operator on a Grey List flag is penalised for the flag's aggregate record.
Historic lag. The profile runs on a 36-month record, so genuine improvement takes years to show, while a single bad inspection registers immediately - the system is quicker to punish than to reward.
Age as a crude proxy. A well-maintained 13-year-old tanker is treated as higher risk than a neglected 11-year-old one.
Increased administrative burden from the ETA72, ETA24, ATA and ATD reporting obligations, falling largely on the master and the agent.
Frequency and duration for high-risk ships. A 5 to 6 month cycle of expanded inspections is a heavy operational and commercial burden, and expanded inspections are long.
Residual inconsistency. Deficiency coding and the exercise of professional judgement still vary between PSCOs and between States, so the same condition may be recorded differently in different ports.
Severe consequences of banning, which can effectively end a ship's commercial life in the region, with limited and slow appeal - an appeal does not suspend the detention.
Perverse incentives. The regime can encourage cosmetic preparation for inspection and the avoidance of honest self-reporting, rather than genuine improvement.

blocks.h: 10. How owners and managers should respond

blocks.p: The correct answer to this limb is not "comply with the regulations". It is a management programme aimed at the profile itself, and it has five parts.

1. Manage the profile as a measured asset. Calculate the Ship Risk Profile for every vessel using the Paris MoU calculator, know each ship's category and the date its window opens, and treat movement toward Low Risk as a board-level KPI alongside off-hire and fuel. Model the effect of a prospective detention before it happens.

2. Attack the controllable parameters, and choose the uncontrollable ones. Deficiencies and detentions are within the operator's control and are where effort pays. Flag and RO performance are not controllable day to day - but they are selectable. Flag choice and class choice become risk decisions with a measurable inspection consequence, and a White List flag whose administration has completed the IMO audit, with a high-performing RO, is worth paying for.

3. Protect company performance as a fleet-wide asset. Because one ship's detention degrades every sister ship's profile, the company must run fleet-wide corrective action: analyse every deficiency across the fleet, apply the lesson to all vessels rather than the one inspected, and use the ISM Code's own machinery - root cause analysis, corrective and preventive action, internal audit and management review - to close the loop. Due diligence on acquisition and on takeover of management must include the incoming ship's and company's PSC record.

4. Prepare the ship and the crew for the inspection they will actually get. Self-inspection regimes and mock PSC inspections built on the published deficiency and detention statistics; particular focus on the recurring detainable areas - ISM implementation, fire safety, life-saving appliances, MLC working and living conditions, and pollution prevention; and readiness for the expanded inspection scope if the ship is high risk or one of the five types over 12 years old. Familiarisation so that officers can demonstrate systems in operation rather than merely produce certificates. Concentrated Inspection Campaign topics are announced in advance and should be prepared for specifically.

5. Handle the process professionally when it happens. Rigorous compliance with the ETA72, ETA24, ATA and ATD obligations, since failure is itself an unexpected factor that invites inspection. A senior officer to accompany the PSCO throughout. Deficiencies rectified before departure wherever possible, and where not, agreement of a proper rectification plan - never a detention jumped and never a failure to proceed to an agreed repair yard, both of which trigger an immediate ban. Where a finding is genuinely unjustified, the company may appeal to the national PSC authority or through the flag State Administration, but the appeal does not lift the detention, so the operational answer is always to fix first and argue afterwards.

The strategic point to close on: under the NIR, inspection frequency has become a commercial variable that management can move. A company that gets its fleet into the Low Risk band buys itself fewer inspections, less disruption, a better chartering position and lower cost - so the response to the NIR is not defensive compliance but the recognition that quality management now has a directly measurable financial return.

Eight marks each, and they test different skills. Limb (a) is recall of a system: profile, categories, windows, priorities, inspection types, reporting, banning. Limb (b) is evaluation and application - pros, cons, and a management response - and it is the limb that separates candidates, because most will write four thin advantages and stop.

The examiner has printed three tasks in limb (b): pros, cons, and how would owners/managers respond. That third task carries real weight and needs a structured programme, not a sentence about maintaining the ship properly. The route gives it five headings so it cannot be skimped.

Note the printed stem is defective - it reads "Explain the salient features NIR", with a word apparently missing. It plainly means the salient features of the NIR, and the answer proceeds on that basis.

blocks.h: The one idea that unlocks limb (a)

blocks.p: Everything in the NIR flows from a single change: targeting moved from the ship's accumulated points to a continuously recalculated risk profile, and the profile decides both HOW OFTEN and WHAT KIND. Once that is stated, the windows, the priorities and the inspection types all follow as consequences rather than as separate facts to be memorised.

Add the second structural change - the shift from 25% of ships per State to a shared commitment to inspect all ships in the region - and you have explained why THETIS had to exist and why the ATA/ATD reporting obligations were introduced. A system that promises to inspect every ship must know where every ship is.

blocks.h: Company performance is the answer to 'what was NEW?'

blocks.p: If asked what was genuinely novel about the NIR, the answer is company performance. Risk profiles and inspection types existed in some form before; ranking the ISM company across its whole fleet by the IMO company number, over 36 months, against the regional average, did not.

It is also the hinge between the two limbs. In limb (a) it is a parameter. In limb (b) it is simultaneously the strongest pro - it reaches the management quality where substandard operation originates - and the sharpest con - a good ship is penalised for its sister vessels' record. A candidate who uses the same fact on both sides of the argument is doing exactly what "pros and cons" asks for.

ul: 1 January 2011 - the NIR enters into force.
5-6 / 10-12 / 24-36 months - the windows for High, Standard and Low Risk. If you remember nothing else numerical, remember these.
36 months - the inspection history period, and the company performance period.
12 years - the age threshold, both for risk and for the five ship types that always get an expanded inspection.
72 / 24 hours - ETA72 for expanded-inspection ships, ETA24 for all ships.
3 detentions in 36 months (Black) or 3 in 24 months (Grey) - the first ban.
3, 12, 24 months, then permanent - the ban durations.
30 inspections in the three-year period - the threshold for a flag to be listed at all.
25% - the OLD individual commitment the NIR replaced.

blocks.h: What was true in December 2024 specifically

blocks.p: The NIR is structurally unchanged since 2011, so this question is not a currency minefield. But three things are sitting-relative and are worth getting right:

ul: the White, Grey and Black Lists in force are the 2023 performance lists, approved by the Committee at its 57th meeting and applied from 1 July 2024. The lists change every July, so "the current list" always means the one adopted the previous summer;
the Russian Federation is suspended from the Paris MoU;

revisions to the Ship Risk Profile aligned with the recast EU Port State Control Directive - including revised methodologies for flag State and RO performance and the incorporation of environmental criteria into the profile - were in preparation and not operative. That Directive applies from 2027. Do not write that environmental parameters form part of the Ship Risk Profile; at this sitting they do not.

blocks.p: That last point is the future-instrument trap on this question, and it is exactly the kind of thing a candidate revising from current material in a later year would get wrong.

ul: Confusing the Ship Risk Profile with the old Target Factor. The NIR replaced one with the other.
Getting the windows wrong, or giving a single figure instead of a range. They are ranges: 5-6, 10-12, 24-36 months.
Reversing Priority I and Priority II. Priority I means the window has PASSED and the ship MUST be inspected; Priority II means it has OPENED and the ship MAY be.
Confusing overriding and unexpected factors. Overriding gives Priority I; unexpected gives Priority II.
Saying only High Risk Ships get expanded inspections. So do all bulk carriers, chemical tankers, gas carriers, oil tankers and passenger ships over 12 years old, whatever their profile.
Omitting company performance - the genuinely new parameter.
Omitting the banning regime, which is a third of limb (a)'s substance.
Answering limb (b) with pros and cons only, and never addressing how owners and managers should respond.
Treating flag and RO performance as things the operator cannot influence at all. They cannot be controlled, but they can be chosen.
Saying environmental criteria are part of the Ship Risk Profile. Not at this sitting.
Confusing the Paris MoU with the Tokyo MoU, which has its own regime and its own lists.

"Your ship was inspected four months ago in Rotterdam and is High Risk. Can it be inspected in Antwerp next week?" It has no priority status until month 5, so there is no obligation - but a member State may still inspect if it thinks fit, and an overriding or unexpected factor would make it Priority I or II immediately.
"A sister ship was detained. Does that affect your ship?" Yes - through company performance, and the profile is recalculated daily, so the effect can be immediate.

"You failed to send the ETA24. What follows?" Failure to comply with reporting obligations is an unexpected factor, making the ship Priority II irrespective of the window, and national penalties may also apply.
"What happens if you sail with an unrectified detention?" Jumping detention leads to a ban, as does failing to sail to an agreed repair yard.
"How long before a first ban can be lifted?" Three months - then 12, then 24 with more stringent conditions, then permanent.
"Does an appeal suspend a detention?" No. The company may appeal to the national authority or through the flag State, but the ship stays detained meanwhile.
When did the NIR come into force, and what did it replace? 1 January 2011; the Target Factor, and the 25% individual inspection commitment.
Name the Ship Risk Profile parameters. Type, age, flag performance and IMO audit, RO performance, company performance, deficiencies and detentions over 36 months.
What are the three categories and their windows? High 5-6 months, Standard 10-12, Low 24-36.
Distinguish Priority I from Priority II. Window passed, must inspect; window open, may inspect.
Give an overriding factor and an unexpected factor. Collision or a discharge of harmful substances; failure to report ETA, or outstanding deficiencies.
Which ships must have an expanded inspection? Every High Risk Ship, and every bulk carrier, chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker or passenger ship over 12 years old.
What reporting is required? ETA72 for expanded-inspection ships, ETA24 for all ships, plus ATA and ATD.
What is THETIS? The NIR information database, fed via SafeSeaNet, which holds the profiles and inspection history.
When is a ship banned? Third detention in 36 months on a black-listed flag, or in 24 months on a grey-listed flag; and after the second ban any further detention.
How is company performance calculated? From the fleet's deficiencies and detentions over 36 months by IMO company number, against the regional average, ranked very low to high.

blocks.p: For limb (a), five beats: PROFILE - WINDOW - PRIORITY - INSPECTION - BAN. Who you are, when you are due, whether you must be done, what kind you get, and what happens if you keep failing. Reporting and THETIS sit underneath as the plumbing that makes it work.
For the profile parameters: TYPE, AGE, FLAG, RO, COMPANY, DEFICIENCIES, DETENTIONS - the first two are what the ship is, the next three are who stands behind it, the last two are what it has done.
For limb (b)'s response programme: MEASURE it, CHOOSE what you can, PROTECT the fleet, PREPARE the ship, HANDLE the day.

blocks.p: Three limitations are recorded and they are worth understanding rather than skipping. No numerical weightings from Table 1 of Annex 7 are asserted anywhere in this answer. The table could not be retrieved from the Paris MoU's own published source by automated means, and a fabricated or half-remembered weighting would be worse than none - so the answer names every parameter and describes each one's qualitative effect, which is what a candidate can realistically deploy in any event. No per-flag listing or detention statistic is asserted, because the lists move every July. And the membership is stated as the organisation states it - 27 maritime authorities with the Russian Federation suspended - without asserting a count of active members, since suspension does not remove membership.

On currency, one instruction for a later editor: the revised Ship Risk Profile aligned to the recast EU Port State Control Directive, including environmental criteria, is a FUTURE instrument at this sitting and must not be presented as operative. That Directive applies from 2027. Anyone updating this object from current Paris MoU material would find the revised profile described as in force and would introduce future contamination into a December 2024 paper.

steps.title: What the NIR is, and what it replaced
points: entered into force 1 January 2011, in parallel with the EU port State control Directive
replaced the TARGET FACTOR with the SHIP RISK PROFILE
profile decides both HOW OFTEN and WHAT KIND of inspection
replaced each State inspecting 25% of individual ships with a SHARED regional commitment to inspect ALL ships
ranked the ISM company by performance for the first time
region: European coastal States and the North Atlantic basin from North America to Europe
at this sitting 27 maritime authorities, with the Russian Federation SUSPENDED

steps.title: The Ship Risk Profile
points: three categories - High Risk, Standard Risk, Low Risk; Standard is the RESIDUAL category
type of ship - chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker, bulk carrier, passenger ship are higher risk
age of ship - over 12 years attracts higher risk
flag performance - White, Grey or Black List, and whether the IMO audit is complete
recognized organization performance
company performance
number of deficiencies and number of detentions over 36 months in the region
RECALCULATED DAILY; a sister ship's inspection can immediately move this ship's profile
weightings are in Annex 7 Table 1 and are not expected to be reproduced

steps.title: Company performance - the new parameter
points: the genuinely novel element of the NIR
formula over the company's fleet deficiencies and detentions in the last 36 months
identified by IMO company number
compared against the average of all vessels inspected in the region
ranked very low, low, medium or high
any refusal of access of one of its ships damages the ranking
intent: reach past the ship to the quality of MANAGEMENT

steps.title: The selection scheme - windows and priorities
points: High Risk 5 to 6 months; Standard Risk 10 to 12 months; Low Risk 24 to 36 months
measured from the last inspection in the region; the span RESTARTS after any inspection
Priority II - window OPENED, ship MAY be selected
Priority I - window PASSED, ship WILL be selected and must be inspected
before the window opens and absent factors, NO priority status - inspection not obligatory
OVERRIDING factor - Priority I irrespective of the window; e.g. collision, discharge of harmful substances
UNEXPECTED factor - Priority II irrespective of the window; e.g. failure to report ETA, outstanding deficiencies, cargo problems

steps.title: Types of inspection
points: initial - certificates, documents, overall condition
more detailed - where CLEAR GROUNDS are established
expanded - defined-scope examination of risk areas
on a periodic inspection an EXPANDED inspection is mandatory for every High Risk Ship
and for every bulk carrier, chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker or passenger ship OVER 12 YEARS OLD, whatever its profile
other Standard and Low Risk Ships get an initial inspection, escalating on clear grounds
any ADDITIONAL inspection is at least a more detailed inspection

steps.title: Reporting obligations and THETIS
points: ETA72 - 72 hours, from ships eligible for expanded inspection
ETA72 content includes hull configuration, cargo and ballast tank condition, volume and type of cargo for tankers, and the date of the last expanded inspection
ETA24 - 24 hours, from ALL ships, at any time regardless of the window
ATA and ATD - actual times of arrival and departure, new under the NIR
THETIS is the NIR information database, fed through SafeSeaNet
FAILURE TO REPORT IS ITSELF AN UNEXPECTED FACTOR - that is the enforcement mechanism

steps.title: Refusal of access - banning
points: extended from certain ship types to ALL types, and from Black List flags to Grey List flags too
black-listed flag - banned after the THIRD detention in the last 36 months
grey-listed flag - banned after the THIRD detention in the last 24 months
after a SECOND ban, any subsequent detention leads to a ban regardless of flag listing
jumping detention, or failing to sail to an agreed repair yard, leads to a ban
lifting - 3 months, then 12 months, then 24 months with more stringent conditions, then PERMANENT
lists published annually from a three-year rolling period, minimum 30 inspections; the 2023 lists applied from 1 July 2024 are operative here

steps.title: Pros of the NIR
points: risk-proportionate use of finite inspection resource
real reward for quality - LRS inspected every 24 to 36 months instead of annually
no escape by routing, because the regional commitment covers all ships
reaches the COMPANY, where substandard operation originates
transparent and predictable - the operator can calculate the profile in advance
escalating published banning drives persistent offenders out, and pressures flags and ROs
harmonisation across member States through common criteria and a common database

steps.title: Cons of the NIR
points: collective punishment - a good ship penalised for sister vessels' detentions
flag and RO parameters largely outside the individual operator's control
36-month historic lag - quicker to punish than to reward
age over 12 years is a crude proxy for condition
administrative burden of ETA72, ETA24, ATA and ATD
5 to 6 month expanded-inspection cycle is heavy for high risk ships
residual inconsistency in deficiency coding and professional judgement between PSCOs
severe consequences of banning, with appeal that does not suspend detention
perverse incentives toward cosmetic preparation rather than genuine improvement

steps.title: How owners and managers should respond
points: MEASURE - calculate the profile for every ship, know the window dates, treat movement to Low Risk as a board-level KPI
CHOOSE - deficiencies and detentions are controllable; flag and RO are not controllable but ARE selectable, so flag and class choice become risk decisions
PROTECT THE FLEET - one detention degrades every sister ship, so corrective action must be fleet-wide, through ISM root cause analysis, CAPA, internal audit and management review
PROTECT THE FLEET - PSC record due diligence on acquisition and on taking over management
PREPARE - self-inspection and mock PSC built on published deficiency statistics; focus on ISM, fire safety, LSA, MLC and pollution prevention
PREPARE - readiness for expanded inspection scope; officers able to DEMONSTRATE systems, not just produce certificates; prepare for announced Concentrated Inspection Campaigns
HANDLE THE DAY - rigorous ETA/ATA/ATD reporting, since failure is an unexpected factor
HANDLE THE DAY - senior officer accompanies the PSCO; rectify before departure; never jump detention or miss the agreed repair yard
HANDLE THE DAY - appeal to the national authority or through the flag State, but the appeal does NOT lift the detention
STRATEGIC CLOSE - inspection frequency is now a commercial variable management can move

questions.understand_first: The NIR is one idea with a lot of consequences, and if you state the idea first the rest of limb (a) writes itself. The idea is that targeting stopped being a score a ship accumulates and became a PROFILE the ship carries - recalculated daily from what the ship is, who stands behind it, and what it has done over 36 months - and that profile decides both how often the ship is inspected and what kind of inspection it gets. The second structural change is just as important: the region stopped promising that each State would inspect a quarter of its callers and started promising that the region collectively would inspect them all. That is why THETIS and the arrival-reporting obligations had to exist at all. Limb (b) is where the marks are won or lost, because it asks three things - pros, cons, and what an owner should actually DO - and the third needs a management programme aimed at the profile itself, not a paragraph about maintaining the ship properly.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) in five beats: PROFILE - WINDOW - PRIORITY - INSPECTION - BAN (steps 2, 4, 4, 5, 7), with reporting and THETIS as the plumbing (6). Profile parameters: what the ship IS (type, age), who STANDS BEHIND it (flag, RO, company), what it has DONE (deficiencies, detentions). Windows: 5-6 / 10-12 / 24-36. Limb (b) response: MEASURE it, CHOOSE what you can, PROTECT the fleet, PREPARE the ship, HANDLE the day (10).

quick_revision.recall_15s: NIR = Paris MoU New Inspection Regime, in force 1 January 2011, alongside the EU PSC Directive. Replaced the Target Factor with the Ship Risk Profile, and replaced each State inspecting 25% of callers with a shared regional commitment to inspect ALL ships. Region: European coastal States and the North Atlantic basin; at this sitting 27 maritime authorities, Russian Federation SUSPENDED. SHIP RISK PROFILE - HRS / SRS / LRS (Standard is the residual). Parameters, over 36 months in the region: type (chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker, bulk carrier, passenger ship are higher risk), age (over 12 years), flag (White/Grey/Black List and IMO audit), RO performance, company performance, number of deficiencies, number of detentions. Recalculated DAILY - a sister ship's detention can move your profile at once. Weightings are in Annex 7 Table 1. COMPANY PERFORMANCE was the new element: fleet deficiencies and detentions over 36 months by IMO company number, against the regional average, ranked very low / low / medium / high; a ban on any ship damages it. WINDOWS from last inspection in the region: HRS 5-6 months, SRS 10-12, LRS 24-36; restarts after any inspection. Priority II = window OPENED, MAY be inspected. Priority I = window PASSED, MUST be inspected. Overriding factor (collision, discharge of harmful substances) → Priority I irrespective of window. Unexpected factor (failure to report ETA, outstanding deficiencies, cargo problems) → Priority II irrespective of window. INSPECTION TYPES: initial; more detailed on clear grounds; expanded. Expanded is mandatory for every HRS and for every bulk carrier, chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker or passenger ship over 12 years old. Any additional inspection is at least more detailed. REPORTING: ETA72 (expanded-inspection ships; includes tanker hull configuration, tank condition, cargo volume and type, date of last expanded inspection), ETA24 (ALL ships, always), ATA and ATD. Data goes to THETIS via SafeSeaNet. Failure to report is itself an unexpected factor. BANNING: Black flag - 3rd detention in 36 months; Grey flag - 3rd detention in 24 months; after a 2nd ban any detention bans regardless of flag; jumping detention or missing the agreed repair yard bans. Lifting: 3, 12, 24 months, then PERMANENT. Lists from a three-year rolling period, minimum 30 inspections; the 2023 lists applied from 1 July 2024 are operative here. PROS: risk-proportionate resource; real reward for quality; no escape by routing; reaches the company; transparent and predictable; escalating banning; harmonisation. CONS: collective punishment via company performance; flag and RO outside daily control; 36-month lag punishes faster than it rewards; age a crude proxy; reporting burden; heavy 5-6 month cycle for HRS; residual PSCO inconsistency; severe banning with appeal that does not suspend detention; cosmetic-compliance incentives. RESPONSE: MEASURE the profile as a KPI; CHOOSE flag and RO deliberately; PROTECT the fleet with fleet-wide CAPA and PSC due diligence on acquisition; PREPARE with self-inspection, mock PSC and CIC readiness; HANDLE the day with rigorous reporting, escorted inspection, rectification before departure, and never jumping detention.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: The Ship Risk Profile, set out in Table 1 of Annex 7 of the Paris MoU Memorandum, classifies every ship as High, Standard or Low Risk from the type and age of the ship, the performance of its flag, recognized organization and ISM company, and the number of deficiencies and detentions recorded in the region over the preceding 36 months; the resulting profile determines both the interval between inspections and the type of inspection the ship receives.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) with pros and cons only and never addressing the third printed task - how owners and managers should respond. That response must be a management programme aimed at the profile itself: measure it, choose flag and RO deliberately, protect the fleet through fleet-wide corrective action because company performance is shared, prepare for the inspection the ship will actually get, and handle the inspection day professionally. In limb (a) the recurring traps are reversing Priority I and Priority II, and saying only High Risk Ships receive expanded inspections when all bulk carriers, chemical tankers, gas carriers, oil tankers and passenger ships over 12 years old do as well. One currency trap: environmental criteria in the Ship Risk Profile belong to the recast EU Directive applying from 2027 and are NOT part of the regime at this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Paris MoU New Inspection Regime question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 What the NIR is and what it replaced. 2 The Ship Risk Profile. 3 Company performance. 4 Windows and priorities. 5 Inspection types. 6 Reporting and THETIS. 7 Banning. (b) 8 Pros. 9 Cons. 10 How owners and managers respond.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) has three printed tasks, and step 10 is the one most answers omit entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When did the NIR enter into force and what two things did it replace?
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 January 2011. It replaced the Target Factor with the Ship Risk Profile, and replaced each member State's commitment to inspect 25 per cent of individual ships calling at its ports with a shared commitment of the region as a whole to inspect all ships visiting its ports and anchorages.
retrieval_cards.why: The second change is what forced THETIS and the arrival-reporting obligations into existence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the Ship Risk Profile parameters.
retrieval_cards.answer: Type of ship; age of ship; performance of the flag, including its White, Grey or Black List position and whether the IMO audit is complete; performance of the recognized organization; performance of the company responsible for ISM management; number of deficiencies; and number of detentions - the last two over the preceding 36 months of inspections in the region.
retrieval_cards.why: Group them as what the ship IS, who STANDS BEHIND it, and what it has DONE.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the periodic inspection window for each risk category.
retrieval_cards.answer: High Risk Ship 5 to 6 months; Standard Risk Ship 10 to 12 months; Low Risk Ship 24 to 36 months, measured from the last inspection in the Paris MoU region. The span restarts after any inspection.
retrieval_cards.why: If only one set of numbers is remembered on this question, it should be these.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish Priority I from Priority II, and the two factors that override the window.
retrieval_cards.answer: Priority II - the window has OPENED and the ship MAY be selected. Priority I - the window has PASSED and the ship WILL be selected and must be inspected. An overriding factor, such as a collision or a discharge of harmful substances, makes a ship Priority I irrespective of the window. An unexpected factor, such as failure to comply with the ETA reporting obligations or outstanding deficiencies, makes it Priority II irrespective of the window.
retrieval_cards.why: Reversing these two pairs is the commonest error in limb (a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which ships must undergo an expanded inspection?
retrieval_cards.answer: On a periodic inspection: every High Risk Ship, AND every bulk carrier, chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker or passenger ship older than 12 years, whatever its risk profile. Other Standard and Low Risk Ships get an initial inspection, escalating to a more detailed inspection where clear grounds are established.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying only High Risk Ships get expanded inspections misses half the population.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is company performance calculated, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: By a formula taking the deficiencies and detentions of the company's whole fleet over the last 36 months, identified through the IMO company number, compared against the average of all vessels inspected in the Paris MoU region, producing a ranking of very low, low, medium or high. Any refusal of access imposed on one of its ships damages the ranking. It matters because it feeds every ship's profile, so one vessel's detention affects the whole fleet.
retrieval_cards.why: It was the genuinely new element of the NIR, and it is both the strongest pro and the sharpest con in limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What reporting obligations does the NIR impose, and what happens if you miss one?
retrieval_cards.answer: ETA72 - 72 hours before arrival from ships eligible for an expanded inspection, including for tankers the hull configuration, cargo and ballast tank condition, and volume and type of cargo. ETA24 - 24 hours before arrival from all ships, at any time regardless of the window. ATA and ATD - actual times of arrival and departure. Data goes to THETIS via SafeSeaNet. Failure to report is itself an unexpected factor, rendering the ship liable to inspection irrespective of the period since the last one.
retrieval_cards.why: The enforcement of the reporting duty is the reporting duty's own breach becoming a targeting trigger.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the banning criteria and the ban durations.
retrieval_cards.answer: A ship on a black-listed flag is banned after the third detention in the last 36 months; on a grey-listed flag, after the third detention in the last 24 months. After a second banning, any subsequent detention leads to a ban regardless of flag listing. Jumping detention or failing to sail to an agreed repair yard also leads to a ban. Bans cannot be lifted until 3 months after the first, 12 months after the second, 24 months after the third with more stringent conditions, and the fourth is permanent.
retrieval_cards.why: Two flags, two periods, four escalating durations - all exact and all examinable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which performance lists were operative at this sitting, and what must NOT be said about the Ship Risk Profile?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2023 performance lists, approved at the 57th Committee meeting and applied from 1 July 2024. Do NOT say that environmental criteria form part of the Ship Risk Profile - the revised profile aligned with the recast EU Port State Control Directive was still in preparation, and that Directive applies from 2027.
retrieval_cards.why: The lists change every July, and the environmental parameters are the future-instrument trap on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the five-part management response an owner should make to the NIR.
retrieval_cards.answer: MEASURE - calculate every ship's profile, know the window dates, treat movement toward Low Risk as a board-level KPI. CHOOSE - deficiencies and detentions are controllable, flag and RO are selectable, so flag and class choice become risk decisions. PROTECT THE FLEET - one detention degrades every sister ship, so corrective action must be fleet-wide, with PSC due diligence on acquisition. PREPARE - self-inspection and mock PSC built on published deficiency statistics, readiness for expanded scope, officers able to demonstrate systems. HANDLE THE DAY - rigorous reporting, escorted inspection, rectify before departure, never jump detention; appeal does not lift the detention.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the third printed task in limb (b) and the one that separates candidates.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Use company performance as both a pro and a con of the NIR.
retrieval_cards.answer: As a pro: it reaches past the individual ship to the quality of fleet management, which is where substandard operation actually originates, and removes the advantage of keeping one showpiece vessel in good order. As a con: it is collective punishment - a well-run ship's profile deteriorates because of detentions on sister vessels it has no connection with, and a newly acquired ship inherits the company's record.
retrieval_cards.why: Deploying one fact on both sides is exactly what a 'pros and cons' limb is asking for.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The 2023 Paris MoU performance lists, applied from 1 July 2024, are the White, Grey and Black Lists operative at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: The lists are recalculated from a three-year rolling period and reissued each July. A later editor working from current Paris MoU material would find a different set described as current. The sitting-date lists are the 2023 lists and must not be advanced.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The revised Ship Risk Profile aligned with the recast EU Port State Control Directive, including environmental criteria, was NOT operative at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT ADD ENVIRONMENTAL PARAMETERS TO THE PROFILE. The recast Directive applies from 2027 and the revised methodologies were in preparation at this sitting. Current Paris MoU material will describe them as adopted or in force; introducing them would be future contamination in a December 2024 paper.

reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. Guidance issued at the NIR's introduction lists the Russian Federation as a full member and describes its national system as feeding THETIS; that description is stale and must not be reinstated.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No numerical weighting from Table 1 of Annex 7 is asserted anywhere in this answer
reverify_before_publication.why: The weighting table could not be retrieved from the Paris MoU's own published source by automated means. A fabricated or half-remembered weighting would be worse than none. If the table is later obtained, weightings may be added - but they must come from the Memorandum itself and must be the version in force at December 2024.

reverify_before_publication.why: Suspension does not remove membership and the organisation's own presentation retains the suspended State in the list. Any figure for active members would be an inference rather than a record.

reverify_before_publication.why: The lists move annually and no per-flag position was verified for this sitting. If a figure is added later it must be the position as at or before December 2024.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs of eight marks each. (a) is recall of a system - what the NIR is, and its salient features: the Ship Risk Profile, the categories, the windows and priorities, the inspection types, the reporting obligations and the banning regime. (b) is evaluation and application, and it prints THREE tasks: the pros, the cons, and how ship owners and managers would respond or rise to the challenge.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks printed as 8 + 8. Limb (a) at eight marks needs the profile, the windows, the priorities, the inspection types and banning - breadth across the system rather than depth on one part. Limb (b) at eight marks splits roughly three for pros, two for cons and three for the response, because the response is a distinct printed task and carries the application marks.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate understands the NIR as a targeting system rather than as a list of inspection types - specifically that the profile decides both frequency and type, and that the regional commitment is collective. In limb (b), that the candidate can argue both ways on company performance and can set out a real management programme rather than generic advice to maintain the ship.
primary_source_plan: Establish the entry-into-force date and what the NIR replaced, from the organisation's own material and from the guidance issued at its introduction
Take the Ship Risk Profile parameters and the three categories from the Paris MoU's own procedures
Take the inspection windows, Priority I and II, and the overriding and unexpected factors from the Selection Scheme
Establish which inspection type each population receives, and the expanded-inspection trigger
Take the banning criteria and durations exactly - two flag colours, two periods, four escalating durations
ESTABLISH THE SITTING-DATE POSITION SEPARATELY: which performance lists were in application in December 2024, the membership position, and whether any revised profile was operative
Do NOT assert weighting numbers that cannot be retrieved from the Memorandum itself
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The NIR's structure is unchanged since 1 January 2011, so the bulk of limb (a) is stable. But the performance lists are reissued annually - the 2023 lists applied from 1 July 2024 are the ones operative here - the Russian Federation is suspended, and the revised Ship Risk Profile aligned to the recast EU Directive is a future instrument that current material will describe as adopted.

blocks.h: 1. What a classification society is, and its two distinct roles

blocks.p: A classification society is a technical body that publishes its own rules for the design, construction and survey of ships, assigns class to a ship that meets them, and maintains that class by periodical survey. Its origin is commercial: underwriters needed an independent judgement of the ship they were asked to insure. Everything else follows from that.
The distinction to make at the outset is that a society wears two hats:

ul: Classification - a private, contractual relationship with the owner, under the society's own rules. Class is not a government function, and the society does not act for the flag State when it assigns it.

Statutory work as a Recognized Organization - work delegated by the flag State under SOLAS regulation XI-1/1, in which the society surveys and certifies against the conventions on the Administration's behalf, subject to the Code for Recognized Organizations, resolutions MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65), mandatory since 1 January 2015. Here the society acts for the flag State - which retains responsibility.

blocks.p: Rules are not written from theory alone. They are built from service experience - damage and defect returns from the surveyed fleet; from casualty investigation; from research and direct calculation, including finite element analysis and fatigue assessment; and from technical committees drawing on owners, builders, makers and the society's own surveyors.

Because a ship trades worldwide and may change flag and society, divergence between societies is itself a hazard, so the members harmonise through IACS: Unified Requirements setting minimum standards each member must implement in its own rules, Unified Interpretations of convention text, Procedural Requirements, and jointly developed rules - most importantly the Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers.

blocks.h: 3. What the structural, mechanical and electrical rules cover

ul: Structural - scantlings of plating, stiffeners and primary members; longitudinal and local strength; fatigue life; corrosion additions and coating requirements; loading conditions and hull girder limits; and the enhanced close-up survey requirements for bulk carriers and tankers.

Mechanical - main propulsion and essential auxiliary machinery; shafting, propellers and gearing; boilers and pressure vessels; piping systems; steering gear; and the type approval of components and materials.

Electrical - generation, distribution and protection, including discrimination and short-circuit capability; essential and emergency services and their sources; cable installation; high-voltage systems; and equipment for hazardous areas.

Design - plan approval of structure, machinery and electrical installations against the rules, review of direct calculations, and type approval of equipment so that approved components need not be re-justified on each ship.

Construction - approval of materials and their manufacturers; certification of components; qualification of welding procedures and welders; witnessing of non-destructive testing and tank testing; survey during construction at the yard; and attendance at trials before the certificate is issued.

Maintenance in service - the periodical survey cycle that keeps class alive: annual, intermediate and renewal or special surveys, docking and in-water surveys, tailshaft and boiler surveys. Alternatives exist where they can be justified - continuous survey of hull or machinery spreading the items across the cycle, and an approved planned maintenance scheme allowing certain machinery items to be credited on the Chief Engineer's records. Where a defect is found the society may impose a condition of class or recommendation with a date for rectification, and class may be suspended or withdrawn if it is not met.

blocks.h: 5. Why compliance with class rules is now mentioned in SOLAS chapter II-1

blocks.p: The reference is SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1, "Structural, mechanical and electrical requirements for ships". It provides that ships shall be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society which is recognized by the Administration in accordance with the provisions of regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration which provide an equivalent level of safety.

The reason it is there is the gap it closes. SOLAS regulates subdivision and damage stability, machinery and electrical installations, fire protection and life-saving. But SOLAS never contained scantling rules - it does not state how thick a plate must be or what section modulus a hull girder must have. That had always been left to the classification societies as a matter of private contract between owner, society and underwriter. The consequence was that, as a matter of convention law, there was no requirement that a ship be built to any structural standard at all: class was commercially indispensable and legally optional.
Regulation II-1/3-1 converts that commercial arrangement into a statutory obligation, and four things follow:

ol: compliance with a recognized society's rules becomes a SOLAS requirement, enforceable by the flag State and inspectable by port State control;
the obligation runs to maintenance, not only to design and construction - so loss or suspension of class becomes a SOLAS non-compliance, not merely a commercial and insurance problem;
the society whose rules are relied on must be recognized under XI-1/1 and must operate under the RO Code, so the standard is not simply whatever any body chooses to publish; and
an Administration may still use its own national standards, but only where they provide an equivalent level of safety - preserving flag State sovereignty without opening a loophole.

blocks.p: This also completes the picture begun by goal-based standards: for bulk carriers and oil tankers the class rules relied on under II-1/3-1 must themselves have been verified at IMO as conforming to the goals and functional requirements under SOLAS II-1/3-10. SOLAS therefore requires compliance with class rules, and separately requires those rules to have been shown to be good enough.
(The printed question refers to "SOLAS ch.ll-1", using two lower-case letter L's. The reference intended is chapter II-1, and within it regulation 3-1.)

blocks.h: 6. The harmonized system, and where these surveys sit

blocks.p: Before harmonization each certificate carried its own survey dates, so a ship could be under survey almost continuously and a certificate could still expire while the ship was at sea. The Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, introduced by the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols and extended to MARPOL by MEPC.39(29) and to Annex VI by MEPC.132(53), aligns the certificates on a common five-year cycle with common anniversary dates and a common window of three months either side, so that surveys can be taken together in one attendance.

The guidance operative at this sitting is the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2023, resolution A.1186(33), adopted 6 December 2023 by the 33rd Assembly, which revokes A.1156(32). The system uses initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal and additional surveys, plus inspection of the outside of the ship's bottom.

blocks.h: 7. Annual versus periodical - the difference and the relevance

rows: Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate, Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate and the International Load Line Certificate
Only the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate and the Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificate
Within three months before or after each anniversary date

Safety Equipment: within three months before or after the second or third anniversary date, taking the place of one of the annual surveys. Safety Radio: within three months before or after each anniversary date

A certificate examination, a visual examination of a sufficient extent of the ship and its equipment, and certain tests to confirm the condition is being properly maintained - including that no unapproved modifications have been made

An inspection with tests when necessary of the equipment, to confirm it complies, is in satisfactory condition and is fit for the service intended, plus a check that certificates, record books, manuals and documentation are on board
A general confirmation that maintenance is being kept up
A more searching examination of the equipment itself

blocks.p: The relevance is that a five-year certificate would otherwise be an unverified assertion. The renewal survey establishes the ship's condition at the start of the cycle; the annual and periodical surveys are the checkpoints that keep that finding credible through it, and their common window is what allows them to be combined into a single attendance rather than surveying the ship piecemeal. The periodical survey exists because life-saving, fire-fighting and radio equipment deteriorates and is consumed in a way structure is not - so equipment gets a searching mid-cycle test, and the radio installation, on which distress communication depends absolutely, gets one every year.

The printed split is 10 + 6, and it must be respected. Limb (a) carries three tasks in ten marks - rule formation, implementation across the lifecycle, and the SOLAS reason - and the third is where the discrimination lies, so it deserves real space rather than a closing sentence. Limb (b) is six marks for a comparison: a table earns them faster than prose, and there is no credit for padding it out.

blocks.h: The heart of limb (a): what gap does II-1/3-1 close?

blocks.p: Most candidates will state that SOLAS II-1/3-1 requires compliance with class rules. Very few will say why that regulation had to exist, and that is the whole question. SOLAS has never contained scantling rules - it does not say how thick a plate must be. Structural standards were always a matter of private contract between owner, society and underwriter. So before II-1/3-1 a ship could in principle satisfy SOLAS while being built to no structural standard whatever, because class was commercially indispensable but legally optional. The regulation makes it legally compulsory, and extends the duty to maintenance - which is what turns loss of class from a commercial problem into a convention breach that port State control can act on.

blocks.h: The two-hats distinction is the other half of limb (a)

blocks.p: Classification is private and contractual; statutory certification as a Recognized Organization is delegated by the flag State under SOLAS XI-1/1 and governed by the RO Code. The same surveyor may do both on the same day, which is exactly why the distinction is worth stating. Note the resolution numbers carefully: the RO Code is MSC.349(92) with MEPC.237(65), mandatory from 1 January 2015. Getting the session number wrong here is an easy and visible slip.

blocks.h: Limb (b) has one fact almost nobody knows

blocks.p: The periodical survey is not simply "the survey that happens periodically". It attaches to only two certificates - Safety Equipment and Safety Radio - and it has a different frequency for each. For the Safety Equipment Certificate it falls at the second or third anniversary and replaces one of the annual surveys. For the Safety Radio Certificate it falls at every anniversary. A candidate who states both frequencies, and notes that the radio survey is annual because distress communication cannot be allowed to degrade unnoticed, has said something precise where most answers say something vague.

blocks.h: Why harmonization was needed at all

blocks.p: The point of HSSC is not the survey types; it is the alignment. Before it, certificates carried independent dates, so a ship might be under survey almost continuously and could still find a certificate expiring at sea. HSSC puts everything on a common five-year cycle with common anniversary dates and a common three-months-either-side window, so surveys can be combined into one attendance. If limb (b) explains the alignment rather than merely listing survey names, it has answered "relevance" as well as "difference".

blocks.h: Which edition of the Survey Guidelines - and why the answer here is NOT the one you will find today

blocks.p: The Survey Guidelines under the HSSC are re-adopted by the IMO Assembly roughly every two years, and each edition revokes the last. At the date of this examination the operative edition was resolution A.1186(33), the 2023 Guidelines, adopted 6 December 2023 by the 33rd Assembly and revoking A.1156(32).

Be careful with anything you read about this now. The 34th Assembly adopted A.1207(34), the 2025 Guidelines, on 3 December 2025 - a full two years after this paper was sat. Current material will tell you that A.1186(33) has been revoked and that citing it is a mistake. For this sitting that is exactly backwards. The substance is unaffected either way: the annual and periodical survey definitions, frequencies and certificate attachments are the same in both editions. Only the resolution number and date differ - which is what makes this the most dangerous kind of error, because an answer citing the wrong edition reads as entirely correct in every other respect.

The general rule this illustrates is worth more than the particular fact: an Assembly boundary is the adoption date, not the meeting month, and any instrument re-adopted on a cycle has to be pinned to your own sitting rather than to whatever is current when you revise.

ul: Treating classification and statutory certification as the same activity. One is private contract; the other is delegated flag State authority.
Saying SOLAS contains the structural rules. It does not - that is precisely why II-1/3-1 refers out to class rules.
Citing the RO Code as MSC.349(90). It is MSC.349(92), with MEPC.237(65).
Saying periodical surveys apply to all certificates. They apply only to the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificates.
Giving one frequency for the periodical survey. There are two, depending on the certificate.
Confusing the periodical survey with the intermediate survey. Both may fall at the second or third anniversary, but the intermediate attaches to different certificates and has a different scope.
Citing A.1207(34) as the Survey Guidelines for this sitting. That resolution was adopted on 3 December 2025, two years after this examination. The edition in force here is A.1186(33).
Forgetting that II-1/3-1 permits national standards of equivalent safety as an alternative to class rules.
Omitting the word maintained from II-1/3-1. It is the word that does the work.

blocks.p:
"Your ship loses class mid-voyage. Is that a SOLAS matter?" Yes. II-1/3-1 requires the ship to be maintained in compliance with the rules of a recognized society, so loss of class is a convention non-compliance and not merely a commercial and insurance issue.

"Must a ship be classed?" Strictly, it must comply with the requirements of a recognized society or with national standards of the Administration providing an equivalent level of safety. In practice class is universal, but the regulation offers the alternative and saying so shows the text has been read.

"When is your periodical survey due?" Ask which certificate. Safety Equipment: second or third anniversary, in place of an annual. Safety Radio: every anniversary.

"Who is responsible if the recognized organization gets it wrong?" The Administration. Recognition delegates the work, not the responsibility - which is the point of the RO Code.

ul: Which SOLAS regulation requires compliance with class rules, and where does the recognition come from? II-1/3-1, with recognition under XI-1/1.
What is the RO Code and when did it become mandatory? MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65), mandatory from 1 January 2015.
Name three IACS instrument types. Unified Requirements, Unified Interpretations, Procedural Requirements.
What is the harmonized survey window? Three months before or after the anniversary date.
Which certificates carry a periodical survey? Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Cargo Ship Safety Radio.
Which resolution carried the HSSC Survey Guidelines at this sitting? A.1186(33), adopted 6 December 2023, revoking A.1156(32).
What is a condition of class? A defect the society requires to be rectified by a stated date, failing which class may be suspended or withdrawn.
What alternatives to open survey exist for machinery? Continuous survey of machinery, and an approved planned maintenance scheme.
Which ships are covered by goal-based standards under II-1/3-10? Bulk carriers and oil tankers.

blocks.p: For limb (a), three lifecycle verbs: approve, witness, survey - plan approval at design, witnessing at construction, periodical survey in service (step 4). For the SOLAS reason, one sentence: SOLAS never had scantlings, so it borrowed class's (step 5). For limb (b), annual is a look, periodical is a test - and periodical belongs to only two certificates (step 7).

blocks.p: The survey material is primary: A.1186(33) annex sections 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4 are the source of the annual, intermediate and periodical definitions and frequencies. Two limitations are recorded. MIW holds no licensed IMO consolidated SOLAS edition, so the text of regulations II-1/3-1, II-1/3-10 and XI-1/1 rests on authoritative secondary reproduction - the substance is not in doubt but the wording is not from a licensed consolidated text. And no count of IACS member societies is asserted anywhere: membership has changed more than once in recent years and a wrong number is worse than no number. One error is worth recording because it recurs: the RO Code is MSC.349(92), not MSC.349(90) as some search summaries suggest.

Finally, the Survey Guidelines edition here is deliberately the 2023 one. A later editor working from current IMO material will find A.1186(33) described as revoked and may "correct" it to A.1207(34). That would introduce a resolution adopted two years after this examination. If a current note is wanted, add it separately and labelled as such.
