questions.understand_first: The odd thing about SOLAS is what it does not contain. It has a great deal to say about stability, fire and life-saving, and nothing at all about how thick a plate has to be. Hull strength was always the classification societies' private business with the owner and the underwriter. Regulation II-1/3-1 is SOLAS pointing at that private rule book and saying: that one, and you must keep to it for the ship's whole life - which is how losing class stopped being a commercial embarrassment and became a breach of the Convention. Limb (b) is a different kind of question: two survey names that sound interchangeable and are not. The periodical survey belongs to only two certificates and runs at two different frequencies, and knowing that is most of the six marks.
questions.memory_cue: Two hats first (1), then rules made from evidence (2) and what they cover (3). Lifecycle verbs: APPROVE at design, WITNESS at construction, SURVEY in service (4). The SOLAS reason is one sentence: SOLAS never had scantlings, so it borrowed class's (5). Then alignment, not survey names (6). Limb (b) closes on annual is a LOOK, periodical is a TEST - and periodical belongs to only two certificates (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Two hats. Classification is a private, contractual relationship with the owner under the society's own rules - not a government function. Statutory work as a Recognized Organization is delegated by the flag State under SOLAS XI-1/1, governed by the RO Code, MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65), mandatory since 1 January 2015; the Administration retains responsibility. Rules are made from service experience and defect returns, casualty investigation, research and direct calculation including FEA and fatigue assessment, and technical committees - harmonised across societies through IACS: Unified Requirements, Unified Interpretations, Procedural Requirements, and the Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers. They cover structural (scantlings, hull girder strength, fatigue, corrosion additions, close-up survey), mechanical (propulsion, shafting, boilers, piping, steering gear, type approval) and electrical (generation, distribution and protection, essential and emergency services, high voltage, hazardous areas). Implementation: plan approval and type approval at design; material and welder qualification, NDT and tank testing witnessed, survey during construction and trials; in service the survey cycle, with continuous survey and an approved planned maintenance scheme as alternatives, and a condition of class where a defect is found - class may be suspended or withdrawn. Why it is in SOLAS: regulation II-1/3-1 requires ships to be designed, constructed AND maintained to the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a society recognized under XI-1/1, or to national standards of equivalent safety. It exists because SOLAS never contained scantling rules - structural standards were private contract, so class was commercially indispensable but legally optional. Now compliance is a convention requirement, it runs to maintenance so loss of class is a SOLAS non-compliance inspectable by port State control, and under II-1/3-10 the rules relied on must themselves be verified as conforming to goal-based standards. (b) HSSC, from the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols and extended by MEPC.39(29) and MEPC.132(53), aligns certificates on a common five-year cycle, common anniversary dates and a common three months either side window so surveys combine into one attendance. Guidelines at this sitting: A.1186(33), HSSC 2023, adopted 6 December 2023, revoking A.1156(32). Annual survey - Safety Equipment, Safety Construction and Load Line certificates; every anniversary, three months either side; certificate examination plus visual examination with certain tests, confirming maintenance and no unapproved modifications. Periodical survey - ONLY Safety Equipment and Safety Radio; Equipment at the second or third anniversary in place of an annual, Radio at EVERY anniversary; an inspection with tests when necessary of the equipment plus a documentation check. Relevance: a five-year certificate would otherwise be an unverified assertion - the renewal survey sets the condition, the annual and periodical surveys keep it credible, and equipment is tested harder because it is consumed in a way structure is not.

quick_revision.major_trap: Failing to explain WHY II-1/3-1 exists - that SOLAS never contained scantling rules, so structural standards were private contract until this regulation made them statutory - or stating a single frequency for the periodical survey when it differs between the Safety Equipment and Safety Radio certificates. There is a third trap peculiar to this sitting: the edition of the HSSC Survey Guidelines. The edition in force here is A.1186(33) of 6 December 2023. A.1207(34) was adopted on 3 December 2025, two years AFTER this examination, and current material will wrongly tell you that citing A.1186(33) is out of date. retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a class society is and its two roles. 2 How rules are made. 3 What the rules cover. 4 Implementation through the ship's life. 5 Why compliance is now in SOLAS II-1. 6 The harmonized system. 7 Annual versus periodical.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 5 are the ten-mark limb (a); steps 6 and 7 are the six-mark limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the two roles a classification society performs.
retrieval_cards.answer: Classification is a private, contractual relationship with the owner under the society's own rules. Statutory certification as a Recognized Organization is work delegated by the flag State under SOLAS XI-1/1, governed by the RO Code, in which the society acts for the Administration - which retains responsibility.
retrieval_cards.why: The same surveyor may do both on the same day, which is exactly why the distinction has to be stated.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1 require?
retrieval_cards.answer: That ships be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society recognized by the Administration under regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration providing an equivalent level of safety.
retrieval_cards.why: Note all three verbs - designed, constructed AND maintained. The third is what makes loss of class a convention breach.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why did SOLAS need regulation II-1/3-1 at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because SOLAS never contained scantling rules. Structural standards were a matter of private contract between owner, society and underwriter, so class was commercially indispensable but legally optional. II-1/3-1 makes compliance a convention requirement, extending to maintenance.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the discriminating point of the whole question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the RO Code and when did it become mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Code for Recognized Organizations, adopted by resolutions MSC.349(92) and MEPC.237(65), mandatory from 1 January 2015 under SOLAS, MARPOL and the Load Line Protocol.
retrieval_cards.why: It is MSC.349(92), not (90) - an easy and visible slip.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When is an annual survey due, and what is its scope?
retrieval_cards.answer: Within three months before or after each anniversary date of the certificate. It consists of a certificate examination, a visual examination of a sufficient extent of the ship and its equipment and certain tests, confirming the condition is being maintained and that no unapproved modifications have been made.
retrieval_cards.why: The 'no unapproved modifications' limb is the part most candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which certificates carry a periodical survey, and when is it due?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate and the Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificate. For Safety Equipment, within three months before or after the second or third anniversary date, taking the place of one of the annual surveys. For Safety Radio, within three months before or after each anniversary date.
retrieval_cards.why: Two certificates, two different frequencies - the fact most answers miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a periodical survey differ in character from an annual survey?
retrieval_cards.answer: An annual survey is largely a visual confirmation that maintenance is being kept up. A periodical survey is an inspection with tests when necessary of the equipment itself, confirming it complies, is in satisfactory condition and is fit for the intended service, together with a documentation check.
retrieval_cards.why: Annual is a look; periodical is a test. Equipment is consumed in a way structure is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which resolution carried the HSSC Survey Guidelines at this sitting - and why must you be careful looking this up now?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1186(33), Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, 2023, adopted 6 December 2023 by the 33rd Assembly, revoking A.1156(32). Be careful because A.1207(34) was adopted on 3 December 2025 - two years AFTER this examination - and current material will tell you A.1186(33) is revoked. For this sitting it is the correct citation.
retrieval_cards.why: The survey substance is identical in both editions, so a wrong citation yields an answer that reads as entirely correct. That is what makes it dangerous.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship loses class mid-voyage. Is that only a commercial problem?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. SOLAS II-1/3-1 requires the ship to be maintained in compliance with a recognized society's rules, so loss of class is a convention non-compliance, enforceable by the flag State and inspectable by port State control.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the practical consequence of the word 'maintained' in the regulation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the periodical survey from the intermediate survey.
retrieval_cards.answer: Both may fall at the second or third anniversary and both may take the place of an annual survey, but they attach to different certificates and have different scopes. The intermediate survey is directed at the ship's condition and structure under the Safety Construction and Load Line certificates; the periodical survey is an equipment inspection with tests under the Safety Equipment and Safety Radio certificates.
retrieval_cards.why: The coincident timing is exactly why they get merged in weak answers.

blocks.h: 1. What root cause analysis is, and why it is required

blocks.p: Root cause analysis (RCA) is a structured method of investigating an event in order to identify the underlying organisational and systemic reasons it occurred, so that corrective action can be taken which prevents recurrence - as distinct from identifying the immediate technical or human failure and stopping there.

The regulatory footing matters, because it explains the method's whole orientation. The Casualty Investigation Code, adopted by resolution MSC.255(84) in 2008 and made mandatory as to Parts I and II by SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 with effect from 1 January 2010, requires a marine safety investigation into every very serious marine casualty - one involving the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment. Critically, the Code provides that a marine safety investigation is conducted to prevent future casualties, and is separate and distinct from, and must not seek to apportion, blame or determine liability.

That separation is the licence for root cause analysis. An investigation that may apportion blame will meet defensive witnesses and will stop at the individual; only an investigation insulated from liability can follow the chain back into the design office, the manning decision and the procedure that was written badly.

The same discipline is required of the company internally by the ISM Code regulation 9: the safety management system must include procedures ensuring that non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences are reported, investigated and analysed with the objective of improving safety and pollution prevention, and the Company must establish procedures for the implementation of corrective action.

blocks.h: 2. The principles of root cause analysis

ol: Seek causes, not culprits. The purpose is prevention, not attribution. Blame stops the enquiry at the last person to touch the system.
Every accident has multiple causes. A single-cause finding is almost always an incomplete investigation.
Go beyond the immediate. Keep asking why until the answer reaches something the organisation controls - a decision, a procedure, a resource, a design.
Base findings on evidence. Physical evidence, records, data and interviews - and gather perishable evidence first.
Establish the sequence before the explanation. Build the timeline of what happened before attempting why.
Distinguish causal factors from contributing conditions. Test each candidate by asking: if this had not existed, would the event have been prevented or mitigated?
A root cause must be actionable. "Human error" is not a root cause because nothing can be done to it; "the procedure did not cover this configuration" is, because it can be rewritten.
Corrective action must address the level at which the cause sits. A systemic cause cannot be corrected by retraining one individual.
Close the loop. Verify that corrective action was implemented and that it worked, and feed the finding back across the fleet.
Just culture. Honest reporting must be safe, or the raw material of the analysis never arrives. The line is drawn at recklessness and wilful violation, not at error.

blocks.h: 3. The steps of a root cause analysis

ol: Recognise and report the event - accident, near miss, non-conformity or hazardous occurrence. Immediate actions to make the situation safe come first.

Preserve and collect evidence. Physical evidence, VDR and alarm data, engine and bridge logs, planned maintenance and defect records, work and rest hours, permits to work, risk assessments, procedures and drawings, and witness accounts taken early while memory is fresh.
Establish the sequence of events. Build a timeline, or an event and causal factor chart, of what actually happened - what, where, when, in what order.
Identify the causal factors. At each step ask what conditions or actions allowed the event to progress, and test each by removal - if it were absent, would the outcome change?

Analyse to root cause. Apply a technique - the five whys, a cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram, fault tree analysis, barrier analysis - to drive each causal factor back to the organisational decision, condition or omission behind it.
Identify the failed defences. Ask which barriers should have stopped this and why each did not - absent, inadequate, bypassed or not maintained.
Develop corrective and preventive action. Corrective action fixes this occurrence; preventive action removes the condition that produced it. Assign an owner and a date to each.
Implement and verify. Confirm the action was taken, and then confirm it was effective - these are two different checks and the second is usually the one omitted.
Communicate and share the lesson - across the fleet, not just to the ship involved - and feed it into risk assessments, procedures, training, design standards and the next management review.

blocks.p: Note that steps 8 and 9 mirror the ISM Code's own machinery of corrective action, internal audit and management review, and the same plan - implement - monitor - evaluate loop that governs the SEEMP. It is one management discipline applied to different subject matter.

blocks.p: Worked example. A main engine lubricating oil pump fails and the engine is damaged.

ul: Proximate cause - the pump bearing seized through loss of lubrication, and the standby pump did not cut in.
Why? The standby pump's auto-start had been isolated during an earlier repair and not restored.
Why? There was no permit-to-work close-out check confirming that isolations were removed.
Why? The permit system's close-out step was not enforced because the form did not require a signature against each isolation.
Why? The form was adopted unchanged from a generic package and was never reviewed against the ship's own systems.
Root cause - the company's safety management system adopted generic procedural documents without ship-specific review, so a defence that existed on paper did not exist in practice.

blocks.p: Correcting only the proximate cause replaces a bearing. Correcting the root cause revises the permit system across the fleet - and in doing so removes a hazard that would equally have produced a different accident somewhere else.

A note on terminology, which is worth a mark: the phrase proximate cause is also a term of art in marine insurance, where it means the dominant or effective cause of a loss for the purpose of deciding whether the loss is covered by a peril insured against. In the casualty-investigation sense used here it means the immediate cause in the causal chain. The two usages are related but are not the same test, and should not be conflated.

Early models were sequential - the domino model, in which an accident is the last of a line of falling dominoes and removing one stops the sequence. They usefully introduced the idea of a chain, but they encouraged the search for a single removable cause, and they place that cause close to the accident.

The model that introduced the terms in the question is the organisational accident model developed by James Reason, commonly represented as defences in depth or the "Swiss cheese" model. In it, a complex system is protected by successive layers of defence - design features, engineered safeguards, procedures, supervision, training, alarms and the crew themselves. Each layer has weaknesses, represented as holes. The holes are not static: they open, close and move. An accident occurs only when the holes in every layer momentarily line up, allowing a hazard to pass through all the defences to the loss.
Within that model, failures divide into two kinds by where they originate and how quickly their effect appears.

Active failures are unsafe acts committed by people in direct contact with the system - the sharp end - whose effects are felt almost immediately. They are the errors and violations of operators: the watchkeeper, the engineer, the pilot, the rating.
They are usefully classified as:

ul: Slips and lapses - skill-based failures of execution or memory, where the intention was correct but the action was not. Example: an engineer intends to open the correct valve and, working from habit on a familiar manifold, opens the adjacent one; or a duty officer omits a step in a checklist he has completed a thousand times.

Mistakes - failures of planning, where the action went as intended but the intention was wrong. Rule-based, where a good rule is misapplied, or knowledge-based, where the situation is novel. Example: an officer misdiagnoses a fluctuating exhaust temperature as an instrumentation fault and continues, when the correct diagnosis was a burning exhaust valve.

Violations - deliberate departures from a rule or procedure. Routine violations become the normal way the job is done because the procedure is cumbersome; situational violations arise because the procedure cannot be complied with in the circumstances, for instance where manning or time does not allow it; exceptional violations occur in unusual situations. Example: a permit to work signed retrospectively because the routine has always been to work first and paper afterwards.

blocks.p: Two things must be said about active failures. They are the most visible element of any accident and the easiest to identify - which is precisely why investigations stop at them. And a routine violation is diagnostic of a latent condition: if a whole department is habitually departing from a procedure, the procedure, the manning or the time allowed is the real finding.

Latent failures - or latent conditions - are the delayed consequences of decisions taken by designers, builders, procedure writers, regulators and senior management. They are present in the system before the accident, often for years, lying dormant and harmless until they combine with local circumstances and active failures to produce a loss. Reason described them as resident pathogens: present in the body of the system, doing nothing until conditions favour them.
They have two kinds of effect - they create error-provoking conditions in the workplace, and they create long-lasting holes or weaknesses in the defences.

rows: Two dissimilar valves, identical in appearance, mounted adjacent with unclear labelling - which makes the slip in section 6 almost inevitable eventually

A checklist adopted unchanged from another ship class and never revised for this installation
Minimum safe manning applied to a workload it does not support; deferred maintenance under budget pressure
Fatigue arising from a manning level that makes the rest-hour regime unachievable in a short-sea trade
Familiarisation that certifies attendance rather than capability
An officer who has never operated the system in the abnormal mode in which it eventually fails
PMS intervals set generically; defect backlog tolerated

Production pressure over safety; reporting discouraged; near misses not investigated
A vessel where near-miss reporting has fallen to zero, which is evidence of suppression, not of safety

blocks.h: 8. Why the distinction matters, and how the two combine

blocks.p: The distinction is not academic; it decides what an organisation does after an accident.

ul: Active failures are hard to prevent and easy to blame. People will always make errors; error is a normal feature of competent human performance, not a defect in it. Disciplining the individual who made the slip changes nothing, because the next person in the same conditions will make the same slip.

Latent conditions are the manageable target. They can be identified proactively - by audit, inspection, risk assessment, near-miss analysis and trend data - before any accident, because they are present in the system all along. This is the entire justification for the ISM Code's audit and review machinery.

The accident needs both. A latent condition alone usually produces nothing; an active failure alone is usually caught by a defence. The loss occurs when an active failure meets a set of latent conditions that have opened the holes in every layer at once - which is why apparently trivial errors sometimes produce catastrophes and identical errors usually produce nothing at all.

Chance is real, and outcome is a poor measure of behaviour. Because the alignment of the holes is partly a matter of timing, the same unsafe act may on one day be a near miss and on another a total loss. That is why near misses must be investigated with the same rigour as accidents - they are free evidence about the state of the defences, delivered without the cost.

Blame destroys the data. If reporting an error is punished, the reports stop, the latent conditions become invisible, and the organisation loses the only early warning it has. Hence just culture: distinguish honest error, which is reported and learned from, from recklessness and wilful violation, which are not excused.

blocks.p: The practical conclusion, and the right note to end on: root cause analysis is the technique that converts an active failure into information about latent conditions. The proximate cause tells you what happened at the sharp end; the root cause tells you which hole in which defence let it through, and that is the only finding a company can actually act on across a fleet.

Eight marks each, and the two limbs are closely related but must not be merged. Limb (a) is method - principles, steps, and one clean distinction. Limb (b) is theory applied - it names a concept from accident causation models and asks for discussion with suitable examples.

The single easiest way to lift this answer above the average is to join the two limbs at the end: root cause analysis is the technique by which an active failure is converted into information about latent conditions. Most candidates answer the two limbs as though they were unrelated questions on the same paper. They are the same idea from two directions.

Note also that limb (b) prints "giving suitable examples". Examples are not decoration here; they are part of the printed instruction, and an answer that defines active and latent failures abstractly has left marks on the table.
Get these two sentences right and limb (b) has a spine:

ul: Active failures are unsafe acts committed by people in direct contact with the system, whose effects are felt almost immediately.

Latent failures are the delayed consequences of decisions taken by designers, procedure writers and management, which lie dormant in the system until they combine with local triggering conditions and active failures to produce a loss.

blocks.p: The two discriminators buried in those definitions are WHO (sharp end versus blunt end) and WHEN (immediate versus delayed, often by years). If time is short, say those two things and give one example of each.

blocks.h: Reason's model - attribute it, and use the right image

blocks.p: The terms come from the organisational accident model developed by James Reason, usually drawn as defences in depth or the Swiss cheese model. Naming the model and its author is worth a mark and takes four words.

But use the image accurately. The point of the model is not that there are holes; it is that the holes move, and that an accident happens only when they line up through every layer at once. That is what explains the two things candidates find puzzling: why a trivial slip occasionally causes a catastrophe, and why the same slip usually causes nothing. It also produces the strongest single argument in limb (b) - since alignment is partly a matter of timing, outcome is a poor measure of behaviour, and near misses therefore deserve the same investigation as accidents.

If a diagram is drawn, keep it small and label it: successive slices representing design, engineered safeguards, procedures, supervision and the operator; holes in each; one trajectory passing through all of them. Do not spend five minutes on it.

blocks.h: The regulatory hook that most answers miss

blocks.p: This looks like a pure management-theory question, and answers that treat it that way score respectably and no better. The hook that lifts it is the Casualty Investigation Code, MSC.255(84) of 2008, Parts I and II made mandatory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 with effect from 1 January 2010, which requires a safety investigation into every very serious marine casualty - total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment.

The provision that actually matters for this question is the Code's statement that a marine safety investigation is conducted to prevent future casualties and is separate and distinct from, and must not seek to apportion, blame or determine liability. That is not incidental - it is the reason root cause analysis is possible at all. An investigation that can attribute liability meets defensive witnesses and stops at the individual. Making that connection explicitly is the mark of a management-level answer.

The internal counterpart is ISM Code regulation 9: non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences reported, investigated and analysed with the objective of improving safety, and corrective action procedures established. Together these give you the external duty and the internal duty.

blocks.h: Do not say 'human error' is a root cause

blocks.p: This is the most valuable single point in limb (a). "Human error" is a proximate cause, never a root cause, because nothing can be done to it - you cannot issue a corrective action against human nature. The test of a root cause is that it is actionable: it names something the organisation controls and could change. "The officer misread the gauge" is not actionable. "The gauge was unlabelled and identical to the adjacent one" is.

The same test disposes of the other weak findings that appear in real investigation reports - "lack of situational awareness", "failure to follow procedure", "complacency". Each is a restatement of what happened, not an explanation of why it was allowed to happen.
The worked example in the model answer runs a five-whys chain from a seized bearing to a generic procedure adopted without ship-specific review. Two cautions worth carrying:

ul: Five is not a rule. Stop when you reach something the organisation controls and can change, whether that takes three steps or seven.

A single chain is a simplification. Real accidents have several converging chains, which is why the fishbone diagram and fault tree analysis exist - they allow multiple branches where the five whys allows one. Saying this shows you understand the technique's limits rather than reciting it.
Defining active and latent failures without examples, when the stem prints "giving suitable examples".
Treating latent as meaning "hidden equipment defect". A latent condition is a decision and its consequences - a procedure, a manning level, a design choice - not a dormant mechanical fault.
Saying "human error" is a root cause.
Confusing proximate cause in casualty investigation with proximate cause in marine insurance. Note the difference expressly; it earns a mark.
Presenting the Swiss cheese holes as fixed. They move, and that is the point of the model.
Giving the steps of RCA but omitting verification of effectiveness, which is the step organisations actually omit.
Omitting the fleet-wide sharing of the lesson - the finding is worthless if it stays on one ship.
Not naming a technique. The five whys, fishbone, fault tree and barrier analysis are cheap marks.
Attributing the Swiss cheese model to IMO. It is Reason's model, adopted into IMO guidance.
Ignoring near misses, which is where the model's practical payoff lies.

"Give me a latent failure on your last ship." Have one ready that is a decision, not a defect - a generic checklist, a PMS interval never revised, a manning level that made the rest-hour regime unachievable.
"Whose fault was the accident?" Resist. The Casualty Investigation Code separates safety investigation from blame and liability precisely so that the question is not asked in these terms.

"Why investigate a near miss when nothing happened?" Because whether an event becomes a loss depends partly on the chance alignment of the holes, so a near miss is evidence about the state of the defences delivered without the cost.

"Your crew routinely bypasses a procedure. Is that a violation or a latent condition?" Both - and the routine violation is diagnostic of the latent condition. If everyone departs from the procedure, the procedure, the manning or the time allowed is the finding.

"Which is easier to eliminate, active or latent?" Latent, because they are present in the system all along and can be found proactively by audit and risk assessment. Active failures are a permanent feature of human performance.
Define active and latent failure. Unsafe acts at the sharp end with immediate effect; delayed consequences of blunt-end decisions, dormant until triggered.
Who developed the model? James Reason - the organisational accident or Swiss cheese model.
Name three RCA techniques. Five whys, cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram, fault tree analysis - and barrier analysis.
Distinguish proximate from root cause. Immediate event in the chain versus the underlying organisational reason it could occur.
Which resolution is the Casualty Investigation Code, and what made it mandatory? MSC.255(84), 2008; SOLAS XI-1/6 from 1 January 2010, for Parts I and II.
What is a very serious marine casualty? One involving total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment.
Which ISM Code regulation deals with accidents and corrective action? Regulation 9.
Classify errors. Slips and lapses (skill-based), mistakes (rule- and knowledge-based), and violations (routine, situational, exceptional).
Why must an investigation be separate from blame? Because attribution produces defensive witnesses and stops the enquiry at the individual, leaving the latent conditions in place.

blocks.p: For limb (a), the RCA sequence in five beats: COLLECT - SEQUENCE - CAUSAL FACTORS - ROOT - CORRECT AND VERIFY. Gather the evidence, build the timeline, find what mattered, drive each one back to something the organisation controls, then fix it and prove the fix worked.
For proximate versus root: SHARP END versus BLUNT END, and NOW versus YEARS AGO. Correcting the proximate cause restores the situation; correcting the root cause prevents the recurrence.

For limb (b): ACTIVE = who was there, felt at once. LATENT = who decided, felt much later. And the closing line that joins the limbs - RCA is how an active failure becomes information about latent conditions.

blocks.p: This is the least date-sensitive question on the paper, and that is itself worth knowing when planning revision time. The Casualty Investigation Code is unamended at this sitting, the ISM Code provisions relied on are long settled, and the accident causation material is established literature rather than a regulatory instrument that moves.

Four limitations are recorded. MIW holds no licensed copy of the Casualty Investigation Code or the ISM Code, so their provisions rest on the adopting resolution and authoritative reproduction, and nothing is quoted verbatim at length. The active/latent distinction and the defences-in-depth model are attributed to Reason and to the human-factors literature; they are widely reproduced in IMO and flag State guidance but are not themselves the text of an IMO instrument, and the answer does not present them as one. No casualty statistic is asserted - figures for the proportion of casualties attributed to human factors circulate widely, vary by study and period, and none was verified for this sitting, so the argument is made without leaning on a number. And the RCA techniques are presented as established industry techniques, not as convention requirements, because that is what they are.

questions.understand_first: Two limbs that look separate and are actually the same idea approached from opposite ends. Limb (a) asks how you investigate backwards from an event to something the organisation can change. Limb (b) asks about the model that explains why events happen at all - Reason's organisational accident model, in which an accident requires an unsafe act at the sharp end to coincide with weaknesses that management put into the system long before. Put them together and the answer has a spine: root cause analysis is precisely the technique by which an active failure is converted into information about latent conditions. The regulatory hook that most candidates miss is the Casualty Investigation Code's insistence that a safety investigation is separate from blame and liability - that separation is not a nicety, it is the thing that makes root cause analysis possible, because an investigation that can attribute liability will never get past the last person to touch the system.

Close on the join: RCA turns an active failure into information about latent conditions (8).

quick_revision.major_trap: Offering 'human error' as a root cause. It is a proximate cause and never a root cause, because nothing can be done to it - the test of a root cause is that it names something the organisation controls and could change. retrieval_cards.why: Three limbs, exactly stated - and the threshold that makes investigation mandatory rather than discretionary.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the steps of a root cause analysis.
retrieval_cards.answer: Recognise and report, making the situation safe first; preserve and collect evidence; establish the sequence of events; identify the causal factors and test each by removal; analyse to root cause using a technique; identify which defences failed and why; develop corrective and preventive action with an owner and a date; implement and verify both implementation and effectiveness; communicate the lesson fleet-wide.
retrieval_cards.why: Verification of effectiveness and fleet-wide sharing are the two steps organisations actually omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is 'human error' never a root cause?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a root cause must be actionable - it must name something the organisation controls and could change. No corrective action can be issued against human nature. 'The officer misread the gauge' is not actionable; 'the gauge was unlabelled and identical to the adjacent one' is. The same test disposes of 'lack of situational awareness', 'failure to follow procedure' and 'complacency'.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most valuable point in limb (a), and the one that distinguishes a management-level answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish proximate cause from root cause.
retrieval_cards.answer: The proximate cause is the event or condition directly preceding and producing the outcome - at the sharp end, immediate in time, and correcting it only restores the situation. The root cause is the underlying systemic or organisational reason the proximate cause was able to occur - at the blunt end, often years earlier, and correcting it prevents recurrence and usually prevents other events too.
retrieval_cards.why: Sharp end versus blunt end, now versus years ago, restore versus prevent.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does 'proximate cause' mean in marine insurance, and why note the difference?
retrieval_cards.answer: In marine insurance it means the dominant or effective cause of a loss, for deciding whether the loss arises from a peril insured against. In casualty investigation it means the immediate cause in the causal chain. They are related but are not the same test and should not be conflated.
retrieval_cards.why: Noting the distinction expressly earns a mark and prevents an answer drifting into insurance law.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define active failures and give three classes with examples.
retrieval_cards.answer: Unsafe acts committed by people in direct contact with the system, whose effects are felt almost immediately. Slips and lapses - skill-based failures of execution or memory, such as opening the adjacent valve from habit on a familiar manifold. Mistakes - planning failures, rule-based or knowledge-based, such as misdiagnosing a fluctuating exhaust temperature as an instrument fault when it was a burning exhaust valve. Violations - deliberate departures from procedure, whether routine, situational or exceptional, such as a permit to work signed retrospectively.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem prints 'giving suitable examples', so the examples are part of the requirement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define latent failures and give three examples from different origins.
retrieval_cards.answer: The delayed consequences of decisions taken by designers, builders, procedure writers, regulators and management, present in the system before the accident and lying dormant until combined with local triggering conditions and active failures. Reason called them resident pathogens. Examples: two dissimilar valves identical in appearance mounted adjacent with unclear labelling (design); a checklist adopted unchanged from another ship class and never revised for this installation (procedure); a manning level that makes the rest-hour regime unachievable in a short-sea trade (resourcing).
retrieval_cards.why: A latent condition is a DECISION and its consequences - not a dormant mechanical defect.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain Reason's model accurately, including the point most people miss.
retrieval_cards.answer: The organisational accident model, drawn as defences in depth or the Swiss cheese model: successive layers of defence - design, engineered safeguards, procedures, supervision, training, alarms and the crew - each with weaknesses represented as holes. The point most miss is that the holes are not static: they open, close and move, and an accident occurs only when the holes in every layer momentarily line up so a hazard passes through all the defences.
retrieval_cards.why: The moving holes explain why a trivial slip occasionally causes a catastrophe and usually causes nothing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your crew routinely bypasses a procedure. Is that a violation or a latent condition?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both, and the routine violation is diagnostic of the latent condition. If a whole department habitually departs from a procedure, the real finding is that the procedure, the manning or the time allowed is unworkable - which is a management decision, not an individual failing.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows the candidate can read an active failure as evidence rather than as a culprit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why investigate a near miss when nothing was lost?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because whether an event becomes a loss depends partly on the chance alignment of weaknesses in the defences, so outcome is a poor measure of behaviour. A near miss is evidence about the current state of the defences delivered without the cost of an accident - and it is the main proactive source of latent-condition data.
retrieval_cards.why: The practical payoff of the whole model, and a standard oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which is the more manageable target, active or latent failures, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: Latent conditions. Active failures are a permanent feature of competent human performance and cannot be eliminated - the next person in the same conditions makes the same slip. Latent conditions are present in the system all along and can therefore be found proactively, before any accident, by audit, inspection, risk assessment, near-miss analysis and trend data. That is the justification for the ISM Code's audit and management review machinery.
retrieval_cards.why: It converts the theory into a management conclusion, which is what a Class I examiner is looking for.

reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. Both are long settled and no amendment was identified as at this sitting, but the Code text is taken from the adopting resolution rather than a licensed consolidated source.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The provisions of the Casualty Investigation Code and the ISM Code as stated in this answer
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW holds no licensed copy of either instrument. The provisions rest on the adopting resolution and authoritative reproduction, and nothing is quoted verbatim at length.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The active/latent failure distinction and the defences-in-depth model are attributed to James Reason and to the human-factors literature, not presented as IMO text
reverify_before_publication.why: They are widely reproduced in IMO and flag State guidance but are not themselves the text of an IMO instrument. A later editor must not attach a resolution number to them.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no casualty statistic is asserted anywhere in this answer
reverify_before_publication.why: Figures for the proportion of marine casualties attributed to human factors circulate widely, vary by study and period, and none was verified for this sitting. The argument is deliberately made without leaning on a number; if one is added later it must be sourced and dated at or before December 2024.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The five whys, fishbone, fault tree, event and causal factor charting and barrier analysis are presented as established industry techniques rather than convention requirements
reverify_before_publication.why: No instrument mandates a particular RCA technique. The answer should not be edited to imply that any of them is required by SOLAS or the ISM Code.

blocks.h: 1. What the MLC is, and why its structure is unusual

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 is an International Labour Organization convention, adopted at the 94th (Maritime) Session of the International Labour Conference, which consolidated some sixty-eight earlier maritime labour Conventions and Recommendations into a single instrument. It is widely described as the fourth pillar of the international regulatory regime for quality shipping, standing alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW.

Its structure is not the usual ILO shape, and that is deliberate: it had to be firm on rights but flexible on implementation, and amendable at the speed the industry changes rather than by adopting a fresh convention each time.
The Convention is in three parts:

ol: The Articles - the treaty framework. General obligations, definitions and scope, the amendment procedures, entry into force, and the fundamental rights and principles. This is the part that binds a Member as a matter of treaty law.
The Regulations - the core requirements, set out by subject. Each Regulation states a purpose and the substantive obligation in short form.
The Code - the detail of how the Regulations are to be implemented.

blocks.p: The Code is itself in two parts, and the distinction is the single most examinable point in limb (a):

ul: Part A - Standards, which are mandatory. A ratifying Member must give effect to them.
Part B - Guidelines, which are not mandatory but to which a Member must give due consideration in deciding how to implement the Part A Standard.

blocks.p: The three levels stack vertically on the same subject, and they share a numbering scheme, which is what makes the Convention navigable. For any topic there is a Regulation x.y, a mandatory Standard Ax.y and a Guideline Bx.y. So Regulation 5.1.3 (Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC) is amplified by mandatory Standard A5.1.3 and by Guideline B5.1.3.

Flexibility is delivered by two further devices. Article VI paragraph 3 permits a Member to implement a Part A Standard through a provision that is substantially equivalent - one that gives full effect to the general object and purpose of the provision - provided this is recorded. And Title 3 permits certain exemptions by the competent authority. Both must be declared, which is where the DMLC in limb (b) comes in.
The Regulations and the Code are organised into five Titles, each covering the same subject matter at all three levels:

rows: Minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship
Minimum age; medical certification; training and qualifications; recruitment and placement services
Seafarers' employment agreements; wages; hours of work and hours of rest; entitlement to leave; repatriation; compensation for loss of the ship; manning levels; career and skill development
Accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering
Accommodation and recreational facilities; food and catering, including the ship's cook
Health protection, medical care, welfare and social security protection
Medical care on board and ashore; shipowners' liability; health and safety protection and accident prevention; access to shore-based welfare facilities; social security
Flag State responsibilities including inspection and certification; port State responsibilities; and labour-supplying responsibilities

blocks.p: A useful way to hold them: Titles 1 to 4 run in the order a seafarer meets them - getting the job, the terms of the job, living on board, staying well - and Title 5 is how all of it is enforced. Limb (b) of this question lives entirely in Title 5.

blocks.h: 4. The amendment position at this sitting

blocks.p: The Convention is "as amended", and stating that accurately is worth a mark because it shows the instrument is being treated as live:

ul: 2014 amendments - in force 18 January 2017. Financial security for repatriation and abandonment (Regulation 2.5, Standard A2.5.2) and for shipowners' liability for death or long-term disability (Regulation 4.2, Standard A4.2.1). These also added two matters to Appendix A5-I.
2016 amendments - in force 8 January 2019. Harassment and bullying brought into Guidelines B4.3.1 and B4.3.6.
2018 amendments - in force 26 December 2020. The seafarer employment agreement, wages and entitlements continue during captivity following piracy or armed robbery.

2022 amendments - approved at the 110th session of the International Labour Conference in June 2022 and entering into force on 23 December 2024. Among them: seafarers to be informed of their rights under the financial-security system operated by private recruitment and placement services; facilitation of prompt repatriation, with emphasis on abandonment; recreational facilities to include social connectivity, with reasonable access to ship-to-shore telephone and internet access; and food and drinking water free of charge, with meals nutritious, balanced and of sufficient quantity and quality.

blocks.p: The 2022 amendments enter into force on 23 December 2024 - that is, in the very month of this examination. The precise and safe way to state it is by the date: "the 2022 amendments were approved in June 2022 and enter into force on 23 December 2024". That is correct whether the paper is sat before or after that day, and it demonstrates the distinction between approved and in force which is exactly what a Class I examiner is testing.

blocks.h: 5. The certification chain - where the DMLC sits

blocks.p: Under Regulation 5.1.3, certification is mandatory for ships of 500 GT or over engaged in international voyages, and ships of 500 GT or over flying the flag of a Member and operating from a port, or between ports, in another country. A shipowner whose ship falls outside those categories may request certification. But note Regulation 5.1.4: all ships covered by the Convention are subject to inspection for all its requirements, whether or not they are certified - certification and inspection are not the same duty.
Two documents are produced, and they do different jobs:

ul: the Maritime Labour Certificate - evidence that the ship has been inspected and found to meet the national requirements implementing the Convention. Maximum validity five years (Standard A5.1.3 paragraph 1), subject to an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates. An interim certificate may be issued on delivery of a new ship, on change of flag, or when a shipowner assumes responsibility for a ship new to it - for a period not exceeding six months, and it is not renewable;
the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance (DMLC) - the document that says what the ship was measured against and how compliance is maintained. It is attached to the Certificate.

blocks.p: Both the Certificate and the DMLC must be carried on board, with a copy posted in a conspicuous place where it is available to the seafarers, and a copy made available to seafarers on request (paragraph 12).

blocks.h: 6. DMLC Part I - the flag State's declaration

blocks.p: Part I is drawn up by the competent authority - that is, by the flag State, not by the shipowner - in the form corresponding to the model in Appendix A5-II. Under Standard A5.1.3 paragraphs 9 and 10(a) it must:

ol: identify the list of matters to be inspected in accordance with the Convention - the Appendix A5-I list;

identify, in each of those areas, the national requirements embodying the relevant provisions of the Convention, by reference to the national legal provisions and, to the extent necessary, concise information on their main content;
refer to any ship-type specific requirements under national legislation;
record any substantially equivalent provisions adopted under Article VI paragraph 3; and
clearly indicate any exemption granted by the competent authority as provided in Title 3.

blocks.p: Appendix A5-I lists the matters that must be inspected and found to meet national requirements before a certificate is issued. At this sitting there are SIXTEEN of them - the original fourteen, plus the two added by the 2014 amendments:

ol: minimum age;
medical certification;
qualifications of seafarers;
seafarers' employment agreements;
use of any licensed or certified or regulated private recruitment and placement service;
hours of work or rest;
manning levels for the ship;
accommodation;
on-board recreational facilities;
food and catering;
health and safety and accident prevention;
on-board medical care;
on-board complaint procedures;
payment of wages;
financial security for repatriation; and
financial security for shipowners' liability.

blocks.p: The last two were added by the 2014 amendments, in force 18 January 2017. A great deal of material - including the ILO's own 2015 FAQ - still refers to "the 14 areas", because it predates that amendment. At this sitting the correct figure is sixteen, and a candidate who says "fourteen, plus two added by the 2014 amendments, so sixteen" has demonstrated command of the instrument rather than recall of a slogan.

blocks.h: 7. DMLC Part II - the shipowner's declaration

blocks.p: Part II is drawn up by the shipowner and is certified by the competent authority or by a recognized organization duly authorized for the purpose. Under Standard A5.1.3 paragraph 10(b) it must identify:

ul: the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance, between inspections, with the national requirements stated in Part I; and
the measures proposed to ensure that there is continuous improvement.

blocks.p: So the two Parts answer two different questions, and this symmetry is the cleanest way to hold the whole of limb (b):

rows: Issued under the authority of the competent authority; a duly authorized RO may issue it with the Certificate
Certified by the competent authority or a duly authorized recognized organization
WHAT must be complied with - the national law implementing the sixteen A5-I matters
HOW this ship complies, and keeps complying, day to day
National legal provisions per A5-I area; ship-type specific requirements; substantial equivalences; Title 3 exemptions
Measures for ongoing compliance between inspections; measures for continuous improvement
Generic to the flag, with ship particulars added

blocks.p: Guideline B5.1.3 paragraph 4 states the purpose of the whole document, and it is worth quoting in substance: the declaration should above all be drafted in clear terms designed to help all persons concerned - flag State inspectors, authorized officers in port States, and seafarers - to check that the requirements are being properly implemented. Appendix B5-I gives an example of both Parts.

blocks.h: 8. The welfare measures covered, and how they bite

blocks.p: Reading the sixteen A5-I matters as welfare provision rather than as a list, the DMLC covers four groups:

ul: Who may be employed and on what terms - minimum age, medical certification, qualifications, employment agreements, regulated recruitment and placement, payment of wages;
Fatigue and manning - hours of work or rest, and manning levels for the ship;

Living conditions - accommodation, on-board recreational facilities, food and catering. This is the group the 2022 amendments reach, adding social connectivity including reasonable internet access to recreational facilities and requiring food and drinking water free of charge;

Health, redress and protection against destitution - health and safety and accident prevention, on-board medical care, on-board complaint procedures, and the two financial security matters covering abandonment and repatriation and death or long-term disability.

blocks.p: The enforcement chain in Title 5 is what makes these real. The flag State inspects and certifies, directly or through an authorized recognized organization. The port State may inspect under Regulation 5.2.1: the Certificate and DMLC are prima facie evidence of compliance, but where there are clear grounds - or a seafarer complaint - a more detailed inspection follows, and deficiencies may lead to detention. The on-board complaint procedure, itself one of the sixteen matters, gives the seafarer a route that does not depend on a port call. And under Standard A5.1.3 paragraph 14 the Certificate ceases to be valid if the inspections are not completed, if it is not endorsed after the intermediate inspection, on change of flag, when the shipowner ceases to assume responsibility for the ship, or when substantial changes are made to the structure or equipment covered in Title 3.

Eight marks each, and the two limbs reward completely different things. Limb (a) is a structure question - it wants the three levels, the Part A/Part B distinction and the five Titles by name, and it is answered fastest as a short hierarchy plus a table. Limb (b) is a function question: not "what is the DMLC" but what each Part contains and who produces it, read against welfare. The instruction "briefly" in limb (b) is not an invitation to write less - it is the examiner saying do not narrate the whole of Title 5.

The highest-value single sentence in the whole answer is the one that says Part I is drawn up by the competent authority and Part II by the shipowner. It is the fact most often stated backwards, and it is the fact that proves the candidate has handled a real DMLC.

blocks.h: The date this question turns on

blocks.p: The 2022 amendments to the MLC entered into force on 23 December 2024 - in the month of this examination. That is not a coincidence you can ignore, and it is not a difficulty either, provided you handle it the way an examiner wants: by the date, not by the tense.

Write "the 2022 amendments were approved at the 110th session of the International Labour Conference in June 2022 and enter into force on 23 December 2024". That sentence is correct whichever side of 23 December the paper is sat, and it displays the approved / adopted / in force distinction that Class I examiners test repeatedly. What you must not write is a bare "the 2022 amendments are now in force" or "are not yet in force" - either may be wrong by a matter of days, and both look like guesswork.

The same discipline explains why the amendment list is worth carrying in full. An answer that describes the MLC as adopted in 2006 and stops is describing an instrument that has moved four times since.

blocks.h: Fourteen or sixteen? The A5-I trap

blocks.p: Almost every revision source says the DMLC covers "the 14 areas". That was true when the Convention entered into force in 2013, and the ILO's own FAQ, published in 2015, still says fourteen - while noting that if the 2014 amendments entered into force, two more would be added.

They did, on 18 January 2017. Appendix A5-I has carried sixteen matters ever since, the two additions being financial security for repatriation and financial security for shipowners' liability. At a December 2024 sitting the answer is sixteen. The safest form of words is "the original fourteen matters, plus the two financial security matters added by the 2014 amendments, so sixteen at present" - which is right, shows the working, and cannot be marked down.

blocks.h: The vertical structure is the thing to hold, not the list

blocks.p: Candidates memorise the five Titles and then cannot say how the Convention actually works. The mechanism is the vertical stack on a shared numbering scheme: for any subject there is a Regulation x.y stating the purpose and obligation, a Standard Ax.y which is mandatory, and a Guideline Bx.y which is not mandatory but must be given due consideration.

Once you have that, everything else follows. You can locate any provision from its number. You can explain why Part B matters despite not being mandatory - a Member that departs from it must be able to justify how it still gives effect to the Part A Standard. And you can explain substantial equivalence under Article VI paragraph 3 as the deliberate flexibility that let so many States ratify, with the DMLC Part I as the place it must be declared so the flexibility is transparent rather than hidden.

ul: Inverting the DMLC Parts. Part I is the competent authority's; Part II is the shipowner's. This is the single most common error on this question.
Saying the Maritime Labour Certificate is valid for four years. It is a maximum of five, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary.
Saying the DMLC covers fourteen areas. Sixteen since 18 January 2017.
Saying Part B is optional and can be ignored. It is not mandatory, but a Member must give due consideration to it.
Describing the MLC as adopted in 2006 with no mention of amendments. It has been amended in 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022.
Writing flatly that the 2022 amendments 'are in force' or 'are not yet in force' at this sitting. Give the date - 23 December 2024.

Saying only certified ships are inspected. All ships covered are subject to inspection for all requirements under Regulation 5.1.4; certification is mandatory only for ships of 500 GT and over in the two categories of Regulation 5.1.3.
Calling the interim certificate renewable. It is issued once, for a maximum of six months, and no further interim certificate follows.
Listing four Titles, or naming Title 5 as something other than compliance and enforcement.

"Who signs DMLC Part I?" The competent authority, or someone directly empowered by it; it is issued under the authority of the competent authority, and a duly authorized RO may issue it together with the Certificate.

"What is a substantially equivalent provision, and where would you find one?" A national provision giving full effect to the general object and purpose of a Part A Standard, adopted under Article VI paragraph 3 - and recorded in DMLC Part I.
"Your ship has just changed flag. What happens to the certificate?" It ceases to be valid on change of flag (Standard A5.1.3 paragraph 14); an interim certificate may be issued for up to six months.
"A seafarer asks to see the DMLC. Must you show it?" Yes - a copy must be posted conspicuously where it is available to seafarers, and made available on request.

"What does the port State do with the DMLC?" The Certificate and DMLC are prima facie evidence of compliance; with clear grounds or on a complaint, a more detailed inspection follows and deficiencies may lead to detention.
Name the three parts of the Convention. Articles, Regulations, Code (Part A Standards, Part B Guidelines).

Name the five Titles. Minimum requirements; conditions of employment; accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering; health protection, medical care, welfare and social security; compliance and enforcement.
Which ships must be certified? 500 GT and over on international voyages, and 500 GT and over operating from or between ports in another country.
What is the certificate's validity and what happens mid-term? Maximum five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary.
How many matters are in Appendix A5-I? Sixteen - the original fourteen plus two financial security matters added by the 2014 amendments.
Which amendments deal with abandonment? The 2014 amendments, financial security under Regulation 2.5 and Standard A2.5.2; the 2022 amendments strengthen prompt repatriation.
Which amendments cover captivity after piracy? The 2018 amendments, in force 26 December 2020.
What did the 2022 amendments add about connectivity? Recreational facilities should include social connectivity, with reasonable access to ship-to-shore telephone and internet.

blocks.p: For the structure: A-R-C - Articles, Regulations, Code; and the Code is A is mandatory, B is not. Numbering: x.y, Ax.y, Bx.y on the same subject.
For the five Titles, follow the seafarer: GET the job (1), the TERMS of the job (2), LIVE on board (3), STAY WELL (4), and who CHECKS (5).
For the DMLC: Part I is WHAT (the State says what the law is); Part II is HOW (the owner says how this ship keeps to it). Or shorter - I is the law, II is the ship.

ul: Article VI - Part A mandatory, Part B due consideration; Article VI(3) substantial equivalence
Regulation 5.1.1 and Standard A5.1.2 - flag State inspection and certification system; authorization of recognized organizations
Regulation 5.1.3 - mandatory certification: 500 GT and over on international voyages, and 500 GT and over operating from or between ports in another country
Standard A5.1.3 paragraph 1 - maximum five-year validity; Appendix A5-I list
Standard A5.1.3 paragraphs 5-8 - interim certificate, maximum six months, not renewable, no DMLC required for it
Standard A5.1.3 paragraphs 9 and 10(a) - DMLC Part I, drawn up by the competent authority
Standard A5.1.3 paragraph 10(b) - DMLC Part II, drawn up by the shipowner, certified by the competent authority or an authorized RO

Regulation 5.2.1 - port State inspection; certificate and DMLC as prima facie evidence
Appendix A5-I - the sixteen matters; Appendix A5-II - the model forms; Appendix B5-I - the example DMLC

blocks.p: Three limitations are recorded. MIW holds no licensed consolidated MLC, 2006 as amended, so the Articles, Regulations, Standards and Appendices rest on the ILO's published material rather than a licensed consolidated text, and nothing is quoted verbatim at length. The detailed content of the individual 2022 amendments is stated at the level recorded in flag State and industry circulars, and no paragraph-level citation of the amending instrument is made. And no ratification count or tonnage figure is asserted - those move continuously and none was verified for this sitting.

One correction is recorded because it is instructive. An automated summary of the ILO source used during research reported the certificate validity as four years and reversed who draws up DMLC Parts I and II. Both were wrong; both were caught against the primary text. It is a clean illustration of why the standing rule is to read the instrument rather than a summary of it - the summary was fluent, plausible and wrong on the two highest-value facts in the question.

notes: THE INTAKE FLAG WAS WRONG, AND THIS IS THE HIGHEST-RISK QUESTION ON THE PAPER. The intake recorded STABLE / LOW with no classes, and the allocation carried QP2412 forward as the only 2024 paper with ZERO temporal flags. Corrected to HIGH.

THE BOUNDARY LANDS INSIDE THE SITTING MONTH. The 2022 amendments to the MLC, 2006 were approved at the 110th session of the International Labour Conference in June 2022 and ENTERED INTO FORCE ON 23 DECEMBER 2024. This examination is a December 2024 sitting.

THE EXAMINATION DAY IS NOT ESTABLISHABLE FROM THE SOURCE. The source copy prints 'DECEMBER 2024' and the serial EM - 2412, and no day of the month. It therefore cannot be determined whether the paper was sat before or after 23 December 2024.

HOW THIS IS HANDLED, AND WHY IT IS NOT A BLOCKER. No date is assumed. The answer states the position BY DATE rather than by tense - 'approved in June 2022, entering into force on 23 December 2024' - which is correct on either side of the boundary. Under playbook section 20 the boundary itself IS established from a certain primary date; what is unknown is only the examination day, and the answer is drafted to survive that unknown. The study guide instructs the candidate to use the same construction and warns expressly against writing a bare 'now in force' or 'not yet in force'.

THIS IS ALSO THE SHARPEST AVAILABLE POINT ON THE QUESTION. A sitting that falls exactly on an entry-into-force date is the cleanest possible illustration of the approved / adopted / in force distinction, which is precisely what a Class I examiner rewards. The coincidence is turned into the answer's strongest material rather than treated as a difficulty.

SECOND TEMPORAL FINDING - APPENDIX A5-I HAS SIXTEEN MATTERS, NOT FOURTEEN. The 2014 amendments entered into force on 18 JANUARY 2017 and added financial security for repatriation and financial security for shipowners' liability to Appendix A5-I. The ILO's own FAQ, fourth edition 2015, still states fourteen and describes the two additions as conditional on the 2014 amendments entering into force - which they subsequently did. Any secondary source predating 2017, and a great deal of revision material that copies it, is stale on this point at this sitting.

FULL AMENDMENT CHAIN ESTABLISHED DATE BY DATE rather than inherited: 2014 amendments in force 18 January 2017; 2016 amendments in force 8 January 2019 (harassment and bullying, Guidelines B4.3.1 and B4.3.6); 2018 amendments in force 26 December 2020 (employment agreement and wages continue during captivity after piracy or armed robbery); 2022 amendments in force 23 December 2024.
NOT YET AT THIS SITTING: any amendment adopted after 2022 is outside this paper. Material describing later MLC developments belongs to a subsequent sitting and must not be back-read into this object.

A RESEARCH-STAGE ERROR IS RECORDED RATHER THAN CONCEALED. An automated summary of the ILO source reported the Maritime Labour Certificate validity as four years and inverted the drawing-up responsibility for DMLC Parts I and II. Both were corrected against the primary text before drafting. Recorded because both are load-bearing facts in limb (b) and the summary was fluent and wrong.

questions.understand_first: Two questions in one, and they test different things. Limb (a) asks how the Convention is BUILT - and the reason it is built that way is that the MLC had to consolidate some sixty-eight earlier instruments, bind States firmly on rights, leave them room on method, and still be amendable without convening a new conference. That produces the three levels (Articles, Regulations, Code) and the mandatory-versus-due-consideration split inside the Code, all running vertically on a shared numbering scheme across five Titles. Limb (b) then lands on the one document where that architecture becomes visible on a ship: the DMLC, whose Part I is the flag State saying WHAT its law requires and whose Part II is the shipowner saying HOW this particular ship keeps to it. Get those two authorships the right way round and most of limb (b) follows. One date matters more than any other on this paper: the 2022 amendments enter into force on 23 December 2024, in the month of this examination.
questions.memory_cue: Structure is A-R-C: Articles, Regulations, Code - and in the Code, A is mandatory, B is not (steps 1-2). Numbering stacks: x.y, Ax.y, Bx.y. Five Titles follow the seafarer: GET the job, the TERMS, LIVE aboard, STAY WELL, who CHECKS (3). Amendments by date, not tense (4). Then the DMLC: Part I is the LAW, Part II is the SHIP (6, 7) - or I says WHAT, II says HOW.

quick_revision.recall_15s: MLC, 2006 - ILO, 94th (Maritime) Session; consolidated some 68 earlier instruments; the fourth pillar with SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW. Three parts: ARTICLES (treaty framework, obligations, definitions, amendment), REGULATIONS (core requirements, each with a purpose), CODE - Part A STANDARDS, MANDATORY; Part B GUIDELINES, not mandatory but must be given DUE CONSIDERATION. Shared numbering: Reg x.y / Std Ax.y / Gdl Bx.y on one subject. Article VI(3) substantial equivalence; Title 3 exemptions - both declared in DMLC Part I. FIVE TITLES: 1 minimum requirements to work on a ship (age, medical, qualifications, recruitment and placement); 2 conditions of employment (SEA, wages, hours of work/rest, leave, repatriation, loss of ship, manning, career development); 3 accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering; 4 health protection, medical care, welfare and social security; 5 compliance and enforcement (flag State, port State, labour-supplying). AMENDMENTS: 2014 in force 18 Jan 2017 (financial security for repatriation and shipowners' liability; added 2 matters to A5-I); 2016 in force 8 Jan 2019 (harassment and bullying); 2018 in force 26 Dec 2020 (SEA and wages continue during captivity after piracy); 2022 approved June 2022, IN FORCE 23 DECEMBER 2024 (recruitment financial-security information, prompt repatriation/abandonment, social connectivity and internet access, free food and drinking water). CERTIFICATION (Reg 5.1.3): mandatory at 500 GT+ on international voyages, and 500 GT+ operating from or between ports in another country; others on request. Reg 5.1.4 - ALL covered ships are inspected for ALL requirements, certified or not. Certificate: max FIVE years, intermediate inspection between the 2nd and 3rd anniversary. Interim: max SIX months, NOT renewable, no DMLC needed for it. DMLC PART I - drawn up by the COMPETENT AUTHORITY: identifies the A5-I list, the national requirements in each area, ship-type specific requirements, substantial equivalences, and any Title 3 exemption. DMLC PART II - drawn up by the SHIPOWNER, certified by the competent authority or an authorized RO: measures for ongoing compliance between inspections, and measures for continuous improvement. Part I = WHAT; Part II = HOW. Appendix A5-I: SIXTEEN matters - age, medical, qualifications, SEA, recruitment and placement, hours of work/rest, manning, accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering, health and safety, medical care, complaint procedures, wages, + financial security for repatriation, + financial security for shipowners' liability. Both documents carried on board, copy posted conspicuously. Port State (5.2.1): certificate and DMLC are prima facie evidence; clear grounds or complaint -> more detailed inspection -> possible detention.
