quick_revision.major_trap: Inverting the two Parts of the DMLC. Part I is the competent authority's statement of national law; Part II is the shipowner's statement of how the ship complies. Two further traps sit alongside it. Appendix A5-I now contains SIXTEEN matters, not fourteen - the two financial security matters were added by the 2014 amendments, in force 18 January 2017, and most revision material (including the ILO's own 2015 FAQ) predates that. And the 2022 amendments enter into force on 23 December 2024, the month of this examination: state the date rather than writing 'now in force' or 'not yet in force', because the examination day is not printed on the paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the MLC structure and DMLC question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the MLC is and why its structure is unusual. 2 The three levels - Articles, Regulations, Code. 3 The five Titles. 4 The amendment position at this sitting. 5 The certification chain. 6 DMLC Part I. 7 DMLC Part II. 8 The welfare measures and how they are enforced.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 4 are the eight-mark limb (a); steps 5 to 8 are the eight-mark limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the three parts of the MLC, and what is the difference inside the Code?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Articles, the Regulations and the Code. The Code is in Part A, containing mandatory Standards, and Part B, containing Guidelines which are not mandatory but to which a Member must give due consideration. They run vertically on a shared numbering scheme - Regulation x.y, Standard Ax.y, Guideline Bx.y on the same subject.
retrieval_cards.why: The vertical stack is the mechanism; the Titles are only the index.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the five Titles of the MLC.
retrieval_cards.answer: Title 1 Minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship; Title 2 Conditions of employment; Title 3 Accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering; Title 4 Health protection, medical care, welfare and social security protection; Title 5 Compliance and enforcement.
retrieval_cards.why: Follow the seafarer - get the job, the terms, live aboard, stay well, who checks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who draws up DMLC Part I, and who draws up Part II?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part I is drawn up by the COMPETENT AUTHORITY - the flag State - in the form of the model in Appendix A5-II. Part II is drawn up by the SHIPOWNER and certified by the competent authority or a duly authorized recognized organization. Standard A5.1.3 paragraph 10.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most commonly inverted fact on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must DMLC Part I contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: The list of matters to be inspected under Appendix A5-I; in each of those areas, the national requirements implementing the Convention, by reference to the national provisions plus concise content where necessary; ship-type specific requirements; any substantially equivalent provisions adopted under Article VI paragraph 3; and any exemption granted by the competent authority under Title 3.
retrieval_cards.why: Substantial equivalences and exemptions are declared here - it is where the Convention's flexibility becomes transparent.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must DMLC Part II contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: The measures adopted by the shipowner to ensure ongoing compliance, between inspections, with the national requirements stated in Part I; and the measures proposed to ensure that there is continuous improvement.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Between inspections' and 'continuous improvement' are the two phrases that earn the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many matters are listed in Appendix A5-I, and why do most sources say fourteen?
retrieval_cards.answer: Sixteen. The original fourteen, plus financial security for repatriation and financial security for shipowners' liability, added by the 2014 amendments which entered into force on 18 January 2017. Sources written before 2017 - including the ILO's own 2015 FAQ - say fourteen.
retrieval_cards.why: A date-sensitive number that almost all revision material gets wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which ships must be certified, for how long, and what is the interim certificate?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ships of 500 GT and over engaged in international voyages, and ships of 500 GT and over operating from a port, or between ports, in another country - Regulation 5.1.3. Maximum validity five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates. An interim certificate may be issued on delivery of a new ship, on change of flag, or when a shipowner takes on a ship new to it, for not more than six months, and it is not renewable.
retrieval_cards.why: Five years and six months are both commonly misremembered, and the interim's non-renewability is a favourite oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are uncertified ships inspected under the MLC?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Regulation 5.1.4 provides that all ships covered by the Convention are subject to inspection for all its requirements, whether or not they are certified. Certification under Regulation 5.1.3 is an additional duty for the ships that fall within it.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely equate the scope of certification with the scope of the Convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the MLC amendment chain with entry-into-force dates.
retrieval_cards.answer: 2014 amendments - 18 January 2017, financial security for repatriation and for shipowners' liability. 2016 amendments - 8 January 2019, harassment and bullying. 2018 amendments - 26 December 2020, employment agreement and wages continue during captivity after piracy or armed robbery. 2022 amendments - approved June 2022 at the 110th session of the International Labour Conference, entering into force 23 December 2024.
retrieval_cards.why: Describing the MLC as a 2006 instrument and stopping there ignores four sets of amendments.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How should the 2022 amendments be described at a December 2024 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: By date: approved at the 110th session of the International Labour Conference in June 2022 and entering into force on 23 December 2024. Do not write a bare 'now in force' or 'not yet in force' - the examination day is not printed on the paper, and the date formulation is correct either way.
retrieval_cards.why: The sitting falls on the entry-into-force boundary, which makes it the cleanest possible illustration of approved versus in force.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a substantially equivalent provision, and where is it recorded?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under Article VI paragraph 3, a national law or measure that gives full effect to the general object and purpose of a Part A Standard, adopted where a Member is not in a position to implement that Standard in the manner set out. It must be recorded in DMLC Part I.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains how so many States with differing legal systems were able to ratify, and it links limb (a) to limb (b).

reverify_before_publication.claim: The 2022 amendments to the MLC, 2006 entered into force on 23 December 2024, within the month of this sitting, and the answer states the position BY DATE rather than by tense
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT RESOLVE THIS INTO A TENSE. The examination day is not printed on the source copy, so no statement that the amendments 'were' or 'were not' in force at the sitting can be supported. The date formulation is deliberate and is correct on either side of 23 December. A later editor who 'tidies' it into past tense would be asserting an examination date that is not in evidence.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Appendix A5-I contains SIXTEEN matters at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: The 2014 amendments entered into force 18 January 2017 and added two financial security matters. A great deal of material, including the ILO's 2015 FAQ, still says fourteen; an editor working from such a source would 'correct' sixteen back to fourteen and would be wrong for any sitting after January 2017.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No MLC amendment adopted after 2022 is reflected in this object
reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. Later MLC developments belong to subsequent papers and must not be back-read into a December 2024 answer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Articles, Regulations, Standards and Appendices as stated in this answer
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW holds no licensed consolidated MLC, 2006 as amended. These rest on the ILO's published material on the Convention rather than a licensed consolidated text, and nothing is quoted verbatim at length.

The Hague Rules 1924 and the Hague-Visby Rules (the 1968 Visby Protocol and the 1979 SDR Protocol) were used for the definition of 'carriage of goods' as covering the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship (Article I(e)); the carrier's obligations of due diligence to make the ship seaworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage and properly and carefully to load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods (Article III rules 1 and 2); the catalogue of exceptions (Article IV rule 2(a) to (q)) including the nautical fault and fire exceptions, perils of the sea, inherent defect quality or vice of the goods, insufficiency of packing, latent defects not discoverable by due diligence, and the catch-all at (q) with its burden of proof on the carrier; the package or unit limitation as amended by the Visby and SDR Protocols; and the one-year time bar under Article III rule 6. blocks.h: 1. Why the duration of responsibility matters

blocks.p: The period of responsibility decides which legal regime applies to a loss, and therefore who bears it. If the cargo is damaged at a moment falling outside the convention period, the Rules do not govern; liability is then determined by the contract of carriage and by general law, where the carrier may lawfully exclude liability altogether. If the damage occurs inside the period, the Rules apply compulsorily - and under Article III rule 8 of the Hague and Hague-Visby Rules any clause reducing the carrier's liability below the Rules' standard is null and void.

So the same physical damage, to the same cargo, on the same voyage, can produce entirely different outcomes depending on when it happened. That is the statement the question asks to be explained with examples.

blocks.h: 2. Hague and Hague-Visby - tackle to tackle

blocks.p: Under Article I(e), "carriage of goods" covers the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time when they are discharged from the ship. This is the classic "tackle to tackle" period.
Two consequences follow, and they are the heart of limb (a):

ul: the period covers only the sea carriage stage. Anything happening before loading - while the goods sit in a shed, on the quay or in the carrier's inland custody - and anything after discharge - in the terminal, in a warehouse, awaiting collection - falls outside the compulsory regime;

in those gaps the carrier may, and in practice does, contract out of liability by a "before and after" clause. The Rules do not prohibit it, because Article III rule 8 only strikes down clauses derogating from liability under the Rules, and outside the period there is no liability under the Rules to derogate from.

blocks.p: The Rules also apply only where a bill of lading or similar document of title is issued (Article I(b)), and "goods" excludes live animals and deck cargo stated as carried on deck and so carried (Article I(c)) - two further gaps in the compulsory cover.

Example. A consignment is damaged by rain while lying on the quay at the load port awaiting loading. Under Hague-Visby that damage falls outside the period of responsibility, and the carrier can rely on an exclusion clause in the bill of lading. Had the identical damage occurred an hour later, with the goods already across the ship's rail, the carrier would be answerable under Article III rule 2 unless it could bring itself within an Article IV exception.

The Hamburg Rules 1978 were written to close exactly that gap. Under Article 4, the carrier's period of responsibility covers the goods for the whole time the carrier is in charge of them at the port of loading, during the carriage, and at the port of discharge - the "port to port" period.

The Article then defines the boundaries precisely: the carrier is deemed to be in charge from the time it has taken over the goods from the shipper, or from an authority or third party to whom the goods must be handed over for shipment under law or regulation at the port of loading; and it remains in charge until it has delivered the goods to the consignee, or placed them at the consignee's disposal in accordance with the contract or local usage, or handed them over to an authority or third party to whom they must be handed over under law or regulation at the port of discharge.

The regime is materially harsher on the carrier in other respects too, and the period is only part of it: Article 5 imposes presumed fault - the carrier is liable for loss occurring while the goods were in its charge unless it proves that it and its servants took all measures that could reasonably be required to avoid the occurrence and its consequences - and there is no nautical fault exception and no long catalogue of excepted perils. The time bar is two years (Article 20) rather than one.

Example. The same rain damage on the quay at the load port, after the carrier has taken the goods into its charge, now falls inside the period. The carrier is liable unless it can show it took all measures reasonably required.

blocks.h: 4. Rotterdam - door to door, and not in force

blocks.p: The Rotterdam Rules 2008 go further again. Under Article 12 the period of responsibility begins when the carrier or a performing party receives the goods for carriage and ends when the goods are delivered - a "door to door" period which is not tied to the ports at all, and which can include inland road, rail or inland waterway legs of a contract that is wholly or partly by sea.

This is the point on which candidates most often go wrong: the Rotterdam Rules are NOT IN FORCE. Adopted in 2008 and opened for signature in Rotterdam in 2009, they require twenty ratifications before entering into force under Article 94, and that threshold had not been reached at this sitting. They are therefore a proposed regime and must be described as such - their significance is as the direction of travel, not as applicable law.

Article 12 does allow the parties to agree the time and location of receipt and delivery, subject to limits, and Article 13(2) permits an agreement that the shipper or consignee performs loading, handling, stowing or discharging - the convention's recognition of FIOS terms.

blocks.h: 5. The comparison, and the Indian position

rows: Tackle to tackle - loading to discharge (Art I(e))
Port to port - in charge at load port, carriage, discharge port (Art 4)
Due diligence for seaworthiness; proper care of cargo; long list of exceptions
Presumed fault with a modified list of exonerations; no nautical fault exception
In force and dominant in world trade
In force, but not adopted by the major maritime trading nations
Applies - Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 as amended in 1993

blocks.p: The Indian position at this sitting. The governing statute is the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925, which was amended in 1993 to give effect to the Hague-Visby Rules including the Visby and SDR Protocol amendments. It operates alongside the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856, which governs the transfer of rights of suit to the consignee or endorsee of a bill of lading. India is not a party to the Hamburg Rules or the Rotterdam Rules. So for an Indian contract of carriage the period of responsibility is the tackle-to-tackle period.

Worked comparison on one set of facts. A consignment is taken into the carrier's custody at the load port terminal on the 1st, loaded on the 3rd, discharged on the 20th, and remains in the discharge port terminal until collected on the 25th. Damage occurs on the 2nd and again on the 22nd.

ul: Hague-Visby - neither loss is inside the period. Both fall to the contract terms, and a "before and after" clause will usually defeat both claims.

Hamburg - both losses are inside the period, because the carrier was in charge of the goods at the load port on the 2nd and at the discharge port on the 22nd. The carrier is liable for both unless it discharges the Article 5 burden.

Rotterdam - both would be inside the period, and had the carrier also received the goods at an inland point the cover would extend there too. But the Rules are not in force, so this outcome is hypothetical.

blocks.p: That single set of facts is the clearest way to "explain this statement with examples", because it produces three different answers from one fact pattern.

blocks.h: 6. The grain claim - how it is framed

blocks.p: The facts are: a bulk carrier discharged a cargo of grain; the consignee received some cargo in damaged condition; the consignee claims against the shipowner.

The consignee's route is short. If the bill of lading was clean, it is prima facie evidence under Article III rule 3 that the goods were shipped in apparent good order and condition - and conclusive evidence in the hands of a good-faith third-party transferee under the Visby amendment. If the cargo is out-turned damaged, the consignee has established, on the face of it, that the goods were good in and bad out, and the burden shifts to the carrier to bring itself within a defence.
So the shipowner is not asked to prove it was careful in the abstract. It must point to a specific defence.

blocks.h: 7. The excepted perils that apply to grain

blocks.p: The catalogue is in Article IV rule 2. The ones that matter on these facts are:

ol: Inherent defect, quality or vice of the goods - rule 2(m). This is the shipowner's principal defence in a grain claim, and it also covers wastage in bulk or weight. Grain is a hygroscopic organic cargo: if it is loaded at a moisture content above the safe limit, it will self-heat, sweat, cake, mould and discolour in the hold no matter how carefully the ship is operated. Damage that is the working out of the cargo's own condition at shipment is not the carrier's responsibility.

Act or omission of the shipper or owner of the goods - rule 2(i). Where the shipper loaded wet, heated or contaminated grain, or misdescribed it, or where damage arises from the shipper's own loading arrangements.
Insufficiency of packing - rule 2(n). Less obvious for a bulk cargo, but it can bite where the shipper was responsible for a protective arrangement that failed.

Perils, dangers and accidents of the sea - rule 2(c). Available where heavy weather of a severity that could not reasonably be guarded against caused water ingress or shifting - but this requires real evidence of exceptional conditions, not merely a rough passage, and the ship must have been seaworthy for the voyage contemplated.

Act, neglect or default of the master or crew in the navigation or MANAGEMENT of the ship - rule 2(a). The classic and difficult distinction: an error in the management of the ship is excepted, but a failure in the care of the cargo is not. Ventilation is the battleground for grain - if the ventilation failure is characterised as care of cargo, the exception does not help.
Latent defects not discoverable by due diligence - rule 2(p), for example a hatch cover or pipe defect that reasonable inspection would not have revealed.
Fire - rule 2(b), unless caused by the actual fault or privity of the carrier - relevant where self-heating has progressed to combustion.

The catch-all - rule 2(q): any other cause arising without the actual fault or privity of the carrier and without the fault or neglect of its agents or servants. Note that here the burden of proof is expressly on the carrier, so it is a defence of last resort.

blocks.h: 8. The overriding obligations that can defeat every defence

blocks.p: The exceptions are not free-standing. Two obligations sit above them, and a shipowner who has breached either will usually lose despite an otherwise good exception:

ul: Seaworthiness - Article III rule 1. The carrier must exercise due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage to make the ship seaworthy, properly man, equip and supply her, and make the holds fit and safe for the reception, carriage and preservation of the goods. That last limb is cargoworthiness and is where grain claims are won and lost: holds must be clean, dry, free of previous cargo residues and infestation, and the hatch covers weathertight. Under Article IV rule 1, if the loss arises from unseaworthiness the carrier is liable unless it proves due diligence - and the burden of proving due diligence is on the carrier.

Care of the cargo - Article III rule 2. The carrier must properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods. For grain this means the ventilation regime above all - ventilating according to an accepted rule when the dew point conditions require it, and not ventilating when it would cause condensation - together with temperature monitoring, hold bilge soundings and pumping, and protection during rain.

blocks.p: The practical position is therefore this: inherent vice is a complete answer to a grain claim only if the ship was cargoworthy and the cargo was properly cared for. If the hatch covers leaked, or the ventilation records are missing or show a regime that made condensation inevitable, the owner will be held to have caused or contributed to the loss and the exception will fail.
Even where liability cannot be avoided altogether, three further defences reduce or extinguish the claim:

ol: Notice of loss - Article III rule 6. Notice in writing must be given before or at the time of removal of the goods, or within three days where the loss or damage is not apparent. Absence of notice is prima facie evidence of delivery in accordance with the bill of lading, though it does not by itself bar the claim.

Time bar - Article III rule 6. The carrier and the ship are discharged from all liability unless suit is brought within one year of delivery or of the date when the goods should have been delivered. This is a hard defence and defeats many claims outright. (Under Hamburg and Rotterdam the period is two years.)

Limitation of liability - Article IV rule 5, as amended by the Visby and SDR Protocols: the package or unit limit or the weight-based limit, whichever is the higher. For a bulk cargo such as grain there are no packages, so the weight-based limit is the operative one - a point specific to these facts and worth making. The right to limit is lost only where the damage resulted from an act or omission done with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result.

blocks.p: Two further points complete the picture. Under the Article 4 bis Himalaya provision the carrier's defences and limits extend to its servants and agents, though not to independent contractors. And a claim must be brought by a person with title to sue - under the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 the rights of suit pass to the consignee or endorsee to whom property in the goods passes upon or by reason of the consignment or endorsement, so a consignee without title cannot maintain the claim at all.

blocks.h: 10. The evidence that makes the defence work

blocks.p: A defence of inherent vice is only as good as the record supporting it. In practice the shipowner needs:

ul: the pre-loading hold inspection and cleanliness certificate, and a hatch cover weathertightness test record - ultrasonic or hose test - to establish cargoworthiness;
the pre-shipment cargo survey, and above all the moisture content and temperature of the grain at loading, which is the single most valuable document in the case;

mate's receipts and any clausing - if the grain was visibly wet, heated or contaminated at loading, the mate's receipt and the bill should have been claused, and a clean bill issued over a claused mate's receipt is a serious problem for the owner;
complete ventilation records showing the rule applied and the dew point readings on which each decision was based, plus hold temperature logs and bilge sounding and pumping records;
weather records and the deck log for any heavy weather relied on, and the draught survey figures at load and discharge port for any shortage element;
prompt appointment of a surveyor at the discharge port, jointly with the cargo interests where possible, and preservation of samples;
notification of the P&I Club at once, since the Club will appoint surveyors and lawyers and the owner's cover depends on cooperation.

blocks.p: Conclusion on the facts. The shipowner's best defence is inherent vice under Article IV rule 2(m), supported where the evidence allows by act or omission of the shipper under rule 2(i), and backed by the one-year time bar and the weight-based limitation as fallbacks. But that defence stands or falls on the owner being able to prove it exercised due diligence to make the holds fit for the grain and that it properly ventilated and cared for the cargo throughout - because if either fails, the exception fails with it.

Eight marks each on two limbs that look unrelated and are in fact the same subject seen from two sides. Limb (a) is comparative law - three conventions, one variable. Limb (b) is applied law - one fact pattern, and the question is what the owner can actually say.

The printed instruction in limb (a) is "explain this statement with examples", and that is what most answers omit. Three convention definitions recited in sequence is a description, not an explanation. The efficient way to earn the explanation marks is a single fact pattern run through all three regimes - the model answer uses damage on day 2 in the load port terminal and day 22 in the discharge port terminal, which produces three different results from one set of facts and demonstrates exactly why the duration matters.

Limb (b) prints "what defence is available to the ship owner?" - singular in form, plural in substance. Give the excepted perils, the overriding obligations that can defeat them, and the procedural and quantum defences, then land on which one actually wins on these facts.

blocks.h: The one sentence that makes limb (a) an explanation

blocks.p: The period of responsibility decides which regime applies, and therefore who bears the loss - because outside the period the carrier can lawfully exclude liability, and inside it Article III rule 8 makes any such clause null and void.

State that at the outset and everything after it is illustration rather than recitation. It also gives you the reason the Hamburg and Rotterdam Rules were drafted at all: each successive convention extends the period because the previous one left a gap in which the carrier could contract out.

ul: Hague / Hague-Visby - TACKLE TO TACKLE. Article I(e): from the time the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship.
Hamburg - PORT TO PORT. Article 4: the whole time the carrier is in charge of the goods at the port of loading, during the carriage and at the port of discharge.
Rotterdam - DOOR TO DOOR. Article 12: from receipt of the goods for carriage to delivery - not tied to ports, and capable of covering inland legs.

blocks.p: Three phrases, three Articles. If time is very short, those three lines plus the one-sentence reason plus the Rotterdam status point will carry most of limb (a).

The Rotterdam Rules are not in force. They were adopted in 2008, opened for signature in 2009, and require twenty ratifications under Article 94. That threshold was not met at this sitting and the Convention is not applicable law anywhere.

Writing about them in the present tense as though they governed is a straightforward and highly visible error, and it is exactly the adopted versus in force distinction that Class I examiners test across every subject. Describe them as the intended successor regime, explain what they would change, and say plainly that they are not in force. Note also that the Hamburg Rules, while genuinely in force, have not been adopted by the major maritime trading nations - so "in force" and "commercially dominant" are two different things, and saying so shows real command.

blocks.h: The Indian position - state it, and state it as at the sitting

blocks.p: For an Indian examination this must appear. At this sitting the governing statute is the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925, amended in 1993 to give effect to the Hague-Visby Rules, operating alongside the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 for the transfer of rights of suit. India is not a party to the Hamburg or Rotterdam Rules.

So the Indian period of responsibility is tackle to tackle. A candidate who explains the three regimes and then says which one actually governs an Indian carriage has answered a question about law rather than about conventions.

blocks.h: Limb (b): the shape of a cargo claim

blocks.p: Understand the burden and limb (b) writes itself. The consignee proves good in, bad out - and a clean bill of lading does the first half for it, being prima facie evidence under Article III rule 3 and conclusive in the hands of a good-faith transferee under Visby. The burden then shifts to the carrier to bring itself within a defence.
So the answer must name defences, not assert care. And the defences come in three layers:

ol: The excepted perils - Article IV rule 2, of which (m) inherent defect, quality or vice is the grain defence.
The overriding obligations that can defeat them - seaworthiness and cargoworthiness under Article III rule 1, and care of cargo under Article III rule 2.
The procedural and quantum defences - notice, the one-year time bar, and limitation.

blocks.h: Why inherent vice is the right answer for grain - and why it is fragile

blocks.p: Grain is hygroscopic and organic. Loaded above its safe moisture content it will self-heat, sweat, cake, mould and discolour whatever the ship does. Article IV rule 2(m) exists precisely for damage that is the working out of the cargo's own condition at shipment - and it expressly covers wastage in bulk or weight as well, which handles any shortage element of the claim.

But the defence is conditional, and this is the point that separates a good answer. Under Article IV rule 1, where loss arises from unseaworthiness the carrier is liable unless it proves due diligence, and the burden of proving due diligence is on the carrier. So the owner must first show the holds were fit and safe for the reception, carriage and preservation of grain - clean, dry, free of residues and infestation, hatch covers weathertight - and then show it properly ventilated and cared for the cargo under Article III rule 2. Leaking hatch covers or missing ventilation records will destroy an inherent vice defence, because the damage will be attributed to the ship rather than to the cargo.

That is why the model answer ends on evidence. In a real grain claim the case is usually decided by three documents: the moisture content at loading, the hatch cover weathertightness test, and the ventilation records.

A small point that is specific to these facts and therefore valuable. Article IV rule 5 as amended gives the package or unit limit or the weight-based limit, whichever is higher. A bulk grain cargo has no packages or units, so the weight-based limit is the operative one. Candidates who quote a per-package figure for a bulk cargo have not thought about the facts they were given.

Article IV rule 2(a) excepts neglect or default of the master or crew in the navigation or in the management of the ship. It does not except failures in the care of the cargo, which is Article III rule 2 territory. The line between "management of the ship" and "care of the cargo" has generated more litigation than any other provision in the Rules, and ventilation is the classic battleground for grain: the owner will argue the decision was ship management; the cargo interest will argue it was cargo care. Flagging that contest, rather than reciting the exception, is what a management-level answer does.

ul: Describing the Rotterdam Rules as in force. They are not, and require twenty ratifications under Article 94.
Reciting three definitions without examples, when the stem prints "explain this statement with examples".
Omitting the Indian position entirely in an Indian examination.
Saying Hague-Visby covers the whole voyage. It covers loading to discharge only.
Treating inherent vice as an unconditional defence. It fails if the ship was uncargoworthy or the cargo was not properly cared for.
Forgetting that under Article IV rule 1 the burden of proving due diligence is on the carrier.
Quoting a per-package limit for a bulk cargo that has no packages.
Omitting the one-year time bar, which is often the most effective defence of all.
Confusing the nautical fault exception with a general excuse - it covers navigation and management of the ship, not care of the cargo.
Forgetting title to sue under the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856.
Ignoring the effect of a clean bill of lading on the burden of proof.
"When does the carrier's responsibility begin under Hague-Visby?" When the goods are loaded on - not when they enter the carrier's custody.
"Are the Rotterdam Rules the current law?" No. Adopted 2008, not in force; twenty ratifications required.
"Which Rules apply to your Indian voyage charter with a bill of lading?" Hague-Visby, through the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 as amended in 1993.

"The grain was wet when loaded but you issued a clean bill. Where does that leave you?" In serious difficulty - the clean bill is prima facie, and conclusive against a good-faith transferee, so the owner may be estopped from proving the true condition at shipment.
"Your ventilation records are missing. Does inherent vice still help?" Probably not - the owner must show it properly cared for the cargo under Article III rule 2, and without records it cannot.
"How long does the consignee have to sue?" One year under Hague-Visby; two years under Hamburg and Rotterdam.
Give the three periods of responsibility in one phrase each. Tackle to tackle; port to port; door to door.
Which Article gives each? Hague-Visby Article I(e); Hamburg Article 4; Rotterdam Article 12.
What is the Indian governing statute? The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925, amended 1993 for Hague-Visby.

What is the carrier's seaworthiness obligation? Due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage, including making the holds fit and safe for the reception, carriage and preservation of the goods.
Name five excepted perils. Nautical fault; fire without actual fault or privity; perils of the sea; inherent vice; act or omission of the shipper.
Which exception applies to grain? Inherent defect, quality or vice - Article IV rule 2(m), which also covers wastage in bulk or weight.
Where does the burden of proof sit on due diligence? On the carrier - Article IV rule 1.
What is the time bar? One year from delivery or from when the goods should have been delivered.
Which limitation applies to bulk grain? The weight-based limit, because there are no packages.
What three documents decide a grain claim? Moisture content at loading, hatch cover weathertightness test, and ventilation records.

blocks.p: For limb (a): TACKLE - PORT - DOOR, and each convention extends the period because the last one left a gap. Add the status line: Hague-Visby governs, Hamburg is in force but marginal, Rotterdam is not in force at all. Then India: 1925 Act as amended in 1993 = Hague-Visby = tackle to tackle.

For limb (b), three layers: EXCEPTIONS - OBLIGATIONS - LIMITS. What I can rely on (Art IV r 2, especially inherent vice); what can defeat it (Art III r 1 seaworthiness and r 2 cargo care); and what caps it anyway (notice, one-year bar, weight-based limitation). And the evidence triad: MOISTURE, HATCHES, VENTILATION.

blocks.p: Four limitations are recorded. MIW holds no licensed consolidated text of the Hague-Visby, Hamburg or Rotterdam Rules, nor of the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925; the Articles relied on rest on the conventions as adopted and on authoritative reproduction, and nothing is quoted verbatim at length. No ratification count is asserted for either the Rotterdam or the Hamburg Rules - those figures move, and what matters and is certain is the status: Rotterdam not in force, Hamburg in force but not adopted by the major maritime trading nations. And the printed facts do not say whether the bill was shipped or received-for-shipment, or whether the charter was on FIOST terms; both would materially change the analysis, so both are flagged rather than assumed.

One currency instruction for a later editor: the Indian statutes stated here are those in force at December 2024 - the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 as amended in 1993, and the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856. India's carriage and bills of lading legislation was subsequently replaced, and the replacement statutes must not be read back into a December 2024 answer. This is the same discipline that keeps the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 rather than the 2025 Act throughout this paper.

questions.understand_first: Two limbs that are really one subject. Limb (a) asks why it matters WHEN the carrier's responsibility starts and stops, and the answer is that the period decides which regime applies and therefore who bears the loss - because outside the period the carrier can lawfully exclude liability, while inside it any such clause is void. Each successive convention extends the period precisely because the last one left a gap: tackle to tackle, then port to port, then door to door. The trap is that the widest of the three, Rotterdam, is not in force. Limb (b) then puts you inside the period with a real claim, and the shape of a cargo claim is what matters: a clean bill of lading proves the goods were good in, damaged out-turn proves they were bad out, and the burden is on the owner to name a defence. For grain that defence is inherent vice - but it is conditional, because it fails if the holds were not fit or the ventilation was not properly managed. Which is why a grain claim is usually decided by three documents: moisture content at loading, hatch cover testing, and ventilation records.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the duration of the carrier's responsibility matter at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it decides which regime governs the loss, and therefore who bears it. Outside the period the Rules do not apply and the carrier may lawfully exclude liability by contract; inside the period Article III rule 8 makes any clause relieving the carrier below the Rules' standard null and void. retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the period of responsibility under each of the three conventions, with the Article.
retrieval_cards.answer: Hague and Hague-Visby - tackle to tackle, from when the goods are loaded on to when they are discharged from the ship, Article I(e). retrieval_cards.prompt: What governs carriage of goods by sea in India at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925, amended in 1993 to give effect to the Hague-Visby Rules, together with the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 for the transfer of rights of suit. India is not a party to the Hamburg Rules or the Rotterdam Rules, so the Indian period of responsibility is tackle to tackle.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Run one fact pattern through all three regimes.
retrieval_cards.answer: Goods into the carrier's custody at the load port on day 1, loaded day 3, discharged day 20, collected day 25; damage on day 2 and day 22. Hague-Visby - neither loss is inside the period, so both fall to the contract terms and a 'before and after' clause usually defeats them. Hamburg - both are inside, and the carrier is liable unless it discharges the Article 5 burden. Rotterdam - both inside, and inland legs would be covered too, but the Rules are not in force.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the consignee frame a cargo claim, and what does a clean bill of lading do?
retrieval_cards.answer: The consignee must show the goods were good in and bad out. A clean bill of lading is prima facie evidence under Article III rule 3 that the goods were shipped in apparent good order and condition, and conclusive evidence in the hands of a good-faith third-party transferee under the Visby amendment. Damaged out-turn then shifts the burden to the carrier to bring itself within a defence.
retrieval_cards.why: Understanding where the burden sits is what makes limb (b) a legal answer rather than an assertion of care.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which excepted peril is the shipowner's principal defence to a grain claim, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article IV rule 2(m) - wastage in bulk or weight, or any other loss or damage arising from inherent defect, quality or vice of the goods. Grain is hygroscopic and organic: loaded above its safe moisture content it will self-heat, sweat, cake, mould and discolour however carefully the ship is operated, and that damage is the working out of the cargo's own condition at shipment.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is inherent vice an unconditional defence?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Article III rule 1 requires due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage to make the ship seaworthy and the holds fit and safe for the reception, carriage and preservation of the goods, and Article IV rule 1 puts the burden of proving due diligence on the carrier. Article III rule 2 requires the cargo to be properly and carefully cared for. Leaking hatch covers or missing ventilation records will defeat the defence, because the damage is then attributed to the ship rather than to the cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: The conditionality is the point that separates a good answer from a list of exceptions.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain the navigation-versus-cargo-care distinction and why it matters for grain.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article IV rule 2(a) excepts neglect or default of the master or crew in the navigation or in the management of the ship, but not failures in the care of the cargo, which is Article III rule 2 territory. Ventilation of a grain cargo is the classic battleground: the owner argues the decision was ship management and excepted, the cargo interest argues it was cargo care and not.
retrieval_cards.why: It has generated more litigation than any other provision in the Rules, and flagging the contest shows real understanding.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the procedural and quantum defences under Hague-Visby.
retrieval_cards.answer: Notice of loss in writing before or at the time of removal, or within three days where the damage is not apparent - absence of notice is prima facie evidence of delivery as per the bill. A one-year time bar from delivery or from when the goods should have been delivered, after which the carrier and ship are discharged from all liability. And limitation under Article IV rule 5 - the package or unit limit or the weight-based limit, whichever is higher.
retrieval_cards.why: The one-year time bar is often the most effective defence of all and is regularly omitted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which limitation limb applies to a bulk grain cargo?
retrieval_cards.answer: The weight-based limit. Article IV rule 5 as amended gives the package or unit limit or the weight-based limit, whichever is higher - and a bulk cargo has no packages or units, so only the weight limb can operate.
retrieval_cards.why: Quoting a per-package figure for a bulk cargo shows the facts were not read.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which three documents usually decide a grain cargo claim?
retrieval_cards.answer: The moisture content and temperature of the grain recorded at loading; the hatch cover weathertightness test record, ultrasonic or hose test; and the complete ventilation records showing the rule applied and the dew point readings behind each decision. Supported by hold inspection and cleanliness certificates, mate's receipts and any clausing, hold temperature logs, bilge soundings, weather records and draught surveys.
retrieval_cards.why: A defence of inherent vice is only as good as the record supporting it.

blocks.h: 1. What the SEEMP is, and where the four steps live

blocks.p: The Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) is required by regulation 26 of MARPOL Annex VI. It is a ship-specific, operational management document that must be kept on board, developed and reviewed taking into account the guidelines adopted by the Organization. The guidelines operative at this sitting are the 2024 Guidelines, resolution MEPC.395(82), adopted on 4 October 2024, which revoke the 2022 Guidelines, MEPC.346(78).

Note the numbering. The SEEMP requirement sits at regulation 26, not regulation 22 - Annex VI chapter 4 was renumbered by MEPC.328(76) with effect from 1 November 2022. Within chapter 4 the goal is stated at regulation 20, the fuel oil data collection system at regulation 27 and the operational carbon intensity indicator at regulation 28.
The plan has three Parts, and it matters for this question that the four steps belong to Part I:

ul: Part I - Ship Management Plan to Improve Energy Efficiency, required by regulation 26.1, applying to any ship of 400 GT and above. This is the part built on the four-step cycle.

Part II - Ship Fuel Oil Consumption Data Collection Plan, required by regulation 26.2, applying to any ship of 5,000 GT and above. It describes the methodology for collecting the data required by regulation 27 and reporting it to the Administration.

Part III - Ship Operational Carbon Intensity Plan, required by regulations 26.3 and 28.8. It carries the attained annual operational CII methodology, the required CII for the next three years, a three-year implementation plan, and its own process for self-evaluation and improvement.

blocks.p: Section 3.6 of the Guidelines states the cycle directly: Part I should be developed as a ship-specific plan by the company and should reflect efforts to improve energy efficiency and reduce carbon intensity through four steps - planning, implementation, monitoring, and self-evaluation and improvement - and "these components play a critical role in the continuous cycle". Section 3.7 adds the standing qualification that safety considerations are paramount at all times.

The Guidelines are unusually emphatic here. Section 4.1.1: planning is the most crucial stage, because it determines both the ship's current energy and carbon-intensity status and the improvement that can be expected - so sufficient time should be devoted to it. Planning has four components:

ol: Ship-specific measures. Establish what the ship actually does now, identify measures already taken and how effective they have been, and identify what more can be adopted. The Guidelines warn that not all measures suit all ships, or the same ship under different operating conditions, and that some are mutually exclusive.

Company-specific measures. Efficiency does not depend on single-ship management alone: repair yards, owners, operators, charterers, cargo owners, fuel suppliers, ports and traffic management all bear on it, so a company-level plan and coordination is recommended.
Human resource development. Awareness-raising and training for personnel ashore and on board - the Guidelines call this both a planning component and a critical element of implementation.

Goal setting. For ships subject to regulation 28 the goal should be consistent with the continuous CII improvement required by that regulation. Whatever is chosen, the goal should be measurable and easy to understand.

blocks.p: Examples. Ship-specific: speed optimisation; weather routeing; hull and propeller condition management with a coating and polishing regime; trim optimisation; confirming berth availability and arrival time with the destination port so the ship is not steaming hard to wait at anchor. Company-specific: negotiating "just-in-time" arrival with terminals, which needs early communication between operator, port and traffic management and cannot be delivered from the bridge alone. Mutually exclusive: a fixed-pitch propeller re-pitched for a lower service speed rules out later gains from speed increase; slow steaming and main-engine derating interact with waste-heat recovery output. Goal: "reduce AER by 5% year on year, consistent with the required CII for the next three years" - measurable, and tied to the regulation.

Section 4.2.1: once the measures are identified it is essential to establish a system for carrying them out. That means developing procedures for energy management, defining the tasks associated with them and assigning those tasks to responsible personnel, with defined levels of authority and lines of communication, and procedures for internal audit and management review where relevant. Part I should say how each measure is to be implemented, who is responsible, and the start and end dates of each. The Guidelines note that building this system can be treated as part of planning.
Section 4.2.2 adds record-keeping, and two points that are easy marks because they are counter-intuitive:

ul: if an identified measure cannot be implemented, the reason should be recorded for internal use - a plan that quietly drops a measure has lost the evidence its next self-evaluation needs;

events and operational conditions outside the crew's control - waiting for berths, extended port dwell times, operation in severe adverse weather - should be documented, because they affect the ship's rating and cannot be reconstructed later.

blocks.p: Examples. The Chief Engineer is named as responsible for the hull and propeller condition regime, with an inspection at each dry-docking and in-water polishing at defined fouling thresholds; the Master is named for trim and speed compliance against the passage plan; the shore superintendent for retrofit scheduling. A measure such as a shaft generator retrofit that is deferred because the yard slot moved is recorded, with the reason, so that next year's evaluation does not read it as a failure of the measure itself.

Section 4.3.1: energy efficiency should be monitored quantitatively, by an established method and preferably by an international standard. The monitoring tool should target the goal indicator set at planning - AER, cgDIST, EEOI or another CII - and a ship subject to regulation 28 is likely to use the CII itself, calculated in accordance with the Guidelines developed by the Organization.

ul: 4.3.4 - monitoring at regular intervals for consistency of data and to assist verification; fuel oil consumption monitored using daily reporting, such as noon reports, or at higher frequency.

4.3.5 - continuous, consistent and reliable data collection is the foundation of monitoring, so a monitoring system with data-collection procedures and assigned personnel must be developed - again, at the planning stage.

4.3.6 - to avoid unnecessary administrative burden, monitoring should be done as far as possible by shore staff where data can be transferred automatically, using existing required records such as the official and engineering logbooks and the oil record book.
4.3.7 - where a ship diverts to engage in search and rescue, that data should not be used in energy efficiency monitoring and should be recorded separately.

blocks.p: Examples. Noon reports feeding an automated performance system that separates hull-fouling degradation from weather effect; a shaft power meter and mass flow meters giving fuel consumption independent of tank soundings; the CII tracked monthly against the required value so the corrective action is taken in month seven, not discovered in the annual return.
Section 4.4.1: this is the final phase of the management cycle, and its purpose is to produce meaningful feedback for the planning stage of the next cycle. Section 4.4.2 gives four purposes:

ol: evaluate the effectiveness of the planned measures and of their implementation;
deepen understanding of the ship's operation - what types of measure do and do not function effectively, and how and why;
comprehend the trend of efficiency improvement for that ship; and
develop the improved plan for the next cycle by identifying further opportunities.

blocks.p: Note the second and third. The Guidelines do not ask only "did it work?" but "why did it work, and what is the trend" - which is what converts a year's data into a better plan rather than a score.

Examples. Evaluation shows weather routeing delivered most of the claimed saving on North Atlantic legs but almost none on short coastal legs, so the next cycle applies it selectively and reinvests the effort in trim optimisation. Hull coating performance is found to degrade faster on a trade with long idle periods in warm water, so the next cycle shortens the polishing interval rather than blaming the coating. For a ship subject to regulation 28, Part III carries this further: where the ship is rated D for three consecutive years or E in a single year, a plan of corrective actions must be developed and included in the SEEMP - self-evaluation with a statutory consequence.

blocks.h: 6. Why the cycle is critical, not merely administrative

blocks.p: The question asks for the critical role of each component, so the answer must say why removing any one of them breaks the whole:

rows: Establishes the baseline and selects measures that suit this ship and this trade
Measures are adopted by fashion rather than fit; savings cannot be claimed because there is no baseline to claim them against
Converts intention into assigned, dated, auditable action
The plan becomes a document carried for inspection rather than a way the ship is run
Supplies the quantitative evidence, consistently and continuously
Effectiveness is a matter of opinion; the CII return is unverifiable and adverse weather cannot be distinguished from poor operation
Turns the data into a better plan and explains why measures worked
The cycle does not close - the same plan is re-issued each year and improvement stops

blocks.p: The cycle is also what makes the plan ship-specific and living rather than generic: section 3.6 notes that with each iteration some elements of Part I will necessarily change while others may remain. And it is what connects an operational management document to a regulatory outcome - the same four beats reappear in Part III, where planning becomes the required CII for the next three years and the three-year implementation plan, monitoring becomes the attained annual operational CII, and self-evaluation becomes the plan of corrective actions.

Finally, note what the SEEMP is not. It is operational, not technical: the EEDI and EEXI fix what the ship is, once. The SEEMP governs how it is operated, continuously - which is why it is a cycle and they are not.

Sixteen marks, one limb, and the question names its own four sections. That is a gift and a trap. The gift is that the structure is handed to you. The trap is that four equal paragraphs of description will not score sixteen marks, because the printed command is "describe with suitable examples, the critical role of each of these components" - three separate demands. You must (i) describe each step, (ii) give examples, and (iii) say why each is critical. An answer that does only the first has answered roughly a third of the question.

The route therefore spends one step per component, attaches examples inside each, and then adds a dedicated step on criticality - the table at step 6 - which is where the "critical role" marks are actually banked. Framing at step 1 is worth the space because it lets you say something most candidates cannot: that the four steps are the framework of Part I specifically, not of the whole plan.

blocks.h: Which guidelines - and why this sitting is different from earlier 2024 sittings

blocks.p: The SEEMP Guidelines are re-adopted periodically and each edition revokes the last. At this examination the operative edition is MEPC.395(82), the 2024 Guidelines, adopted 4 October 2024 - only two months before the paper was sat - which revoked MEPC.346(78), the 2022 Guidelines.

That is a real discriminator between sittings of the same year. A candidate revising from a January, February or March 2024 paper would cite MEPC.346(78), and by December that citation is superseded. The intermediate step is worth knowing because it shows the pace: MEPC.388(81) amended the 2022 Guidelines at MEPC 81 in the spring, and MEPC.395(82) then replaced them outright in the autumn. Two changes inside one calendar year, on a paper the intake had flagged as carrying no temporal risk at all.

blocks.h: The regulation number is the other easy mark to lose

blocks.p: A great deal of older material - textbooks, circulars and notes written before 2023 - cites the SEEMP as MARPOL Annex VI regulation 22. That was correct until chapter 4 was renumbered by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022. Since then the SEEMP is regulation 26, with Part I at 26.1, Part II at 26.2 and Part III at 26.3 (read with 28.8). Getting this right, and being able to say why the older number exists, is a visible sign of current reading.
The neighbouring numbers are worth carrying too: regulation 20 the goal of chapter 4, regulation 27 the data collection system, regulation 28 the CII.

blocks.h: Where the paper's decarbonisation position stood in December 2024

blocks.p: If the answer reaches for context, it must be the context of this sitting. EEXI and CII entered into force on 1 January 2023, so at this examination 2023 is the first full CII data year and the first ratings have been issued during 2024 on that data. The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, resolution MEPC.377(80) of 7 July 2023, is the operative strategy. And MEPC 82, held 30 September to 4 October 2024, began the review of the short-term measures - CII, SEEMP and EEXI - referring it to a correspondence group and an intersessional working group reporting to MEPC 83 in 2025. That review had produced no amendment at this sitting. Do not write that the short-term measures have been revised, and do not import any mid-term measure as adopted.

blocks.h: The five facts from section 4 that most answers miss

ul: Planning is expressly the "most crucial stage" (4.1.1). Say so and attribute it - it converts a generic opening into a cited one.
Some measures are mutually exclusive (4.1.3). Almost nobody says this, and it demonstrates real engineering understanding rather than a list of green measures.
Reasons for non-implementation must be recorded (4.2.2). Counter-intuitive, and precise.
Conditions outside the crew's control should be documented (4.2.2) - waiting for berths, port dwell, severe weather - because they affect the rating.
Search and rescue data is excluded and recorded separately (4.3.7). A small, exact, memorable point that proves the Guidelines were opened.
Citing the SEEMP as regulation 22. It has been regulation 26 since 1 November 2022.
Citing MEPC.346(78) as the operative guidelines. They were revoked by MEPC.395(82) on 4 October 2024, before this sitting.
Presenting the four steps as the structure of the whole SEEMP. They are the framework of Part I.
Describing the steps without giving examples, when the question prints "with suitable examples".
Describing the steps without saying why each is critical, when the question prints "the critical role of each".
Confusing the SEEMP with the EEDI or EEXI. Those are technical and one-off; the SEEMP is operational and continuous.
Writing that Part I applies to ships of 5,000 GT and above. That is Part II; Part I is 400 GT and above.
Treating monitoring as something done only for the annual return. The Guidelines require regular intervals and daily fuel reporting.
Asserting that MEPC 82 revised the CII. It opened a review; no amendment existed at this sitting.
"Whose plan is it?" Part I is developed as a ship-specific plan by the company (3.6) - not written on board, though it is implemented on board.

"Is the SEEMP audited?" For ships not subject to regulation 28 the Guidelines say expressly there is no requirement to define a goal, publish it, or be subject to external inspection, survey or audit in respect of the SEEMP (4.1.7.2). For ships subject to regulation 28 the position is different, because Part III is verified. Knowing that the answer splits is worth a mark.
"What happens if the ship rates badly?" D for three consecutive years, or E in one year, triggers a plan of corrective actions in the SEEMP.
"Why must adverse weather be recorded?" Because it affects the rating and cannot be reconstructed after the fact - 4.2.2.
"Where does safety come in?" Section 3.7 - safety considerations are paramount at all times, and the trade may determine which measures are feasible.
Which regulation requires the SEEMP, and which guidelines are current? Regulation 26 of MARPOL Annex VI; the 2024 Guidelines, MEPC.395(82).
What are the three Parts and their thresholds? Part I 400 GT and above; Part II 5,000 GT and above; Part III with the CII regime under regulations 26.3 and 28.8.
Name the four steps. Planning, implementation, monitoring, self-evaluation and improvement.
Which step do the Guidelines call the most crucial, and why? Planning - it fixes the baseline and the achievable improvement.
Give two ship-specific and one company-specific measure. Speed optimisation and hull condition management; just-in-time arrival negotiated with the terminal.
What must be recorded when a measure is not implemented? The reason, for internal use.
What data is excluded from energy efficiency monitoring? Data from search and rescue diversions, recorded separately.
How does Part III mirror the cycle? Required CII and three-year implementation plan; attained annual CII; plan of corrective actions.

blocks.p: PIMS - Plan, Implement, Monitor, Self-evaluate. It is a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle wearing IMO clothes, which is why section 3.3 says a company already running ISO 14001 should treat efficiency monitoring as part of its existing management system, and section 3.4 allows Part I to form part of the safety management system.

For the four sub-parts of planning: SHIP, COMPANY, PEOPLE, GOAL - ship-specific measures, company-specific measures, human resource development, goal setting. For the four purposes of self-evaluation: did it work, why, what is the trend, what next.

blocks.p: The four steps, their content and every section number in this answer are taken from MEPC.395(82) read directly. Three limitations are recorded. MIW holds no licensed consolidated MARPOL Annex VI, so the regulation numbering and content are established from the recitals and cross-references inside MEPC.395(82) rather than from a licensed Annex VI text, and no regulation is quoted verbatim. No CII rating statistic is asserted - the first ratings were issued during 2024 on 2023 data, but no published distribution was verified for this sitting. And the MEPC 82 review of the short-term measures is recorded as in progress with no outcome, because that is its status at this sitting.

One currency instruction for any later editor: MEPC.395(82) is the correct edition here and must not be advanced. The guidelines are re-adopted periodically, and the review opened at MEPC 82 reported to MEPC 83 in 2025 - after this examination. Anything arising from that review belongs to a later paper, not this one.

notes: THE INTAKE FLAG WAS WRONG. The intake recorded STABLE / LOW with no classes, and the allocation carried QP2412 forward as the only 2024 paper with ZERO temporal flags. This question alone refutes that: the operative guidelines changed TWICE during 2024, the second time only two months before the sitting. Corrected to HIGH.

THE DECIDING FACT. MEPC.395(82), the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines, was adopted on 4 OCTOBER 2024 at MEPC 82 and by operative paragraph 3 REVOKES MEPC.346(78), the 2022 Guidelines. December 2024 falls two months after that adoption, so MEPC.395(82) is the operative edition at this sitting.

THE CHAIN WITHIN 2024, from the resolution's own preamble: MEPC.346(78) (2022 Guidelines) -> amended by MEPC.388(81) at MEPC 81 in spring 2024 -> replaced outright by MEPC.395(82) at MEPC 82 on 4 October 2024. Two movements inside the examination year.

THIS IS THE CONCRETE CASE AGAINST INHERITING A JANUARY TREATMENT. A January, February or March 2024 answer to this question would correctly cite MEPC.346(78). By December that citation is revoked. The standing instruction's warning that a January treatment must not be assumed valid eleven months later is demonstrated here rather than merely asserted.

RENUMBERING, verified from the resolution rather than recalled. The SEEMP is required by MARPOL Annex VI REGULATION 26 - the preamble of MEPC.395(82) says so, and section 1.3 attributes Part I to 26.1, Part II to 26.2 and Part III to 26.3 with 28.8. Regulation 22 is the PRE-2021 numbering, superseded by MEPC.328(76) with effect from 1 November 2022. Pre-2023 material citing regulation 22 is stale at this sitting.

REVIEW IN PROGRESS, NOT COMPLETE. MEPC 82 (30 September to 4 October 2024) opened the review of the short-term GHG measures - CII, SEEMP and EEXI - and referred it to a correspondence group and an intersessional working group reporting to MEPC 83 in 2025. At this sitting the review has produced NO amendment. The answer records it as in progress and asserts no outcome. A donor written for any 2025 or 2026 sitting would carry that outcome and it must not be back-read.

DECARBONISATION STAGE AT THIS SITTING. EEXI and CII entered into force 1 January 2023, so 2023 is the FIRST full CII data year and the first ratings were issued during 2024. The operative strategy is the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, MEPC.377(80) of 7 July 2023 - not the 2018 Initial Strategy it superseded. No mid-term measure is described as adopted, because none was at this sitting.
NO CLAIM DEPENDS ON THE EXAMINATION DAY within December 2024. MEPC.395(82) had been in force since 4 October, nearly three months before the earliest possible sitting day.

questions.understand_first: This question hands you its own structure, which is why it is easier to answer adequately than to answer well. The four steps are printed in the stem, so describing them earns only part of the marks; the printed command asks for the CRITICAL ROLE of each, WITH EXAMPLES. So the real task is to show that the four steps are a closed loop in which each stage is load-bearing - plan without monitoring and you cannot prove a saving; monitor without self-evaluation and the cycle never closes. Two framing facts separate a current answer from a stale one: the four steps are the framework of PART I of the SEEMP, not of the whole plan, and the guidelines that describe them were re-adopted as MEPC.395(82) on 4 October 2024, two months before this examination, revoking the 2022 edition.
questions.memory_cue: PIMS - Plan, Implement, Monitor, Self-evaluate. It is Plan-Do-Check-Act in IMO clothes. Inside planning: SHIP, COMPANY, PEOPLE, GOAL (2). Implementation is who, what, by when (3). Monitoring is quantitative, continuous, shore-side (4). Self-evaluation asks did it work, why, what trend, what next (5). Then close with break one link and the loop fails (6).

quick_revision.recall_15s: SEEMP = MARPOL Annex VI regulation 26 (NOT reg 22 - renumbered by MEPC.328(76) from 1 Nov 2022). Ship-specific, operational, kept on board. Guidelines at this sitting: MEPC.395(82), adopted 4 October 2024, revoking MEPC.346(78) (which MEPC.388(81) had amended earlier in 2024). Chapter 4: reg 20 goal, reg 27 data collection, reg 28 CII. Three Parts: Part I (reg 26.1, 400 GT+) - the four-step cycle; Part II (reg 26.2, 5,000 GT+) - fuel oil data collection plan; Part III (regs 26.3 and 28.8) - operational carbon intensity plan. Section 3.6 states the four steps and calls them critical to the continuous cycle; 3.7 safety paramount. 1 PLANNING (4.1) - the MOST CRUCIAL stage; ship-specific measures (some are mutually exclusive), company-specific measures, human resource development, goal setting - measurable and easy to understand, consistent with continuous CII improvement. 2 IMPLEMENTATION (4.2) - establish a system: procedures, defined tasks, responsible personnel, levels of authority, lines of communication, start and end dates; record-keeping; record the reason if a measure cannot be implemented; document conditions outside the crew's control (berth waiting, port dwell, severe weather) because they affect the rating. 3 MONITORING (4.3) - quantitative, by an established method; tool targets the goal indicator (AER, cgDIST, EEOI, CII); regular intervals, fuel by noon reports or better; continuous consistent reliable data is the foundation; do it shore-side where possible using logbooks and the oil record book; search and rescue data excluded and recorded separately. 4 SELF-EVALUATION (4.4) - final phase, feeds the next planning stage; four purposes: evaluate effectiveness, deepen understanding of what works and why, comprehend the trend, develop the improved plan. Why critical: no baseline means no provable saving; no assignment means a document not a practice; no consistent data means opinion; no evaluation means the loop never closes. Part III mirrors it - required CII and three-year implementation plan, attained annual CII, and a plan of corrective actions if rated D three years running or E once. Contrast: EEDI/EEXI are technical and one-off; the SEEMP is operational and continuous.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the SEEMP four-step question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the SEEMP is and where the four steps live. 2 Planning. 3 Implementation. 4 Monitoring. 5 Self-evaluation and improvement. 6 Why the cycle is critical rather than administrative.
retrieval_cards.why: Step 6 is where the 'critical role' marks are banked; steps 2 to 5 carry the examples inside them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which regulation requires the SEEMP, and which guidelines are operative at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 26. The operative guidelines are the 2024 Guidelines, resolution MEPC.395(82), adopted 4 October 2024, which revoke the 2022 Guidelines MEPC.346(78).
retrieval_cards.why: Two citation traps in one card - the old regulation 22 numbering and the superseded 2022 guidelines.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why do many sources cite the SEEMP as MARPOL Annex VI regulation 22?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because that was the numbering before MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 was renumbered by resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022. Since then the SEEMP is regulation 26, with Part I at 26.1, Part II at 26.2 and Part III at 26.3 read with 28.8.
retrieval_cards.why: Pre-2023 textbooks and notes are still in circulation and all carry the old number.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three Parts of the SEEMP and the ships each applies to.
retrieval_cards.answer: Part I, Ship Management Plan to Improve Energy Efficiency - any ship of 400 GT and above. Part II, Ship Fuel Oil Consumption Data Collection Plan - any ship of 5,000 GT and above. Part III, Ship Operational Carbon Intensity Plan - required by regulations 26.3 and 28.8 for ships subject to the CII.
retrieval_cards.why: The four steps belong to Part I only, and the two tonnage thresholds are commonly transposed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the planning stage consist of, and what do the Guidelines say about its importance?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 4.1.1 calls it the most crucial stage, because it determines both the current status of energy use and carbon intensity and the improvement that can be expected. It has four components: ship-specific measures, company-specific measures, human resource development, and goal setting - the goal to be measurable and easy to understand.
retrieval_cards.why: Attributing 'most crucial stage' to the Guidelines converts a generic opening into a cited one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does section 4.1.3 say about combining efficiency measures?
retrieval_cards.answer: That not all measures can be applied to all ships, or even to the same ship under different operating conditions, and that some of them are mutually exclusive.
retrieval_cards.why: Almost no candidate says this, and it demonstrates engineering judgement rather than a list of green measures.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must the implementation system contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: Procedures for energy management; defined tasks assigned to responsible personnel; defined levels of authority and lines of communication; procedures for internal audit and management review where relevant; and, for each measure, how it is to be implemented, who is responsible and the start and end dates.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Who, what, by when' is the whole of step 2 and is what makes the plan auditable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Two things must be recorded under section 4.2.2 that candidates rarely mention. What are they?
retrieval_cards.answer: First, if an identified measure cannot be implemented, the reason should be recorded for internal use. Second, events and operational conditions outside the crew's control - waiting for berths, extended port dwell times, operation in severe adverse weather - should be documented, because they may affect the ship's rating.
retrieval_cards.why: Both are counter-intuitive, both are precise, and the second links implementation to the CII outcome.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does monitoring require, and what data is expressly excluded?
retrieval_cards.answer: Quantitative monitoring by an established method, preferably an international standard, using a tool targeting the goal indicator - AER, cgDIST, EEOI or another CII; at regular intervals, with fuel oil consumption monitored by daily reporting such as noon reports; supported by a monitoring system established at the planning stage and carried out as far as possible by shore staff. Data obtained during a search and rescue diversion is excluded and recorded separately.
retrieval_cards.why: The SAR exclusion is small, exact and memorable, and proves the Guidelines were opened.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the four purposes of self-evaluation under section 4.4.2?
retrieval_cards.answer: To evaluate the effectiveness of the planned measures and their implementation; to deepen understanding of the ship's operation - what works, how and why; to comprehend the trend of efficiency improvement; and to develop the improved management plan for the next cycle.
retrieval_cards.why: The middle two are what convert data into a better plan rather than a score.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the SEEMP from the EEDI and EEXI.
retrieval_cards.answer: EEDI and EEXI are technical indices fixing what the ship is - design efficiency, assessed once. The SEEMP is an operational management plan governing how the ship is run, continuously, through a repeating four-step cycle.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why the SEEMP is a cycle and the indices are not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What was the status of the CII and SEEMP review at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: MEPC 82, held 30 September to 4 October 2024, OPENED a review of the short-term GHG measures - CII, SEEMP and EEXI - and referred it to a correspondence group and an intersessional working group reporting to MEPC 83 in 2025. No amendment existed at this examination.
retrieval_cards.why: Material written for a 2025 or 2026 sitting carries the outcome of that review; back-reading it into a December 2024 answer is future contamination.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: One limb, sixteen marks, and the stem names its own four sections. The printed command is 'describe with suitable examples, the critical role of each of these components in improving energy efficiency of ships' - three demands: describe, exemplify, and justify criticality. Description alone answers about a third of it.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks, undivided. Roughly three marks per step for description plus examples, and four for the criticality argument and the framing that locates the cycle in Part I. An answer that gives four equal descriptive paragraphs and stops will not reach the upper band.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate has read the SEEMP guidelines rather than a summary of them. The tell-tales are: knowing the four steps are the framework of Part I; that planning is expressly called the most crucial stage; that some measures are mutually exclusive; that reasons for non-implementation and conditions outside the crew's control must be recorded; and that search and rescue data is excluded from monitoring. Correct citation of regulation 26 and of the current guidelines edition is the currency test.
