blocks.h: 1. The Code, and what made it mandatory

blocks.p: The IMO Instruments Implementation Code (III Code) is the annex to resolution A.1070(28), adopted by the Assembly on 4 December 2013. Operative paragraph 3 revoked resolution A.1054(27), the Code for the Implementation of Mandatory IMO Instruments, 2011, which had been the basis of the voluntary audit scheme.

The Code is recommendatory in its own drafting - it says what a State "should" do - but its use was made mandatory by amending the treaty instruments themselves: A.1083(28), A.1084(28) and A.1085(28) amended Load Lines 1966, Tonnage 1969 and COLREG 1972; MSC.366(93), MSC.373(93), MSC.374(93) and MSC.375(93) amended SOLAS 1974, STCW 1978, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; and MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) amended MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol. That chain is what turns the Code into the standard against which a Member State is audited under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme.

The Code has four parts - Part 1 Common Areas, Part 2 Flag States, Part 3 Coastal States, Part 4 Port States - and each of Parts 2, 3 and 4 ends with an Evaluation and review section. Limb (b) is simply that section of Part 2 opened up.

Paragraph 1 states the objective in a single sentence: to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment, and to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization. The second half matters as much as the first - the Code is an assistance instrument, written because the Organization accepted that some States face real difficulty in complying fully.

Paragraph 2 qualifies it. States view the Code according to their own circumstances and should be bound only for the implementation of those instruments to which they are Contracting Governments or Parties; by virtue of geography and circumstance some States have a greater role as a flag State, others as a coastal or port State. The Code is therefore not a uniform checklist applied identically everywhere.

Two general provisions frame everything that follows. Paragraph 4 makes States responsible for promulgating laws and regulations and taking all other steps necessary to give those instruments full and complete effect. Paragraph 5 requires that, in acting against pollution, States must not transfer damage or hazards from one area to another, nor transform one type of pollution into another.

blocks.h: 3. The strategy recommended to the flag State

blocks.p: Paragraph 3 answers the second task in limb (a). To meet the objective a State is recommended to:

ul: develop an overall strategy to ensure that its international obligations and responsibilities as a flag, port and coastal State are met (3.1);
establish a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy ensures effective implementation and enforcement of the relevant international mandatory instruments (3.2); and
continuously review the strategy to achieve, maintain and improve overall organizational performance and capability as a flag, port and coastal State (3.3).

blocks.p: Read together those three are a develop - monitor - review cycle, not a document written once. Paragraph 9 completes it: the State should communicate its strategy, including information on its national legislation, to all concerned.

Paragraph 7 tells the State what its legislation and administrative procedures must actually address - nine areas: jurisdiction; organization and authority; legislation, rules and regulations; promulgation of the applicable mandatory instruments; enforcement arrangements; control, survey, inspection, audit, verification, approval and certification functions; the selection, recognition, authorization, empowerment and monitoring of recognized organizations and nominated surveyors; investigations required to be reported to the Organization; and reporting to the Organization and other Administrations. Paragraph 8 adds the three initial actions a Government must be capable of when a new or amended instrument enters into force: the ability to promulgate laws giving effective jurisdiction and control, a legal basis for enforcement including investigative and penal processes, and sufficient personnel with maritime expertise.

blocks.h: 4. Which IMO instruments the Code covers

blocks.p: This limb has two correct answers and they are not the same, which is where marks are usually lost.
First, the Code's own scope. Paragraph 6 says the Code addresses those aspects necessary to give full and complete effect to the applicable international instruments pertaining to six subject areas:

ul: safety of life at sea;
prevention of pollution from ships;
standards of training, certification and watchkeeping for seafarers;
load lines;
tonnage measurement of ships; and
regulations for preventing collisions at sea.

blocks.p: Note what is absent: maritime security is not one of the six. The preamble to the resolution speaks of safety, security and protection of the marine environment, but the operative scope at paragraph 6 does not extend to the ISPS Code or SOLAS chapter XI-2.

Second, the treaty instruments under which use of the Code is mandatory, which therefore define the audit scope. These are the instruments listed in resolution A.1187(33), the 2023 Non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code, adopted 6 December 2023: SOLAS 1974 with its 1978 and 1988 Protocols; MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol; STCW 1978 and the STCW Code; Load Lines 1966 and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; Tonnage 1969; and COLREG 1972. A.1187(33) revoked the 2021 list, A.1157(32), and has been the current list for twelve months at this sitting.

A precise point available here, and worth a mark for showing the resolution has been opened: A.1187(33) is organised in seven annexes, and Annex 7 lists the amendments expected to be accepted and to enter into force between 1 January 2024 and 1 July 2024. At this sitting that window has closed - those amendments are in force, and the annex now reads as a record of what came into effect during the year rather than as a forecast. A candidate who notices that the obligations list is itself dated, and moves with the calendar, is demonstrating exactly the distinction between adopted, expected to enter into force and in force that this Code exists to police.

blocks.h: 5. Key performance indicators for flag State evaluation

blocks.p: Paragraph 42 requires a flag State to evaluate its performance on a periodic basis with respect to the administrative processes, procedures and resources needed to meet its obligations under the instruments to which it is a Party. Paragraph 43 then lists the measures, inter alia:

ul: port State control detention rates;
flag State inspection results;
casualty statistics;
communication and information processes;
annual loss statistics, excluding constructive total losses (CTLs); and
such other performance indicators as may be appropriate.

blocks.p: The stated purpose is diagnostic, and reproducing it earns the mark: the indicators exist in order to determine whether staffing, resources and administrative procedures are adequate to meet its flag State obligations. They are for the State's own periodic self-evaluation - not a return filed with IMO.
Paragraph 44 then recommends ten areas for regular review:

ol: fleet loss and accident ratios, to identify trends over selected time periods;
the number of verified cases of detained ships in relation to the size of the fleet;
verified cases of incompetence or wrongdoing by holders of certificates or endorsements issued under its authority;
responses to port State deficiency reports or interventions;
investigations into very serious and serious casualties and the lessons learned from them;
technical and other resources committed;
results of inspections, surveys and controls of the ships in the fleet;
investigation of occupational accidents;
the number of incidents and violations under the applicable international pollution prevention regulations; and
the number of suspensions or withdrawals of certificates, endorsements or approvals.

blocks.p: (This paper prints five marks for limb (b) where the January and March 2024 sittings printed four. The extra mark is bought by giving paragraph 44 in its own right rather than compressing it into paragraph 43 - so name the paragraph 43 measures, state their diagnostic purpose, and then give at least six of the paragraph 44 review areas.)
Part 2 runs from paragraph 15 to paragraph 44. Its shape is implementation - delegation - enforcement - surveyors - investigations - review.

ul: Implementation (15-17). Issue national legislation and guidance implementing the safety and pollution conventions, and assign responsibility for keeping it updated. Paragraph 16 requires a safety and environmental protection programme with five minimum elements, of which the load-bearing one is 16.2: compliance verified by an audit and inspection programme independent of any body issuing the certificates. Paragraph 17 requires ships to be sufficiently and efficiently manned, on the Principles of Safe Manning.

Delegation (18-21). A flag State authorising a recognized organization must determine that it has adequate technical, managerial and research capability; base the authorisation on a formal written agreement; issue specific instructions for a ship found unfit to proceed to sea; supply its national law and interpretations; and require records to be kept. Paragraph 20 requires an oversight programme with supplementary surveys and competent supervising staff.

Enforcement (22-27). Prohibit a ship from sailing until it complies; inspect periodically to verify that the actual condition of ship and crew matches the certificates; verify seafarer familiarity and the complement's ability to coordinate in an emergency; provide penalties of adequate severity; and institute proceedings after investigation irrespective of where the violation occurred. Paragraphs 26 and 27 permit certification only after determining that all applicable requirements are met.

Surveyors and investigations (28-41). Surveyors qualified against a defined standard under a documented qualification system, and issued an identification document (37). Marine safety investigations by impartial and objective investigators, taking account of the Casualty Investigation Code, with the report forwarded to the Organization together with the flag State's observations (38-41).

blocks.h: 7. Coastal State and port State responsibilities

blocks.p: Parts 3 and 4 open with the same principle, at paragraphs 45 and 52: coastal and port States have rights as well as obligations, and when they exercise those rights they incur additional obligations. Both must implement policy through national legislation and guidance (46, 54) and ensure their legislation and procedures deliver consistent implementation and verification (47, 55).

Coastal State (Part 3). Paragraph 48 lists the rights, obligations and responsibilities, inter alia: radiocommunication services; meteorological services and warnings; search and rescue services; hydrographic services; ships' routeing; ship reporting systems; vessel traffic services; and aids to navigation - eight service areas. Note that they are services to shipping, not controls over ships. Paragraph 50 requires a control and monitoring programme to allocate statistical data for trend analysis, to establish mechanisms for timely response to pollution incidents in its waters, and to cooperate with flag and port States in casualty investigations.

Port State (Part 4). Paragraph 53 records that the port State role derives from a combination of treaties, conventions, national laws and in some cases bilateral and multilateral agreements. Paragraph 56 gives three obligations: provision of appropriate reception facilities or the capability to accept all waste streams regulated under IMO instruments; port State control; and keeping a register of fuel oil suppliers. Paragraph 59 carries the no more favourable treatment principle - the conditions of the instruments are imposed on the ships of non-parties as well as parties. Paragraphs 60 and 61 require a PSC programme consistent with the relevant Assembly resolution - at this sitting A.1185(33), the Procedures for Port State Control, 2023 - carried out only by authorized and qualified port State control officers; paragraph 62 requires those officers to be free from commercial, financial and other pressures, to hold no commercial interest in the port, the ships inspected, repair facilities or support services, and not to be employed by or work on behalf of recognized organizations or classification societies.

Both parts close as Part 2 does: paragraphs 51 and 63 require the coastal State and the port State to periodically evaluate their own performance. That symmetry - implement, enforce, evaluate - is the single most useful thing to carry into the hall, because it lets you build all three States from one remembered shape, which is exactly what five marks for three roles requires.

This question recurs across four MIW-transcribed sittings word-for-word, but this paper does not print the same marks as the January and March 2024 sittings. Those print 6 + 4 + 6. This one prints 6 + 5 + 5. The words are identical; the expected depth is not.

What that means in the hall: limb (b) is now worth more than it looks. Four marks would be covered by naming the paragraph 43 measures. Five will not be - you need paragraph 43 and a real showing of paragraph 44's ten review areas. Conversely limb (c) has lost a mark and now carries five for three States. That is under two marks each, so a discursive treatment of flag State duties will run you out of time. Answer all three on the Code's shared skeleton - implementation, enforcement, evaluation - and you cover three roles in the space most candidates spend on one.

Limb (a) is unchanged at six marks and still hides three tasks: the objective, the strategy, and the instruments. Splitting it across three route steps stops all six marks being spent on the objective sentence.

blocks.h: The mandatory-application chain, and why it matters

blocks.p: Candidates often assert that "the III Code is mandatory" without being able to say why a recommendatory-sounding text binds anybody. The answer is that the Code was never redrafted into obligation language; instead the conventions were amended to require its use. That is why the Code still reads "should" throughout. Being able to say that in one sentence separates a candidate who has read the instrument from one who has read about it.
The audit scheme is the practical consequence. The Code supplies the auditable areas; A.1187(33) supplies the obligation-by-obligation list that auditors and Administrations work from.

blocks.h: The obligations list is dated - and at THIS sitting the date has moved

blocks.p: A.1187(33) was adopted on 6 December 2023 by the 33rd Assembly, revoking the 2021 list A.1157(32). At this December 2024 sitting it has been the current list for twelve months. Material citing the 2021 list is superseded.

The resolution is built in seven annexes, and Annex 7 is headed amendments expected to be accepted and to enter into force between 1 January 2024 and 1 July 2024. Read that heading against the date of your own examination. At a January 2024 sitting the whole window is still ahead and the annex is a forecast - a textbook illustration of adopted but not yet in force. At this sitting, in December 2024, the window has closed: those amendments came into force during the year and the annex is now a record, not a prediction. Same annex, opposite reading, eleven months apart. If you are revising from a solved January 2024 paper, this is the one sentence in it you must turn around.

The printed words are "Which all IMO instruments covered in the code". Two things are being asked at once and the safe answer gives both. The Code's scope at paragraph 6 is expressed as six subject areas, not as a list of conventions. The instruments under which the Code is mandatory are the SOLAS / MARPOL / STCW / Load Lines / Tonnage / COLREG family with their Protocols, listed in A.1187(33).

A count is risky. The audit scope is usually summarised as nine mandatory instruments - SOLAS 1974, SOLAS PROT 1988, MARPOL, MARPOL PROT 1997, STCW 1978, LL 1966, LL PROT 1988, TONNAGE 1969 and COLREG 1972 - but A.1187(33) annex 1 also carries a SOLAS PROT 1978 column, and neither instrument states a number anywhere. List them; do not lead with a count. If a count is wanted, write "the SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG instruments together with their Protocols, commonly summarised as nine".

The absence of maritime security from paragraph 6 is a genuine examinable point, not a drafting slip: the preamble uses the phrase "safety, security and protection of the marine environment" while the operative scope does not extend to security instruments.

ul: Writing a general essay on flag State duties under UNCLOS article 94. That is a different question. The examiner has named a specific Code and wants its paragraphs.
Answering "which instruments" with the six subject areas only, or the convention list only. Give both, and say why they differ.
Confusing the III Code with the ISM Code. The III Code binds States; the ISM Code binds companies and ships.
Treating the performance indicators as a return made to IMO. They are for the State's own periodic self-evaluation under paragraph 42.
Giving the coastal State a control-and-inspection role. Paragraph 48 is a list of services - SAR, hydrography, VTS, aids to navigation.
Answering limb (b) with paragraph 43 alone. At five marks on this paper that is not enough - paragraph 44's review areas are wanted too.
Spending half the answer on limb (c). On this paper it is worth five marks for three States.
Citing A.1054(27), the 2011 Code, as current. It was revoked by A.1070(28).
Describing A.1187(33) Annex 7 as a list of amendments still to come. At a December 2024 sitting that window has closed.
Six subject areas versus the instrument list. The single most likely place to lose marks on this question.
"Should" throughout the Code. If asked whether the Code is mandatory, say that its use is mandatory under the amended conventions while the text remains recommendatory in form.
Excluding constructive total losses. Paragraph 43 says annual loss statistics excluding CTLs. Reproducing that qualifier shows the source has been read.

Two independence requirements, different Parts, different purposes. The flag State's audit programme must be independent of the certifying body (16.2); PSCOs must be free of commercial interest and must not work for recognized organizations (62). Do not merge them.
The marks are not the ones in last year's paper. 6 + 5 + 5 here, 6 + 4 + 6 in January and March 2024.
"Is the III Code mandatory, and how?" - the amendment chain.
"What is IMSAS and what does it audit against?" - the Code supplies the auditable areas; A.1187(33) supplies the obligations list.

"Your flag State has a rising detention rate. What does the Code expect it to do?" - paragraphs 43 and 44: treat it as a performance indicator, review detentions against fleet size, review responses to PSC deficiency reports, and test whether staffing and resources are adequate.

"What must a flag State do before authorising a class society?" - paragraph 18: capability, a formal written agreement, specific instructions for unfit ships, national law and interpretations, records.
"Name three port State obligations under the Code." - reception facilities, port State control, a register of fuel oil suppliers.

"Which State investigates a casualty, and who gets the report?" - paragraphs 38 to 41: the flag State provides qualified impartial investigators irrespective of where the casualty occurred; the report goes to the Organization with the flag State's observations.

blocks.p: Two shapes carry the whole question. The Code's shape is COMMON, FLAG, COASTAL, PORT. The shape inside each State part is implement, enforce, evaluate and review. Everything in limb (c) hangs on the second shape, and limb (b) is simply the "evaluation and review" box of the flag State part opened up.

For the coastal State's eight services, group them as talk, warn, rescue, chart (radiocommunication, meteorological warnings, SAR, hydrographic) and route, report, watch, mark (ships' routeing, ship reporting, VTS, aids to navigation).

ul: Resolution A.1070(28), 4 December 2013 - the III Code. Revoked A.1054(27).
Paragraph 1 objective. Paragraph 2 bound only for instruments to which the State is a Party.
Paragraph 3 the three-part strategy. Paragraph 9 communicate it.
Paragraph 6 the six subject areas. Paragraph 7 the nine areas legislation must address. Paragraph 8 initial actions.
Paragraphs 15-17 flag implementation; 18-21 delegation; 22-27 enforcement; 28-37 surveyors; 38-41 investigations.
Paragraphs 42-44 flag State evaluation and review - the KPIs, and limb (b) in full.

blocks.h: Flag State surveyors and investigations - the detail behind route step 6

blocks.p: Limb (c) is five marks for three States, so the Model Answer gives the flag State the headline of paragraphs 28 to 41 rather than the whole regime. The detail below is worth holding for the oral.

ul: Qualification (para 29). Either appropriate qualifications from a marine or nautical institution with relevant seagoing experience as a certificated officer holding or having held a valid management level certificate of competency; or a degree or equivalent from a tertiary institution in a relevant field of engineering or science; or accreditation as a surveyor through a formalised training programme reaching the same standard.

Experience (paras 30-31). Personnel qualified under 29.1 should have served not less than three years at sea as a deck or engine officer; those qualified under 29.2 should have worked in a relevant capacity for at least three years.

Knowledge (para 36). Knowledge of the applicable international and national rules; of survey, certification, control, investigative and oversight procedures; understanding of the goals of the instruments; professional competency; full safety awareness; and training or experience in the tasks performed.
Identification (para 37). The flag State issues an identification document for the surveyor to carry when performing his or her tasks.

Investigator expertise (para 39). Ready access to expertise in navigation and the Collision Regulations, certificate-of-competency regulations, causes of marine pollution, interviewing techniques, evidence gathering, and evaluation of the effects of the human element.

Reporting threshold (para 40). Any accident involving personal injury necessitating absence from duty of three days or more, and any deaths from occupational accidents and casualties, should be investigated and the results made public.

blocks.p: The Code material is primary throughout: A.1070(28) was read in full and every paragraph number was checked against the source. Two limitations are recorded. The answer deliberately does not lead with a number of instruments - A.1070(28) states six subject areas and no instrument count, and A.1187(33) lists obligations by instrument without totalling them; the figure of nine is offered as a common summary, not as a quotation. And the Framework and Procedures for the Member State Audit Scheme was not re-read this session, so no claim is made about audit periodicity or the scheme's procedural rules.

One currency point is specific to this sitting and must not be "corrected" by a later editor: A.1187(33) of 6 December 2023 is the operative obligations list here, and the A.11xx(33) series generally is the operative Assembly material, because the 34th Assembly did not meet until 3 December 2025 - a full year after this examination.

notes: The intake recorded STABLE / LOW with no classes. Checked rather than trusted, per the standing rule. LOW is confirmed for the operative law, but two classes are added because sitting-relative framing DID have to change.

A.1070(28) is unamended between its adoption on 4 December 2013 and this sitting. Temporal delta on the Code itself: NIL. It is equally the Code at the March 2024 donor sitting, at the January 2024 sitting and at the October 2025 sitting.

A.1187(33), adopted 6 December 2023 by the 33rd Assembly, revoked the 2021 list A.1157(32). At the January 2024 sitting it was ONE month old; at the March 2024 donor sitting THREE months; at THIS sitting TWELVE months. The sentence was re-derived, not copied.

THE JANUARY 2024 FRAMING INVERTS AT THIS SITTING - the single substantive temporal finding on this question. A.1187(33) Annex 7 is headed 'amendments expected to be accepted and to enter into force between 1 January 2024 and 1 July 2024'. QP2401-Q9 correctly treats that annex as FORWARD-LOOKING, because at January 2024 the whole window lies ahead. At December 2024 the window has CLOSED: those amendments are in force and the annex is RETROSPECTIVE. Copying the January treatment would have produced a confidently wrong statement about what is and is not yet in force - on a question whose entire subject is that distinction. Found by re-reading the resolution against this sitting's date rather than inheriting the donor's account of it.

The 33rd Assembly boundary is the ADOPTION date, 6 December 2023, not the meeting month. December 2024 falls after it and BEFORE the 34th Assembly of 3 December 2025, so the A.11xx(33) series is operative and no A.12xx(34) instrument may appear.
The port State limb is anchored to A.1185(33), Procedures for Port State Control 2023, adopted 6 December 2023 and revoking A.1155(32) - the operative PSC procedures at this sitting.

MARKS, NOT LAW, ARE THE REAL DELTA ON THIS QUESTION. The donor prints 6 + 4 + 6 and this paper prints 6 + 5 + 5. The route was re-weighted accordingly: paragraph 44 is given in full to carry limb (b)'s fifth mark, and limb (c) is compressed onto the Code's shared implement-enforce-evaluate skeleton to fit three States into five marks.

NO CLAIM IN THIS ANSWER DEPENDS ON THE EXAMINATION DAY within December 2024. A.1187(33) had been in force for twelve months by any day of that month, and the Annex 7 window closed on 1 July 2024, five months before the earliest possible sitting day.

questions.understand_first: The examiner has named one instrument and is checking whether you have opened it. Every mark on this question is inside resolution A.1070(28). The Code is short - sixty-three paragraphs in four parts - and it is organised exactly the way the question is: common material first, then flag, coastal and port States in that order, each part ending in an evaluation and review section. Limb (b) IS that evaluation section of the flag State part. So if you can hold the Code's own structure, you can rebuild the whole answer from it. Two things are sharper than they look. The question asks "which all IMO instruments" - and the Code answers that with six SUBJECT AREAS, while the instruments it is mandatory under are a different list entirely. And this paper prints 6 + 5 + 5, not the 6 + 4 + 6 of the January and March 2024 sittings, so limb (b) needs more than the paragraph 43 list and limb (c) has to fit three States into five marks.
questions.memory_cue: The Code's four parts give the answer its spine: COMMON, FLAG, COASTAL, PORT. Walk it as WHAT-WHY-HOW-WHICH-MEASURE-WHO: WHAT the Code is (1), WHY it exists - the objective (2), HOW a State meets it - the strategy (3), WHICH instruments it reaches (4), how performance is MEASURED (5), and WHO does what - flag (6), then coastal and port (7). Inside every State part the same three beats: IMPLEMENT, ENFORCE, EVALUATE.

quick_revision.recall_15s: III Code = annex to A.1070(28), 4 December 2013; revoked A.1054(27). Recommendatory in wording, mandatory in use because SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, LL, TONNAGE and COLREG were amended to require it - which is why it still says "should". Four parts: common, flag, coastal, port, each State part ending in evaluation and review. Objective (para 1): enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment and assist States in implementing IMO instruments. Para 2: bound only for instruments to which the State is a Party. Strategy (para 3): develop an overall strategy covering flag, port and coastal roles; establish a methodology to monitor and assess it; continuously review it - a develop-monitor-review cycle; para 9 communicate it. Para 7 nine areas for legislation; para 8 three initial actions. Scope (para 6): six subject areas - safety of life at sea, prevention of pollution, STCW, load lines, tonnage, COLREG. Security is NOT one of them. Instruments under which it is mandatory are listed in A.1187(33) (6 December 2023, revoking A.1157(32), twelve months old at this sitting): SOLAS + Protocols, MARPOL + 1997 Protocol, STCW + Code, LL 1966 + 1988 Protocol, TONNAGE 1969, COLREG 1972. Its Annex 7 covers 1 Jan - 1 Jul 2024, a window already closed at this sitting. KPIs (42-44): para 42 periodic SELF-evaluation; para 43 - PSC detention rates, flag State inspection results, casualty statistics, communication and information processes, annual loss statistics excluding CTLs - purpose is to test whether staffing, resources and procedures are adequate; para 44 - ten review areas including detentions against fleet size, certificate-holder incompetence, responses to PSC deficiency reports, serious casualty investigations, occupational accidents, pollution violations, suspensions and withdrawals. Flag (15-41): legislation and guidance; para 16 five-element programme, 16.2 audit independent of the certifying body; 17 safe manning; 18-21 delegation by formal written agreement plus oversight; 22-27 prohibit sailing, inspect, penalties of adequate severity, proceedings irrespective of where the violation occurred; 28-41 qualified surveyors with an identification document, impartial casualty investigation reported to the Organization. Coastal (45-51): para 48 eight services - radiocommunication, meteorological warnings, SAR, hydrographic, ships' routeing, ship reporting, VTS, aids to navigation. Port (52-63): para 56 three obligations - reception facilities, port State control, register of fuel oil suppliers; 59 no more favourable treatment; 62 PSCO independence; PSC under A.1185(33). 51 and 63 - coastal and port States evaluate their own performance too. This paper prints 6 + 5 + 5, not 6 + 4 + 6.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: A.1070(28) annex paragraph 6 - the Code addresses six subject areas: safety of life at sea; prevention of pollution from ships; standards of training, certification and watchkeeping; load lines; tonnage measurement; and regulations for preventing collisions at sea. Read it with paragraphs 42 to 44, which carry the flag State performance indicators and, at this paper's five-mark weighting for limb (b), must be given in full rather than summarised.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering "which IMO instruments" with only one of the two correct lists. Paragraph 6 gives six SUBJECT AREAS and names no convention; the treaty instruments under which the Code is mandatory are SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG with their Protocols, listed in A.1187(33). Maritime security is in neither the paragraph 6 list nor the Code's operative scope. Second trap, specific to this sitting: A.1187(33) Annex 7 lists amendments expected to enter into force between 1 January and 1 July 2024. At a January 2024 sitting that annex is a FORECAST; at this December 2024 sitting the window has CLOSED and it is a RECORD. Revising from a solved January 2024 paper will give you the forward-looking version, and here it is wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the III Code question, and note what this paper's mark split changes.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The Code and what made it mandatory. 2 (a) The objective. 3 (a) The strategy. 4 (a) Which instruments. 5 (b) The performance indicators. 6 (c) Flag State. 7 (c) Coastal and port State. This paper prints 6 + 5 + 5, so step 5 must give paragraph 44 as well as 43, and steps 6 and 7 together have only five marks for three States.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 2, 3 and 4 split limb (a), which hides three tasks in six marks; the re-weighting is what distinguishes this sitting from January and March 2024.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which resolution contains the III Code, when was it adopted, and what did it revoke?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1070(28), adopted 4 December 2013. Operative paragraph 3 revoked A.1054(27), the Code for the Implementation of Mandatory IMO Instruments, 2011.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the revoked 2011 Code as current is a common and visible error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the objective of the III Code in the Code's own words.
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 1: to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment, and to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization.
retrieval_cards.why: The second half - assistance - is routinely dropped, and it is half the sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What three things does paragraph 3 recommend a State do to meet the objective?
retrieval_cards.answer: Develop an overall strategy covering its flag, port and coastal responsibilities; establish a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy delivers effective implementation and enforcement; and continuously review the strategy to achieve, maintain and improve organizational performance and capability. Paragraph 9 then requires it to be communicated.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the 'strategy recommended to flag state' half of limb (a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: The question asks which IMO instruments the Code covers. Why are there two answers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 6 defines the Code's scope as six SUBJECT AREAS - safety of life at sea, prevention of pollution from ships, STCW, load lines, tonnage measurement, COLREG. Separately, the Code is made mandatory by amendments to the treaty INSTRUMENTS - SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and its Code, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG with their Protocols, listed in A.1187(33). Give both, and say why they differ.
retrieval_cards.why: The highest-value distinction on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which subject area is conspicuously absent from paragraph 6?
retrieval_cards.answer: Maritime security. The preamble speaks of safety, security and environmental protection, but the six subject areas in the operative scope do not include security, so the ISPS Code and SOLAS chapter XI-2 sit outside the Code's stated scope.
retrieval_cards.why: A candidate who lists seven areas including security has not read paragraph 6.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the flag State performance indicators at paragraph 43, and say what they are for.
retrieval_cards.answer: Port State control detention rates; flag State inspection results; casualty statistics; communication and information processes; annual loss statistics excluding constructive total losses; and other appropriate indicators. Their purpose is to determine whether staffing, resources and administrative procedures are adequate to meet the State's flag State obligations.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) is FIVE marks on this paper, so this paragraph is necessary but no longer sufficient - paragraph 44 is wanted too.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name six of the ten areas paragraph 44 recommends for regular review.
retrieval_cards.answer: Fleet loss and accident ratios; detained ships in relation to fleet size; verified cases of incompetence or wrongdoing by certificate holders; responses to port State deficiency reports or interventions; investigations into very serious and serious casualties; technical and other resources committed. The remaining four are inspection and survey results, occupational accident investigation, pollution incidents and violations, and suspensions or withdrawals of certificates.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the material that buys limb (b)'s fifth mark at this sitting's 6 + 5 + 5 split.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A.1187(33) Annex 7 lists amendments expected to enter into force between 1 January and 1 July 2024. How should that be described at a December 2024 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: As a CLOSED window - those amendments are already in force by this sitting, so the annex reads as a record of what took effect during the year, not as a forecast. A January 2024 treatment correctly calls it forward-looking; eleven months later that framing is wrong.
retrieval_cards.why: The same annex reads in opposite directions at two sittings of the same year. It is the sharpest adopted-versus-in-force illustration available on this question, and it inverts.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Two independence requirements appear in the Code. What are they and where?
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 16.2 - the flag State's audit and inspection programme must be independent of any body issuing the certificates, including a delegated entity. Paragraph 62 - port State control officers must be free of commercial, financial and other pressure, hold no commercial interest in the port or ships inspected, and not be employed by or work for recognized organizations or classification societies.
retrieval_cards.why: They serve different purposes in different Parts and are often merged into one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the eight coastal State areas at paragraph 48 and the three port State obligations at paragraph 56.
retrieval_cards.answer: Coastal: radiocommunication services; meteorological services and warnings; search and rescue services; hydrographic services; ships' routeing; ship reporting systems; vessel traffic services; aids to navigation. Port: appropriate reception facilities or capability to accept all regulated waste streams; port State control; and a register of fuel oil suppliers.
retrieval_cards.why: The coastal list is SERVICES to shipping, not controls over ships; and the register of fuel oil suppliers is the port obligation candidates forget.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What single shape do Parts 2, 3 and 4 of the Code share, and why does it matter on this paper?
retrieval_cards.answer: Implementation, then enforcement, then evaluation and review. Paragraphs 42, 51 and 63 are the three evaluation requirements. It matters because limb (c) is worth only five marks for three States at this sitting, and one remembered shape answers all three inside that budget.
retrieval_cards.why: One shape answers limb (c) for all three States and simultaneously locates limb (b).

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three limbs against one named Code. Limb (a) is really three tasks - objective, strategy, instruments - for six marks. Limb (b) is precise recall of one section of the Code for five marks. Limb (c) asks for all three State roles in five marks, which the Code makes tractable because Parts 2, 3 and 4 share a structure.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks printed as 6 + 5 + 5. This is NOT the split of the January or March 2024 sittings, which print 6 + 4 + 6. Limb (b) gains a mark and limb (c) loses one, so paragraph 44 must be given in full and the three State roles must be answered on a shared skeleton. The October 2025 sitting prints the same 6 + 5 + 5.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate has opened A.1070(28). The tell-tales are the paragraph 3 strategy in its three parts, the six subject areas at paragraph 6, the CTL exclusion at paragraph 43, the ten review areas at 44, the eight coastal services at 48 and the three port obligations at 56. General UNCLOS flag-State material scores poorly because it is not what was asked.
primary_source_plan: Obtain A.1070(28) in full rather than a summary - the paragraph numbers are the marks
Map objective, strategy and scope to paragraphs 1, 3 and 6 before drafting
Take the performance indicators verbatim from 43 AND the ten review areas from 44 - the five-mark weighting requires both
Read Parts 3 and 4 in full - the eight services and three obligations are short and exact
Re-read A.1187(33) directly rather than inheriting the donor's account, and check its Annex 7 window against THIS sitting's date
Establish the operative PSC procedures resolution at this sitting for the port State limb
Do not assert an instrument count that neither resolution states
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - for the Code itself: A.1070(28) is unamended and is the Code at this sitting. MODERATE for the companion list and its framing: A.1187(33) was adopted 6 December 2023 and is twelve months old here, and its Annex 7 window closed on 1 July 2024 - so the forward-looking description correct at a January 2024 sitting is wrong at this one.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The Code applies to States generally and India is a Party to the instruments concerned. No Indian statute is load-bearing on this answer, and the Merchant Shipping Act is not engaged.
technical_ambiguities: Whether "which instruments" means the subject areas or the conventions - it means both
How many treaty instruments the audit scope contains - not stated in either resolution
Whether the Code is mandatory, given that it is drafted in "should" language
Whether maritime security falls within the Code's scope - it does not, at paragraph 6
Whether the performance indicators are reported externally or used internally
Whether A.1187(33) Annex 7 is prospective or retrospective - it depends on the sitting date, and at this sitting it is retrospective
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Instrument and mandatory-application chain first, because it licenses everything else; then the three tasks of limb (a) as separate steps; then limb (b) from paragraphs 42, 43 AND 44 at the enlarged five-mark weighting; then limb (c) as flag, then coastal and port together on the shared implementation-enforcement-evaluation skeleton, compressed to fit five marks.

reverify_before_publication.claim: A.1070(28) is unamended and is the III Code operative at the December 2024 sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. The Assembly may amend the Code on the recommendation of MSC and MEPC under operative paragraph 2. Confirm no amendment took effect before December 2024 and that none is being back-read into the answer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: A.1187(33) of 6 December 2023 is the operative Non-exhaustive list of obligations at this sitting, having revoked A.1157(32), and its Annex 7 window is CLOSED
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT REVERSE THIS TO THE JANUARY 2024 FRAMING. A solved January 2024 paper in this same family correctly describes Annex 7 as forward-looking, because at that sitting the 1 January to 1 July 2024 window lay ahead. At December 2024 it has closed. An editor cross-reading the two papers may 'harmonise' them and would reintroduce a wrong statement about what is in force.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The A.11xx(33) series adopted 6 December 2023 is the operative Assembly material at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: The 34th Assembly adopted its resolutions on 3 December 2025, a full year after this examination. No A.12xx(34) instrument may be introduced into this object by a later editor working from current IMO material.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The audit scope is commonly summarised as nine mandatory IMO instruments
reverify_before_publication.why: Stated in the answer as a common summary, not as a quotation. Neither A.1070(28) nor A.1187(33) states a number. If a source that does state one is later located, replace the hedged wording with the cited figure.

reverify_before_publication.claim: IMSAS uses the III Code as its audit standard
reverify_before_publication.why: Established from the mandatory-application chain recited in A.1070(28) and A.1187(33), both read. The Framework and Procedures resolution itself was not re-read, so no claim about periodicity or audit procedure is made.
